M _ {k} (t) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {0} (s) (\hat {c} _ {k} (s) - \epsilon_ {k} (s)) d s \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right].\tag{4.16}
$$

## 4.5 Equilibrium and the Representative Agent

We are now in a position to state the properties of the complete standard financial market we shall be seeking. 

Definition 5.1: Let the endowment processes and utility functions $\{ \epsilon _ { k } , U _ { k } \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { K }$ and the discount rate $\beta ( \cdot )$ of Section 2 be given. We say that a financial market as described in Section 3 and satisfying Condition 3.1 is an equilibrium market (for the economic primitives $\{ \epsilon _ { k } , U _ { k } \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } , \beta )$ , if the following conditions hold. 

(i) Feasibility for the agents: 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {0} (t) \epsilon_ {k} (t) d t \geq \bar {c} _ {k} \cdot E \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {0} (t) d t, k = 1, \ldots , K.\tag{5.1}
$$

(ii) Clearing of the commodity market: 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \hat {c} _ {k} (t) = \epsilon (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.2}
$$

almost surely. 

(iii) Clearing of the stock markets: 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \hat {\pi} _ {k} (t) = \underset {\sim} {0}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.3}
$$

almost surely, where 0 is the origin in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

<sup>˜</sup> (iv) Clearing of the money market: 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} (\hat {X} _ {k} (t) - \hat {\pi} _ {k} ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}}) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.4}
$$

almost surely, where 1 is the vector $( 1 , \ldots , 1 ) ^ { \prime }$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

Here $\hat { c } _ { k } ( \cdot ) , \hat { \pi } _ { k } ( \cdot ) , \hat { X } _ { k } ( \cdot )$ are the unique optimal processes for Problem 4.1; these are given by (4.11)–(4.14) if the strict feasibility condition (4.4) holds for agent $k .$ , and by Convention 4.2 in the case of the nonstrict feasibilit condition (4.3). 

For the remainder of this section we shall focus on characterizing such an equilibrium market. Aided by this characterization, we shall establish in the next section the existence of an equilibrium market and examine the extent to which this equilibruim market is uniquely determined by the economic primitives $\{ \epsilon _ { k } , U _ { k } \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { K }$ and $\beta$ 

We note immediately from (3.5) and (5.2) that a necessary condition for an equilibrium market to exist is that $\epsilon ( t ) \ \geq \ \bar { c } , \quad 0 \ \leq \ t \ \leq \ T ;$ ; in other words, aggregate endowment must always dominate aggregate subsistence consumption. We have imposed a somewhat stronger assumption in Condition 2.1(iii). 

We now provide a simple characterization of an equilibrium market. 

Theorem 5.2: If is an equilibrium market, then 

$$
\epsilon (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} H _ {0} (t)\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.5}
$$

where $\lambda _ { k } \in [ 0 , \infty ) , k = 1 , \ldots , K$ , satisfy the system of equations 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {0} (t) \left[ I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} H _ {0} (t)\right) - \epsilon_ {k} (t) \right] d t = 0, \quad k = 1, \dots , K.\tag{5.6}
$$

$( I f \lambda _ { k } = 0$ , we adopt the convention $I _ { k } \big ( { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } } e ^ { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \beta ( u ) d u } H _ { 0 } ( t ) \big ) = I _ { k } ( \infty ) = \bar { c } _ { k } . \big )$ Conversely, if is a standard, complete financial market satisfying Condition 3.1, and there exists a vector $\underset { \smile } { \Lambda } = ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \dots , \lambda _ { K } ) \in [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ satisfying (5.5) and (5.6), then is an equilibrium market. In either case, the optimal consumption processes for the individual agents are given by 

$$
\hat {c} _ {k} (t) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} H _ {0} (t)\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, \quad k = 1, \dots , K.\tag{5.7}
$$

Proof. First, let us assume that is an equilibrium market. If the strict feasibility condition (4.4) holds for agent $k .$ , then this agent’s optimal consumption process (4.11) is given by (5.7), with $\textstyle \lambda _ { k } \in ( { \frac { 1 } { r _ { k } } } , \infty )$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { X } _ { k } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } ) = E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } H _ { 0 } ( t ) \ d \epsilon _ { k } ( t ) } \end{array}$ dt (see (4.14)); this last equation is (5.6). If the nonstrict feasibility condition (4.3) holds for agent $k$ , then (4.6) shows that (5.6) is equivalent to $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { X } _ { k } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } ) = \mathcal { X } _ { k } ( \infty ) } \end{array}$ , and this equation is solved by any $\lambda _ { k } \in [ 0 , \frac { 1 } { r _ { k } } ]$ ; with such a choice of $\lambda _ { k }$ , we see from Convention 4.2 and Remark 4.4 that (5.7) holds, where now $\hat { c } _ { k } ( t ) \equiv \bar { c } _ { k }$ . Summing (5.7) over k and using the commodity market clearing condition (5.2), we obtain (5.5). 

For the second part of the theorem, we assume that is a standard, complete financial market satisfying Condition 3.1, and that there exists a vector $\Lambda _ { \sim } ^ { { \mathrm { ~ \scriptsize ~ 1 ~ } } } = ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { k } ) \in [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { { \cal K } }$ satisfying (5.5) and (5.6). Since $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { k } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } e ^ { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \beta ( u ) d u } H _ { 0 } ( t ) ) \ge \bar { c } _ { k } , 0 \le t \le T } \end{array}$ , (5.6) implies the “feasibility for agents” condition (5.1). Under this feasibility condition, we have just seen that the optimal consumption process for each agent k is given by (5.7), and now (5.5) implies the clearing of commodity markets (5.2). We sum (4.16) over k and use (5.2) to obtain $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } M _ { k } ( t ) \equiv 0 } \end{array}$ . From (4.15) we see that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \psi _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( s ) d W ( s ) \equiv 0 } \end{array}$ , which implies $\textstyle \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \psi _ { k } ( t ) \equiv 0$ . Summing first (4.12) and then (4.13) over k, we conclude first that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \hat { X } _ { k } ( t ) \equiv 0 } \end{array}$ and next that $\sigma ^ { \prime } ( t ) \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \widehat { \pi } _ { k } ( t ) \equiv 0$ . Since $\sigma ^ { \prime } ( t )$ is nonsingular, we have the clearing of the stock markets (5.3) and then the clearing of the money market (5.4). ␀ 

Remark 5.3: $I f \underset { \sim } { \mathrm { ~  ~ \cal ~ \Lambda ~ } } \in \mathrm { ~  ~ \lbrack 0 , \infty ) ^ { \cal K } ~ }$ satisfies either $( 5 . 5 ) o r ( 5 . 6 )$ , then Λ <sup>˜</sup> <sup>˜</sup> cannot be the zero vector. For suppose it were; then the right-hand side of (5.5) would be $\textstyle \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } { \bar { c } } _ { k } = { \bar { c } } _ { 1 }$ , which is diferent from $\epsilon ( t )$ because of Condition 2.1(iii), and (5.6) would become 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {0} (t) (\bar {c} _ {k} - \epsilon_ {k} (t)) d t = 0, \quad k = 1, \dots , K,
$$

so that summing up over k we would again obtain a contradiction to Condition 2.1(iii). To simplify notation, we define 

$$
{ } ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K } = [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K } \backslash \{ 0 \}\tag{5.8}
$$

to be the K-dimensional nonnegative orthant with the origin $\mathbf { \underset { \sim } { 0 } = ( 0 , \dots , 0 ) }$ removed. 

Theorem 5.2 reduces the search for an equilibrium market to the search for a vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } \left[ 0 , \infty \right) ^ { K }$ , and for a market with state price density $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ so that $\left( 5 . 5 \right)$ <sup>˜</sup>and $( 5 . 6 )$ are satisfied. We can further simplify the search by inverting (5.5), writing the sought $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ as a function of the given aggregate endowment process ( ); cf. (5.16) below. 

Let $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ be given. For $k = 1 , \ldots , K$ , the function $\textstyle y \mapsto I _ { k } { \bigl ( } { \frac { y } { \lambda _ { k } } } { \bigr ) }$ is <sup>˜</sup> identically equal to $\bar { c } _ { k }$ if $\lambda _ { k } = 0 $ ; but if $\lambda _ { k } > 0$ , it is continuous on $( 0 , \infty )$ as well as strictly decreasing on $\left( 0 , \lambda _ { k } U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) \right]$ , and maps $\left( 0 , \lambda _ { k } U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) \right]$ onto $[ \bar { c } _ { k } , \infty )$ . We set 

$$

$$

For $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } \left[ 0 , \infty \right) ^ { k }$ , we define

Because of Condition 2.1(iii), $\epsilon ( t )$ is in the domain of $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ , and we can invert (5.5) to obtain

Corollary 5.4: A standard, complete financial market satisfying Condition 3.1 is an equilibrium market if and only if its state price density process $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is given by $( 5 . 1 6 )$ , where $\underline { { { \Lambda } } } = ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { K } ) \in ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ is a solution to the system of equations

The fol lowing lemma examines one type of nonuniqueness that can occur in the solution of (5.17).

The remainder of this section develops properties of the function $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ of (5.11). We shall see, in particular, that $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ <sup>˜</sup>is the derivative of the function 

$$

(We use here and elsewhere the convention $0 \cdot ( \pm \infty ) = 0 . )$ 

The next theorem shows that $U ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \lambda } )$ is itself a utility function. It plays <sup>˜</sup>the role of the utility function for a “representative $\boldsymbol { a g e n t } ^ { \ast }$ who assigns $\mathrm { \Delta ^ { * } w e i g h t s ^ { * } } \lambda _ { 1 } , \dots , \lambda _ { k }$ to the various agents and, with proper choice of $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } = \left( \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { k } \right)$ , has optimal consumption equal to the aggregate endow-<sup>˜</sup> ment. The weights $\lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { k }$ correspond to the “relative importance” of the individual agents in the equilibrium market. The maximizing values $c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { k }$ in (5.24) give the optimal consumptions of the individual agents when the aggregate endowment is c. 

The reader may wish to skip on first reading the (long and technical) proof of Theorem 5.6. 

Theorem 5.6: Let $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ be given. Then the function $U ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \Lambda } )$ of $( 5 . 2 4 )$ is a utility function as set forth in Definition $\ 3 . 4 . 1$ , and $\bar { c } \triangleq \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \bar { c } _ { k }$ satisfies

Moreover, $U ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \Lambda } )$ is continuously diferentiable on $( \bar { c } , \infty )$ with 

$$

$$

For $k = 1 , \ldots , K$ , define 

$$
\alpha_ {k} \triangleq I (\lambda_ {k} U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k}); \underline {{\Lambda}})

so that 

$$
\min _ {1 \leq k \leq K} \alpha_ {k} = I (m (\underline {{\Lambda}}); \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \bar {c},
$$

and set 

$$
\mathcal {D} \triangleq \{\alpha_ {k} \} _ {k = 1} ^ {K} \backslash \{\bar {c} \}
$$

so that $\mathcal { D } \subset ( \bar { c } , \infty )$ . The derivatives $U ^ { \prime \prime } ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \Lambda } )$ and $U ^ { \prime \prime \prime } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ exist and are continuous on $( \bar { c } , \infty ) \backslash \mathcal { D }$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>, and their one-sided limits exist and are finite at all points in . Moreover, 

$$
U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha +; \underline {{\Lambda}}) - U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha -; \underline {{\Lambda}}) \geq 0, \quad \forall \alpha \in \mathcal {D}.\tag{5.27}
$$

Proof. Using the convention that the maximum over the empty set is $- \infty$ , we see that 

$$
U (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = - \infty \quad \forall c \in (- \infty , \bar {c}).\tag{5.28}
$$

If $c > { \bar { c } } ,$ then the numbers $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { k } \overset { \triangle } { = } \bar { c } _ { k } + \frac { 1 } { K } ( c - \bar { c } ) } \end{array}$ satisfy $c _ { k } > \bar { c } _ { k }$ and $c _ { 1 } +$ $\cdots + c _ { K } = c .$ . From the definition (5.24) of $U ( c ; \Lambda )$ , we have $U ( c ; \Lambda ) \ge$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \lambda _ { k } U _ { k } ( c _ { k } ) > - \infty } \end{array}$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>. Relation (5.25) follows from this inequality and (5.28). 

Now let $c \geq { \bar { c } }$ be given. For each k, set 

$$
\hat {c} _ {k} \triangleq I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right).\tag{5.29}
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \hat { c } _ { k } = I ( \mathcal { H } ( c ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) = c , } \end{array}$ from (5.15). Furthermore, ${ \hat { c } } _ { k } ~ \geq ~ { \bar { c } } _ { k }$ for each k. If $\hat { c } _ { k } > \bar { c } _ { k }$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>for some k, then $\lambda _ { k } > 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \hat { c } _ { k } ) = \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } \mathcal { H } ( c ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) } \end{array}$ whereas if $\hat { c } _ { k } = \bar { c } _ { k }$ , we know only that $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \hat { c } _ { k } ) \leq \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } \mathcal { H } ( c ; \Lambda ) } \end{array}$ . Suppose $c _ { 1 } \geq$ $\bar { c } _ { 1 } , \dotsc , c _ { K } \dotsc \bar { c } _ { K }$ and $c _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + c _ { K } = c$ <sup>˜</sup>. We have from the concavity of each $U _ { k } ( \cdot )$ that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} (c _ {k}) \leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} [ U _ {k} (\hat {c} _ {k}) + (c _ {k} - \hat {c} _ {k}) U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\hat {c} _ {k}) ] \\ = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} (\hat {c} _ {k}) + \mathcal {H} (c; \underline {{\Delta}}) \cdot \sum_ {\{k; \hat {c} _ {k} > \bar {c} _ {k} \}} (c _ {k} - \hat {c} _ {k}) \\ + \sum_ {\{k; \hat {c} _ {k} = \bar {c} _ {k} \}} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\hat {c} _ {k}) (c _ {k} - \hat {c} _ {k}) \end{array}
$$

$$
\leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} (\hat {c} _ {k}) + \mathcal {H} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} (c _ {k} - \hat {c} _ {k}) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} (\hat {c} _ {k}).

In other words, $\hat { c } _ { 1 } , \dots , \hat { c } _ { K }$ attain the maximum in (5.24), and we obtain the representation 

$$
U (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} \left(I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}})\right)\right), \quad c \in (\bar {c}, \infty).\tag{5.30}

At any of these <sup>˜ ˜</sup>points that is also contained in $( 0 , m ( \underset { \sim } { \Lambda } ) ) , ( 5 . 3 1 )$ implies

For $c \in ( \alpha _ { k } , \infty ) \backslash \mathcal { D }$ , we compute 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {d}{d c} \left[ \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} \left(I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right)\right) \right] & = U _ {k} ^ {\prime} \left(I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right)\right) \\ & \cdot I _ {k} ^ {\prime} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \cdot \mathcal {H} ^ {\prime} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \\ & = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \cdot I _ {k} ^ {\prime} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \cdot \mathcal {H} ^ {\prime} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \\ & = \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \cdot \frac {d}{d c} \left[ I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \right], \end{array}
$$

where we have used (5.37) and the fact that $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } : \left( \bar { c } _ { k } , \infty \right) \ \stackrel { \mathrm { o n t o } } { \longrightarrow } \ \left( 0 , U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) \right)$ is the inverse of $I _ { k } : \left( 0 , U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( { \bar { c } } _ { k } ) \right) \ { \stackrel { \mathrm { o n t o } } { \longrightarrow } } \ \left( { \bar { c } } _ { k } , \infty \right)$ . For $c \in ( \bar { c } , \alpha _ { k } ) \backslash \mathcal { D }$ , we have from (5.36) that $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { k } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } \mathcal { H } ( c ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) ) = \bar { c } _ { k } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } \mathcal { H } ( c ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) ) = 0 } \end{array}$ , so once again 

$$
\frac {d}{d c} \left[ \lambda_ {k} U _ {k} \left(I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right)\right) \right] = \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \cdot \frac {d}{d c} \left[ I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \right],\tag{5.38}
$$

but now with both sides equal to zero. 

We have established (5.38) for all $c \in ( \bar { c } , \infty ) \backslash \{ \alpha _ { k } \}$ , provided that $\alpha _ { k } \neq \bar { c } .$ If $\alpha _ { k } = { \bar { c } } .$ , then 

$$
\lambda_ {k} U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k}) = \mathcal {H} (\alpha_ {k}; \Lambda) = m (\underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) > 0.\tag{5.39}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda _ { k } > 0$ and (5.39) implies (5.37), which leads to (5.38) as before. We may now sum (5.38) over $k \in \{ 1 , \ldots , K \}$ and use the representation (5.30) to obtain 

$$
U ^ {\prime} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \Lambda) \cdot \frac {d}{d c} I (\mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}), \quad \forall c \in (\bar {c}, \infty) \backslash \mathcal {D}.
$$

This implies 

$$
U (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = U (\bar {c} + 1, \underline {{\Lambda}}) + \int_ {\bar {c} + 1} ^ {c} \mathcal {H} (\eta ; \underline {{\Lambda}}) d \eta , \quad \forall c \in (\bar {c}, \infty),
$$

and since $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ is continuous, diferentiation yields 5.26. 

Because $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ is continuous, positive, and strictly decreasing on $( \bar { c } , \infty )$ , the function $U ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \Lambda } )$ is strictly concave and increasing on this set. Moreover, $\mathcal { H } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ is continuous from the right at ${ \bar { c } } ,$ and the representation (5.30), <sup>˜</sup>combined with the right continuity (upper semicontinuity) of each $U _ { k } ( \cdot )$ at $\bar { c } _ { k }$ , establishes the right continuity (upper semicontinuity) of $U ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ at ${ \bar { c } } .$ Finally, 

$$
\lim _ {c \to \infty} U ^ {\prime} (c; \Lambda) = \lim _ {c \to \infty} \mathcal {H} (c; \Lambda) = 0.
$$

This concludes the proof that $U ( \cdot ; \mathbb { \lambda } )$ has all the properties required of utility functions by Definition 3.4.1. 

The piecewise continuity of $U ^ { \prime \prime } ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ and $U ^ { \prime \prime \prime } ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ on $( \bar { c } , \infty )$ follows from the properties proved for $\mathcal { H } ^ { \prime } ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ and $\mathcal { H } ^ { \prime \prime } ( \cdot ; \Delta )$ <sup>˜</sup>. Inequality (5.35) is (5.27). ␀ 

## 4.6 Existence and Uniqueness of Equilibrium

In light of Corollary 5.4, the key remaining step in the construction of an equilibrium market is the solution of the system of equations (5.17) for $\Delta \in$ ${ } ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ <sup>˜</sup> . In contrast to the original problem of determining equilibrium price processes, the problem at hand is finite-dimensional. 

Lemma 5.5 shows that we should not expect the system ofequations $( 5 . 1 7 )$ to have a unique solution $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ , since $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; \Lambda )$ and $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; \Lambda ^ { * } )$ can agree even though $\Lambda \neq \Lambda ^ { * }$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>. However, the equality (5.23) guarantees that both $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda }$ and $\boldsymbol { \Lambda } ^ { * }$ <sup>˜</sup> <sup>˜</sup>result in the same optimal consumption processes for the <sup>˜</sup> <sup>˜</sup>individual agents, given by (5.18). 

There is, however, an additional kind of nonuniqueness in (5.17). The representation (5.26) of the function ${ \mathcal { H } } .$ , along with the definition (5.24) of the “representative agent” utility function, allows us to deduce the positive homogeneity properties for $c \geq \bar { c } , \eta > 0$ , and $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ 

$$
U (c; \eta \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \eta U (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}),\tag{6.1}
$$

$$
\mathcal {H} (c; \eta \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \eta \mathcal {H} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}).\tag{6.2}
$$

It follows from (6.2) that if a vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in \Lt ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ satisfies the equa <sup>˜</sup> tions (5.17), then so does every other vector $\eta \Delta$ with $\eta \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , on the <sup>˜</sup> same ray through the origin; for all such vectors, the optimal consumption processes are the same: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {c} _ {k} (t) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \\ \qquad = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\eta \lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \eta \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, \quad k = 1, \ldots , K. \end{array}\tag{6.3}
$$

The first result of this section guarantees the existence of a solution to (5.17) and provides a condition under which the equilibrium optimal consumption processes of the individual agents are uniquely determined. 

Theorem 6.1: There exists a vector $\underset { \smile } { \Lambda } = ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \dots , \lambda _ { k } ) \in \mathbf { \Sigma } ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ satisfying the system of equations $( 5 . 1 7 )$ <sup>˜</sup> . Suppose, moreover, that for each agent k, the Arrow–Pratt “index of risk-aversion” is less than or equal to one, namely 

$$
- \frac {c U _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (c)} \leq 1 \quad f o r a l l \quad c \in (\bar {c} _ {k}, \infty), \quad k = 1, \dots , K,\tag{6.4}
$$

(see Remark $\it 3 . 4 . 4 )$ , and let $M = ( \mu _ { 1 } , \dots , \mu _ { K } ) \in \mathbf \Upsilon ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ be any other <sup>˜</sup> solution of (5.17); then for some positive constant η, we have almost surely 

$$
\eta \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underline {{M}}), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{6.5}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {c} _ {k} (t) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) \\ = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\mu_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M})\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, \quad k = 1, \ldots , K. \end{array}\tag{6.6}
$$

Proof. We first establish existence. Let $\{ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { K } \}$ be the standard basis of unit vectors in $\mathbb { R } ^ { K }$ , and let $\mathbb { K } = \{ 1 , \ldots , K \}$ <sup>˜</sup>. For any nonempty set $\mathbb { B } \subset \mathbb { K }$ , denote by 

$$
\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbb {B}} \triangleq \left\{\sum_ {k \in \mathbb {B}} \lambda_ {k} \underline {{e}} _ {k}; \quad \lambda_ {k} \geq 0 \quad \forall k \in \mathbb {B} \text {   and   } \sum_ {k \in \mathbb {B}} \lambda_ {k} = 1 \right\} \subset^ {*} [ 0, \infty) ^ {K}
$$

the convex hull of $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbb { B } }$ . For every $k \in \mathbb { K }$ , define $R _ { k } : S _ { \mathbb { K } } \to \mathbb { R }$ by 

$$
R _ {k} (\underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \triangleq E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \left[ I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) - \epsilon_ {k} (t) \right] d t,\tag{6.7}
$$

where as usual, $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { k } ( \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } } \mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) ) \overset { \triangle } { = } \bar { c } _ { k } } \end{array}$ if $\lambda _ { k } = 0$ . The function $R _ { k }$ is continuous, and hence the set $F _ { k } \overset { \Delta } { = } \{ \underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in \mathcal { S } _ { \mathbb { K } } ; R _ { k } ( \underset { \sim } { \Lambda } ) \geq 0 \}$ is closed. Note from (5.15) that 

$$
\sum_ {k \in \mathbb {K}} R _ {k} (\underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) [ I (\mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) - \epsilon (t) ] d t = 0\tag{6.8}
$$

holds for every $\Lambda \in \mathsf { \Omega } ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty )$ . We claim that 

$$
\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbb {B}} \subset \bigcup_ {k \in \mathbb {B}} F _ {k}, \quad \forall \mathbb {B} \subset \mathbb {K}, \quad \mathbb {B} \neq \emptyset .\tag{6.9}
$$

Indeed, suppose $\Lambda \in S _ { \mathbb { B } }$ but $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \notin \cup _ { k \in \mathbb { B } } F _ { k } ;$ then $R _ { k } ( \mathbb { \Lambda } ) < 0$ for all $k \in \mathbb { B }$ <sup>˜</sup> Condition (2.1(ii)) implies $R _ { k } ( \boldsymbol { \Delta } ) \leq 0$ for all $k \in \mathbb { K } \backslash \mathbb { B }$ <sup>˜</sup>, so that (6.8) is con-<sup>˜</sup>tradicted. From (6.9) and the lemma of Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz (1929) (e.g., Border (1985), p. 26), we conclude that $\cap _ { k \in \mathbb { K } } F _ { k } \neq \emptyset$ . Let Λ be in this set. The definition of $F _ { k }$ , combined with (6.8), implies $R _ { k } ( \mathbb { \Lambda } ) = 0$ for all $k \in \mathbb { K }$ ; hence $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda }$ satisfies the system (5.17). 

We next assume the risk-aversion condition $( 6 . 4 )$ and characterize the set of all solutions of (5.17) in terms of a particular solution $\displaystyle \Lambda .$ . Let $\tau$ and $\Lambda ^ { * }$ be as in Lemma 5.5. Suppose that $M = \left( \mu _ { 1 } , \dots , \mu _ { K } \right)$ <sup>˜</sup>is another solution of (5.17), and let $M _ { \sim } ^ { * } = ( \mu _ { 1 } ^ { * } , \dots , \mu _ { K } ^ { * } )$ <sup>˜</sup> be defined by the analogue of (5.21): 

$$
\mu_ {k} ^ {*} \triangleq \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} P \text {-ess inf} \left(\min _ {0 \leq t \leq T} T \frac {\mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t) ; M)}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k})}\right), & \text {if} \quad k \in \mathcal {T}, \\ \mu_ {k}, & \text {if} \quad k \in \mathcal {T} ^ {c}, \end{array} \right.\tag{6.10}
$$

and note that $\mu _ { k } ^ { * } \geq \mu _ { k }$ 

If $\lambda _ { k } ^ { * } = 0$ for some k, then Lemma 5.5 implies $k \in \mathcal T$ , and thus 

$$
P \text {-ess} \inf \left(\min _ {0 \leq t \leq T} \frac {\mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t) ; \underline {{\Lambda}})}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k})}\right) = 0.
$$

But $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; \Lambda )$ is bounded from below by $\mathcal { H } ( \gamma _ { 2 } ; \mathbb { \Lambda } ) > 0$ (Condition 2.1(iii)), <sup>˜</sup>so we must have $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) = \infty$ and thus $\mu _ { k } ^ { * } = 0$ <sup>˜</sup>from (4.6). Now define 

$$
\eta \triangleq \max \left\{\frac {\mu_ {k} ^ {*}}{\lambda_ {k} ^ {*}}; k \in \mathbb {K}, \lambda_ {k} ^ {*} \neq 0 \right\}.\tag{6.11}
$$

Because $\lambda _ { k } ^ { * } = 0$ implies $\mu _ { k } ^ { * } = 0$ , we have 

$$
\mu_ {k} ^ {*} \leq \eta \lambda_ {k} ^ {*}, \quad \forall k \in \mathbb {K}.\tag{6.12}

Furthermore, there is an index $\bar { k } \in \mathbb { K }$ such that $\mu _ { \bar { k } } ^ { * } = \eta \lambda _ { \bar { k } } ^ { * } > 0$ . From (6.12) we have

$$

or equivalently, 

$$
\frac {1}{\lambda_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) \geq \frac {1}{\mu_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*}), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{6.13}

Consider the function $\varphi _ { k } ( y ) = y I _ { k } ( y ) , 0 < y < U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( { \bar { c } } _ { k } )$ . With $c = I _ { k } ( y )$ , we have the derivative formula 

$$
\varphi_ {k} ^ {\prime} (y) = I _ {k} (y) + y I _ {k} ^ {\prime} (y) = c + \frac {U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (c)}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}, \quad 0 <   y <   U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k}),
$$

and (6.4) implies that $\varphi _ { k }$ is nonincreasing. Because both $\boldsymbol { \Lambda } ^ { * }$ and $M ^ { * }$ satisfy (5.17), we have, in the notation of (6.7), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} R _ {\bar {k}} (\underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \left[ \varphi_ {\bar {k}} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*})\right) - \frac {1}{\lambda_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) \epsilon_ {\bar {k}} (t) \right] d t \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \leq E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \left[ \varphi_ {\bar {k}} \left(\frac {1}{\mu_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*})\right) - \frac {1}{\mu_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*}) \epsilon_ {\bar {k}} (t) \right] d t \\ = \frac {1}{\mu_ {\bar {k}} ^ {*}} R _ {\bar {k}} (\underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*}) = 0. \end{array}
$$

This shows that equality must hold in (6.13) almost surely, which yields (6.5). 

For any $k \in \mathbb { K }$ , (6.5) and (6.12) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})\right) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\eta \lambda_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M})\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\mu_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M})\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T. \end{array}\tag{6.14}
$$

But (5.17) for both $\Lambda ^ { * }$ and $M ^ { * }$ and (6.5) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*})\right) d t \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) \epsilon_ {k} (t) d t \\ = \frac {1}{\eta} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*}) \epsilon_ {k} (t) d t \\ = \frac {1}{\eta} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*}) I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\mu_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*})\right) d t \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\mu_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {M} ^ {*})\right) d t. \end{array}

Since $e ^ { - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \beta ( u ) d u } \mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; \Lambda ^ { * } )$ is always positive, equality must hold in (6.14) <sup>˜</sup>almost surely; this and Lemma 5.5 imply (6.6). ␀ 

Remark 6.2: Although we do not use this observation, it is interesting to note that $\boldsymbol { \Lambda } ^ { * }$ and $M ^ { * }$ in the proof of Theorem 6.1 are related via $M ^ { * } = \eta \Lambda ^ { * }$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>In light of (6.12), we need only rule out the possibilty $\eta \lambda _ { k } ^ { * } > \mu _ { k } ^ { * }$ <sup>˜ ˜</sup>. From (6.5) and the definitions (5.21), (6.10) of $\lambda _ { k } ^ { * } , \mu _ { k } ^ { * }$ for $k \in \mathcal T$ , such a k must be in ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { c }$ . Lemma 5.5 applied to M shows that $k \in \mathcal { T } ^ { c }$ if and only if the inequality 

$$
\mu_ {k} ^ {*} \leq \frac {\mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t) ; \tilde {M} ^ {*})}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k})}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

does not hold almost surely, i.e., $\begin{array} { r } { P \left[ U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) > \operatorname* { m i n } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \frac { 1 } { \mu _ { k } ^ { * } } \mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t ) ; M ^ { * } ) \right] > } \end{array}$ 0. If $\eta \lambda _ { k } ^ { * } > \mu _ { k } ^ { * }$ , then the above inequality and (6.5), (5.22) imply 

$$
P \left[ U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (\bar {c} _ {k}) > \min _ {0 \leq t \leq T} \frac {1}{\lambda_ {k} ^ {*}} \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda} ^ {*}) \right] > 0;

but for t and $\omega$ chosen such that $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) > \frac { 1 } { \lambda _ { k } ^ { * } } \mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( t , \omega ) ; \Lambda _ { \sim } ^ { * } ) } \end{array}$ , we have the strict inequality

To complete the construction of an equilibrium market, we appeal to Theorem 6.1 and choose a vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } \in \mathbf { \Omega } ^ { * } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { K }$ satisfying the system of <sup>˜</sup> equations (5.17). The positive homogeneity properties of (6.1), (6.2) permi us to assume without loss of generality that 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\epsilon (0); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) = 1.\tag{6.15}

Let us consider the process 

$$

An application of Itˆo’s rule for diferences of convex functions of martingales (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Theorems 3.6.22, 3.7.1 and Problem 3.6.24) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \eta (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} [ U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (s); \underline {{\Lambda}}) \epsilon (s) \nu (s) + \frac {1}{2} U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (\epsilon (s); \underline {{\Lambda}}) \| \rho (s) \| ^ {2} \epsilon^ {2} (s) ] d s \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (s); \underline {{\Lambda}}) \epsilon (s) d \xi (s) \\ \quad + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} [ U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha_ {k} +; \underline {{\Lambda}}) - U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha_ {k} -; \underline {{\Lambda}}) ] L _ {t} (\alpha_ {k}) \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (s); \underline {{\Lambda}}) \epsilon (s) \rho^ {\prime} (s) d W (s), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, \end{array} \tag {6}\tag{6.17}
$$

in conjunction with Theorem 5.6 and equation (2.2). Here $L _ { t } ( \alpha _ { k } )$ is the local time at $\alpha _ { k }$ of the semimartingale $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ , accumulated during [0, t]. On the other hand, if $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is the state price density in a standard, complete financial market $\mathcal { M }$ , then the process 

$$

Theorem 6.4 (Uniqueness of the equilibrium market): Assume that $( 6 . 4 )$ holds. Then the equilibrium money market process $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , the state price density process $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , and the market price of risk process $\theta ( \cdot )$ , are uniquely determined, as are the optimal consumption processes $\hat { c } _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots ,$ $\hat { c } _ { K } ( \cdot )$ of the individual agents. 

Proof. The uniqueness of $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ follows from Corollary 5.4, Theorem 6.1, and the initial condition $H _ { 0 } ( 0 ) = 1$ . The uniqueness of $\hat { c } _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \hat { c } _ { K } ( \cdot )$ also follows from Theorem 6.1. The semimartingale log $H _ { 0 } ( t )$ can be decomposed uniquely as the sum of a finite-variation process $F ( \cdot )$ plus a local martingale $M ( \cdot )$ . But 

$$
\log H _ {0} (t) = - \int_ {0} ^ {t} r (u) d u - A (t) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \theta (u) \| ^ {2} d u - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \theta (u) d W (u),
$$

and the equation $\begin{array} { r } { M ( t ) \ = \ - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \theta ( u ) d W ( u ) , 0 \ \leq \ t \ \leq \ T } \end{array}$ determines the process $\theta ( \cdot )$ . Knowing $\theta ( \cdot )$ and using the equation 

$$
F (t) = - \int_ {0} ^ {t} r (u) d u - A (t) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \theta (u) \| ^ {2} d u,
$$

we determine $\begin{array} { r l } { - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } r ( u ) d u - A ( t ) } \end{array}$ , and hence $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ 

We should not expect the stock mean rate of return vector $b ( \cdot )$ and the volatility matrix $\sigma ( \cdot )$ to be determined by equilibrium conditions, because of the possibility of replacing stocks by mutual funds. Given a market $\mathcal { M } =$ $( r ( \cdot ) , b ( \cdot ) , \sigma ( \cdot ) , S ( 0 ) , A ( \cdot ) )$ , we can form a mutual fund by specifying an initial value $\ddot { S } ( 0 ) > 0$ and the proportion $p _ { j } ( t )$ of the fund that is to be invested in each stock j at time t. The proportion $\begin{array} { r } { 1 - \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { N } p _ { j } ( t ) } \end{array}$ (which may be negative, or may exceed 1) is invested in the money market. The value of the mutual fund will then evolve according to the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \tilde {S} (t) = \tilde {S} (t) [ (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N}) (r (t) d t + d A (t))} \\ & {\qquad + p ^ {\prime} (t) (b (t) d t + \mathbb {1} _ {N} d A (t)) + p ^ {\prime} (t) \sigma (t) d W (t) ]} \\ & {\qquad = \tilde {S} (t) [ r (t) d t + d A (t) + p ^ {\prime} (t) (b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N}) d t + p ^ {\prime} (t) \sigma (t) d W (t) ].} \end{array}
$$

This is just (1.3.3) with $\Gamma ( \cdot ) = \delta ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 , X ( \cdot ) = \tilde { S } ( \cdot )$ , and $\pi ( \cdot ) = \tilde { S } ( \cdot ) p ( \cdot )$ 

Now let us choose a set of N mutual funds $\begin{array} { r c l } { p _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) } & { = } & { ( p _ { 1 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , } \end{array}$ $p _ { 1 N } ( \cdot ) ) ^ { \prime } , \ldots , p _ { N } ( \cdot ) \ = \ ( p _ { N 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , p _ { N N } ( \cdot ) ) ^ { \prime }$ such that the matrix $P ( t ) =$ $( p _ { i j } ( t ) ) _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq N }$ is nonsingular for all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely. Then the values $\tilde { S } ( t ) = ( \tilde { S } _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , \tilde { S } _ { N } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime }$ for these funds evolve according to the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \tilde {S} (t) = d i a g (\tilde {S} (t)) \cdot [ (r (t)   d t + d A (t)) \mathbb {1} _ {N}} \\ & {\qquad + P (t) (b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1})   d t + P (t) \sigma (t)   d W (t) ],} \end{array}
$$

where $d i a g ( \tilde { S } ( t ) )$ denotes the $N \times N$ diagonal matrix with $\tilde { S } _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , \tilde { S } _ { N } ( t )$ in the diagonal positions. We may regard $\tilde { S } _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \tilde { S } _ { N } ( \cdot )$ as a complete set of stocks with mean rate of return vector 

$$
\tilde {b} (t) \triangleq r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} + P (t) [ b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} ]\tag{6.25}
$$

and volatility matrix 

$$
\tilde {\sigma} (t) \triangleq P (t) \sigma (t).\tag{6.26}
$$

The associated market price of risk is 

$$
\hat {\theta} (t) \stackrel {\triangle} {=} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {- 1} (t) [ \tilde {b} (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} ] = \sigma^ {- 1} (t) [ b (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} ] = \theta (t),
$$

the same as the market price of risk associated with the original set of stocks $S _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , S _ { N } ( \cdot )$ 

If $\mathcal { M } = ( r ( \cdot ) , b ( \cdot ) , \sigma ( \cdot ) , S ( \cdot ) , A ( \cdot ) )$ is an equilibrium market for the prim itives introduced in Section 2, then so is $\tilde { \mathcal { M } } = ( r ( \cdot ) , \tilde { b } ( \cdot ) , \tilde { \sigma } ( \cdot ) , \tilde { S } ( \cdot ) , \bar { A } ( \cdot ) )$ Indeed, since $ { \tilde { \theta } } ( \cdot ) = \theta ( \cdot )$ , the markets have a common state price density process $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , and this is all that matters (Theorem 5.2). Thus, equilibrium considerations cannot determine the processes $b ( \cdot )$ and $\sigma ( \cdot )$ 

It follows from Theorem 6.4, however, that under the risk-aversion condi tion (6.4), the equilibrium market is unique up to the formation of mutual $f u n d s$ . If $\mathcal { M } = ( r ( \cdot ) , b ( \cdot ) , \sigma ( \cdot ) , S ( 0 ) , A ( \cdot ) )$ and $\tilde { \mathcal { M } } = \tilde { ( } r ( \cdot ) , \tilde { b } ( \cdot ) , \tilde { \sigma } ( \cdot ) , \tilde { S } ( 0 )$ ， $A ( \cdot ) )$ are two equilibrium markets, the uniqueness of the market price of risk implies 

$$
\sigma^ {- 1} (t) [ b (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} ] = \tilde {\sigma} ^ {- 1} (t) [ \tilde {b} (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} ].
$$

Setting $P ( t ) = \tilde { \sigma } ( t ) \sigma ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ , we have (6.25), (6.26). 

Remark 6.5: Under condition (6.4), the representative agent utility func tion (5.24) that results in equilibrium is determined (up to an irrelevant multiplicative constant) purely endogenously, by the individual agents’ util ity functions $U _ { 1 } , \dots , U _ { k }$ , the discount rate $\beta ( \cdot )$ , and the distribution of the vector of endowment processes $\mathcal { E } ( \cdot ) = ( \epsilon _ { K } ( \cdot ) , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \epsilon _ { k } ( \cdot ) )$ 

The paths of the equilibrium market processes $r ( \cdot ) , A ( \cdot )$ , and $\theta ( \cdot )$ , as well as the individual agents’ optimal consumption processes $\hat { c } _ { k } ( \cdot )$ , depend on the representative agent’s utility function, the discount rate function $\beta ( \cdot )$ the paths of the aggregate endowment process $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ , and the paths of the processes $\nu ( \cdot ) , \rho ( \cdot )$ , and $\xi ( \cdot )$ used in the model (2.2) of $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ . More generally, $r ( \cdot ) , A ( \cdot ) , \theta ( \cdot )$ and $\hat { c } _ { k } ( \cdot )$ are adapted to the filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ , the augmentation by null sets of the filtration generated by the N-dimensional Brownian motion $W ( \cdot )$ 

A more satisfactory result would be for $r ( \cdot ) , A ( \cdot ) , \theta ( \cdot )$ , and $\hat { c } _ { k } ( \cdot )$ to be adapted to the filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ^ { \mathcal { E } } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ generated by the vector $\mathcal { E } ( \cdot ) \ : =$ $( \epsilon _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \epsilon _ { K } ( \cdot ) )$ of endowment processes. This is indeed the case, under the following conditions. 

Assume that instead of (2.2), the individual agents’ endowment processes are given by the system of functional stochastic diferential equations 

$$
d \epsilon_ {k} (t) = \epsilon_ {k} (t) \left[ \nu_ {k} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)) d t + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \rho_ {k j} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)) d W ^ {(j)} (t) \right], \quad k = 1, \dots , K,
$$

where $\nu _ { k } : [ 0 , T ] \times C ( [ 0 , T ] ) ^ { K } \to \mathbb { R }$ and $p _ { k d } : [ 0 , T ] \times C ( [ 0 , T ] ) ^ { K } \to \mathbb { R }$ are progressively measurable functionals as in Definition 3.5.15 of Karatzas and Shreve (1991). If these functionals $\nu ( t , y ) = \{ \nu _ { k } ( t , y ) \} _ { k = 1 , \ldots , K }$ and $\rho ( t , y ) =$ $\{ \rho _ { k j } ( t , y ) \} _ { \stackrel { 1 \leq k \leq K } { 1 \leq j \leq N } }$ are bounded and satisfy the Lipschitz condition 

$$
\| \nu (t, y) - \nu (t, z) \| + \| \rho (t, y) - \rho (t, z) \| \leq L (1 + \sup _ {0 \leq u \leq t} \| y (u) - z (u) \|)
$$

for every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ and $y , z \ \mathrm { i n } \ C ( [ 0 , T ] ) ^ { K }$ , then the system (6.27) has a pathwise unique, strong solution $\mathcal { E } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ . The proof is a straight forward modification of the standard iterative construction (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Theorem 5.2.9). 

The solution to (6.27) satisfies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \epsilon_ {k} (t) = \epsilon_ {k} (0) \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \left[ \nu_ {k} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)) - \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {N} \rho_ {k d} ^ {2} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)) \right] d t \right. \\ \left. + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \rho_ {k j} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)) d W ^ {(j)} (t) \right\} \end{array}
$$

and hence is nonnegative, and positive if $\epsilon _ { k } ( 0 )$ is positive. Provided that at least one $\epsilon _ { k } ( 0 )$ is positive, we may write the diferential of $\begin{array} { r } { \epsilon ( t ) = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \epsilon _ { k } ( t ) } \end{array}$ as 

$$
d \epsilon (t) = \epsilon (t) \nu (t) d t + \epsilon (t) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \rho_ {j} (t) d W ^ {(j)} (t),
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \nu (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \frac {\epsilon_ {k} (t)}{\epsilon (t)} \nu_ {k} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)), \\ \rho_ {j} (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \frac {\epsilon_ {k} (t)}{\epsilon (t)} \rho_ {k j} (t, \mathcal {E} (\cdot)), \quad j = 1, \ldots , N. \end{array}
$$

We are now in the setting of (2.2) with $\xi ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ , except that now all processes are adapted to the filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ^ { \mathcal { E } } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ 

Remark 6.6: The equilibrium market in this chapter is constructed so that the money market and all stocks are in zero net supply (cf. (5.3), (5.4)). Within the framework of this chapter, other assets can be defined and priced, and these can be in positive net supply. For example, the righ to receive agent $k \mathrm { { s } }$ endowment process is in positive net supply. The value of this right at time t is 

$$
\frac {1}{H _ {0} (t)} \cdot E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} H _ {0} (u) \epsilon_ {k} (u) d u \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right],
$$

where $H _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is determined by equilibrium. Any other value would result in an arbitrage opportunity. 

Remark 6.7 (The Consumption-based Capital Asset Pricing Model): Suppose there exists a unique equilibrium market. From (6.16)–(6.22) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t) ; \Lambda)}{U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t) ; \Lambda)} = \beta (t) d t - r (t) d t - d A (t) - \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (t) ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})}{U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t) ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})} \epsilon (t) \rho^ {\prime} (t) d W (t) \\ = \beta (t) d t - \frac {d S _ {0} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} - \theta^ {\prime} (t) d W (t). \end{array} \tag {6.}\tag{6.27}
$$

We see that if there is no discounting $( \beta ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 )$ , then the rate of growth of the instantaneously risk-free asset is the negative of the growth rate of the representative agent’s marginal utility from consumption. Note also that with 

$$
J (x; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \triangleq - \frac {x U ^ {\prime \prime} (x ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})}{U ^ {\prime} (x ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})},\tag{6.28}
$$

we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} b _ {n} (t) - r (t) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \sigma_ {n j} (t) \theta_ {j} (t) \\ \qquad = J (\epsilon (t); \Lambda) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \sigma_ {n j} (t) \rho_ {j} (t) \\ \qquad = J (\epsilon (t); \Lambda) \frac {d \langle S _ {n} , \epsilon \rangle (t)}{S _ {n} (t) \epsilon (t) d t}. \end{array}\tag{6.29}
$$

In other words, the risk premium associated with each risky asset is proportional to the relative covariance between the price of that asset and the aggregate consumption; the proportionality constant is independent of the particular asset and equals the “index of relative risk-aversion” for the representative agent. 

The above two observations are referred to as the consumption-based capital asset-pricing model (CCAPM) for an economy. 

Remark 6.8: Formula (6.22) suggests that even if the singularly continuous component $\xi ( \cdot )$ of the aggregate endowment process is identically zero, the singularly continuous component $A ( \cdot )$ of the money market price can be nonzero. In this case, movements in the equilibrium money market price cannot be captured by the interest rate process $r ( \cdot )$ alone. If $\rho ( \cdot )$ is nonzero, then the local-time process $t \mapsto L _ { t } ( \alpha _ { k } )$ strictly increases each time $\epsilon ( t ) = \alpha _ { k }$ . If in addition, $\xi ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ , then 

$$
A (t) = - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha_ {k} + ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) - U ^ {\prime \prime} (\alpha_ {k} - ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})}{U ^ {\prime} (\alpha_ {k} ; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda})} L _ {t} (\alpha_ {k})\tag{6.30}
$$

strictly decreases (recall (5.27)) each time $\epsilon ( t ) = \alpha _ { k }$ for some k, and is con stant on each open interval in the complement of the set $\{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; \epsilon ( t ) =$ $\alpha _ { k }$ for some $k \}$ . The set $\{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; \epsilon ( t ) = \alpha _ { k } \}$ is empty if $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) = \infty ;$ but if $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( \bar { c } _ { k } ) < \infty$ , then $\{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; \epsilon ( t ) = \alpha _ { k } \}$ is precisely the set of time points at which the optimal consumption process for the kth agent “falls $\mathrm { t o } ^ { \dag }$ or “rises from” the subsistence level $\bar { c } _ { k }$ . (Of course, “falling $\mathrm { t o } ^ { \dag }$ or “rising from” subsistence consumption $\bar { c } _ { k }$ is not a simple concept here, since every point of the set $\{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; \epsilon ( t ) = \alpha _ { k } \}$ is a cluster point of this set.) 

Example 7.7 in the next section demonstrates that the preceding phenomenon does occur. 

## 4.7 Examples

This section comprises several examples in which the various processes of the equilibrium market can be computed more or less explicitly. In Exam ple 7.6 there are two agents with completely diferent utility functions. In Example 7.7 there are two agents with related utility functions, except that the optimal equilibrium consumption of one agent sometimes falls to zero, whereas this quantity for the other agent is always positive. When optimal equilibrium consumption of an agent falls to zero, or rises from zero, the money market price decreases in a singularly continuous manner, i.e., the money market price is continuous but cannot be represented by an interest rate. Example 7.8 considers an ergodic aggregate endowment process. 

Example 7.1 (Logarithmic utility with subsistence consumption): Let $U _ { k } ( c ) = \log ( c - \bar { c } _ { k } )$ , for $c > c _ { k } , k = 1 , \ldots , K$ , where each $\bar { c } _ { k }$ is a nonnegative constant. Then 

$$
U ^ {\prime} (c; \tilde {\Lambda}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \Lambda) = \frac {1}{c - \bar {c}} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k}, \quad c > \bar {c}.
$$

We normalize Λ by setting $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \lambda _ { k } = \epsilon ( 0 ) - \bar { c } _ { : } } \end{array}$ , a strictly positive quantity <sup>˜</sup> because of Condition 2.1(iii); then $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( 0 ) ; \Lambda ) = 1$ . Equation (5.17) become 

$$
\lambda_ {k} = \frac {(\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}) E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \left(\frac {\epsilon_ {k} (t) - \bar {c} _ {k}}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}\right) d t}{\int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} d u}.\tag{7.1}
$$

With $\lambda _ { k }$ defined by (7.1), we have 

$$
H _ {0} (t) = \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \tilde {\Lambda}) = \frac {\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}},\tag{7.2}
$$

and the optimal consumption process for agent k is 

$$
\hat {c} _ {k} (t) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}}{\lambda_ {k} (\epsilon (t) - \bar {c})}\right) = \frac {\lambda_ {k} (\epsilon (t) - \bar {c})}{\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}} + \bar {c} _ {k}, \quad k = 1, \dots , K.
$$

For each agent, $\hat { c } _ { k } ( t ) > \bar { c } _ { k }$ for all t, almost surely. The equilibrium market coeficients of (6.20)–(6.22) become 

$$
r (t) = \beta (t) + \frac {\epsilon (t) \nu (t)}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}} - \frac {\epsilon^ {2} (t) \| \rho (t) \| ^ {2}}{(\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}) ^ {2}},
$$

$$
\theta (t) = \frac {\epsilon (t) \rho (t)}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}, A (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\epsilon (s)}{\epsilon (s) - \bar {c}} d \xi (s).
$$

Example 7.2 (Power utility with subsistence consumption): Let $U _ { k } ( c ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { p } ( c - \bar { c } _ { k } ) ^ { p } } \end{array}$ for $c > \bar { c } _ { k } , k = 1 , . . . , K$ , where $p < 1 , p \neq 0$ , and each $\bar { c } _ { k }$ is a nonnegative constant. Then 

$$
U ^ {\prime} (c; \tilde {\Lambda}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \tilde {\Lambda}) = \left[ \frac {\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \lambda_ {k} ^ {\frac {1}{1 - p}}}{c - \bar {c}} \right] ^ {1 - p}, \quad c > \bar {c}.
$$

We normalize $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda }$ by setting $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \lambda _ { k } ^ { \frac { 1 } { 1 - p } } = \epsilon ( 0 ) - \bar { c } _ { : } } \end{array}$ , so that $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ( 0 ) ; \underline { { \Lambda } } ) = 1$ <sup>˜</sup> Equation (5.17) becomes 

$$
\lambda_ {k} ^ {\frac {1}{1 - p}} = \frac {(\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}) E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \frac {\epsilon_ {k} (t) - \bar {c} _ {k}}{(\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}) ^ {1 - p}} d t}{E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} (\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}) ^ {p} d t}.\tag{7.3}
$$

With $\lambda _ { k }$ defined by (7.3), we have 

$$
H _ {0} (t) = \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (t); \tilde {\Lambda}) = \left(\frac {\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}\right) ^ {1 - p},
$$

and the optimal consumption process for agent k is 

$$
\hat {c} _ {k} (t) = I _ {k} \left(\frac {1}{\lambda_ {k}} \left(\frac {\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}\right) ^ {1 - p}\right) = \lambda_ {k} ^ {\frac {1}{1 - p}} \left(\frac {\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}{\epsilon (0) - \bar {c}}\right) + \bar {c} _ {k}, k = 1, \dots , K.
$$

For each agent, $\hat { c } _ { k } ( t ) > \bar { c } _ { k }$ for all $t ,$ almost surely. The equilibrium market coeficients of (6.20)–(6.22) become 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & r (t) = \beta (t) + \frac {(1 - p) \epsilon (t) \nu (t)}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}} - \frac {(1 - p) (2 - p) \epsilon^ {2} (t) \| \rho (t) \| ^ {2}}{2 (\epsilon (t) - \bar {c})}, \\ & \theta (t) = \frac {(1 - p) \epsilon (t) \rho (t)}{\epsilon (t) - \bar {c}}, A (t) = (1 - p) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\epsilon (s)}{\epsilon (s) - \bar {c}} d \xi (s). \end{array}
$$

The logarithmic formulas of Example 7.1 are recovered by setting $p = 0$ in this example. 

Remark 7.3: In Example 7.2 and with Λ given by (7.3), the ray of vectors $\{ \eta \underline { { \Lambda } } \} _ { 0 < \eta < \infty }$ <sup>˜</sup> is the locus of solutions to the system of equations (7.3), even <sup>˜</sup>for negative powers $p .$ . This shows that condition $( 6 . 4 )$ is not necessary for uniqueness in Theorem $7 . 1 ,$ since in this example 

$$
- \frac {c U _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U _ {k} ^ {\prime} (c)} = \frac {(1 - p) c}{c - \bar {c} _ {k}} > 1 \quad \mathrm{for} \quad c > \bar {c} _ {k}, \quad p <   0.
$$

Remark 7.4: Condition 2.1(ii) is not necessary for the construction the equilibria in Examples (7.1) and (7.2). All that is required is that the expressions appearing on the right-hand sides of (7.1), (7.3) be nonnegative for all k. They will be positive for at least one k because of Condition 2.1(iii). 

Example 7.5 (Constant aggregate endowment): If the aggregate endowment $\epsilon > \bar { c }$ is constant, then the unique vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda }$ satisfying the 

normalization $\mathcal { H } ( \epsilon ; \Lambda ) = 1$ is 

$$
\tilde {\Lambda} = \left(\frac {1}{U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (\hat {c} _ {1})}, \dots , \frac {1}{U _ {K} ^ {\prime} (\hat {c} _ {k})}\right),
$$

where the constants $\hat { c } _ { k } \ge \bar { c } _ { k }$ are the optimal consumption rates 

$$
\hat {c} _ {k} = \frac {E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \epsilon_ {k} (t) d t}{\int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} d t}, \quad k = 1, \ldots , K.
$$

Constant aggregate endowment implies $\nu ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 , \xi ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 , \rho ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ in (2.2), and the local time of $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ <sup>˜</sup> at every point is zero. Therefore, the equilibrium market coeficients (6.20)–(6.22) are 

$$
r (t) = \beta (t), \quad \theta (t) = 0, \quad A (t) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

It should be noted that the individual agents’ endowments can be random and time-varying, which means that agents may still have to trade with one another in order to finance their constant rates of consumption. 

Example 7.6 $( K = 2 , U _ { 1 } ( c ) = \log c , U _ { 2 } ( c ) = \sqrt { c } . )$ : In this case, we have 

$$
U ^ {\prime} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{2 c} \left[ 1 + \sqrt {1 + c \left(\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) ^ {2}} \right], \quad c > 0,
$$

and the optimal consumption rates become 

$$
\hat {c} _ {1} (t) = \frac {2 \epsilon (t)}{1 + \sqrt {1 + \epsilon (t) (\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}) ^ {2}}}, \quad \hat {c} _ {2} (t) = \left(\frac {\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}} \epsilon (t)}{1 + \sqrt {1 + \epsilon (t) (\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}) ^ {2}}}\right) ^ {2}.
$$

The positive constants $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 }$ are uniquely determined by (5.17) with $k = 1$ : 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 2 \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} d t \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (u) d u} \left[ 1 + \sqrt {1 + \epsilon (t) \left(\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) ^ {2}} \right] \frac {\epsilon_ {1} (t)}{\epsilon (t)} d t, \end{array}\tag{7.4}
$$

and the normalization condition (6.15) gives 

$$
\lambda_ {1} = \frac {2 \epsilon (0)}{1 + \sqrt {1 + \epsilon (0) (\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}) ^ {2}}}.\tag{7.5}
$$

Indeed, (7.4) determines $\frac { \lambda _ { 2 } } { \lambda _ { 1 } }$ , and then $\lambda _ { 1 }$ is found from (7.5). 

With the vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } = ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \lambda _ { 2 } ) \in ( 0 , \infty ) ^ { 2 }$ thus determined, the formulae 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & r (t) = \beta (t) + J (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \nu (t) + \frac {1}{2} \| \rho (t) \| ^ {2} K (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}), \\ & \theta (t) = J (\epsilon (t); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) \rho (t), \quad A (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} J (\epsilon (s); \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}) d \xi (s) \end{array}
$$

of (6.20)–(6.22), with 

$$
J (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = - c U ^ {\prime \prime} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) / U ^ {\prime} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}), \quad K (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) = - c U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}) / U ^ {\prime} (c; \underline {{\Lambda}}),
$$

provide the coeficients of the equilibrium market model. 

Example 7.7 (Money market not represented by an interest rate): This example shows that the equilibrium money-market price can have a non trivial singularly continuous component $A ( \cdot )$ , even though the singularly continuous component $\xi ( \cdot )$ of the aggregate endowment process is identi cally zero. There is a discussion of this phenomenon in Remark 6.8. Here we set up a particular model exhibiting the behavior of interest. 

We consider two agents $\left( K = 2 \right)$ with utility functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} U _ {1} (c) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \log c, & c > 0, \\ - \infty , & c \leq 0, \end{array} \right. \\ U _ {2} (c) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \log (c + 1), & c \geq 0, \\ - \infty , & c <   0, \end{array} \right. \end{array}
$$

so that $\bar { c } _ { 1 } = \bar { c } _ { 2 } = \bar { c } = 0$ . Then 

$$
I _ {1} (y) = \frac {1}{y}, \quad I _ {2} (y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (1 / y) - 1, & 0 <   y \leq 1, \\ 0, & y \geq 1, \end{array} \right.
$$

$$
I (y; \widetilde {\Lambda}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}}{y} - 1, & 0 <   y \leq \lambda_ {2}, \\ \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{y}, & y \geq \lambda_ {2}, \end{array} \right.
$$

$$
U ^ {\prime} (c; \tilde {\Lambda}) = \mathcal {H} (c; \tilde {\Lambda}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{c}, & 0 <   c <   \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \\ \frac {\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}}{1 + c}, & c \geq \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}. \end{array} \right.
$$

In the notation of Theorem 5.6, $\begin{array} { r } { \alpha _ { 1 } = 0 , \alpha _ { 2 } = \frac { \lambda _ { 1 } } { \lambda _ { 2 } } } \end{array}$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { D } = \left\{ \frac { \lambda _ { 1 } } { \lambda _ { 2 } } \right\} } \end{array}$ . In the notation of (5.29), (5.30), 

$$
\hat {c} _ {1} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} c, & 0 <   c <   \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \\ \frac {\lambda_ {1} (1 + c)}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}}, & c \geq \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \end{array} \right.\tag{7.6}
$$

$$
\hat {c} _ {2} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} c, & 0 <   c <   \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \\ \frac {\lambda_ {2} (1 + c)}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}} - 1, & c \geq \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \end{array} \right.\tag{7.7}
$$

$$
U (c; \Lambda) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \lambda_ {1} \log c, & 0 <   c <   \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \\ (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}) \log (1 + c) + \lambda_ {1} \log \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2} + \lambda_ {2}}\right) \\ + \lambda_ {2} \log \left(\frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}}\right), & c \geq \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}, \end{array} \right.
$$

and we observe that (cf. (5.27)) 

$$
U ^ {\prime \prime} \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}} +; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}\right) - U ^ {\prime \prime} \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}} -; \underset {\sim} {\Lambda}\right) = \frac {\lambda_ {3} ^ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2})}.
$$

We set $\beta ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ . For the aggregate endowment, we take the process 

$$
\epsilon (t) = 1 + \exp \left\{W (t \wedge \tau) - \frac {1}{2} (t \wedge \tau) ^ {2} \right\}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

where $\tau \ = \ \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \ \in \ [ 0 , T ) ; W ( t ) \ = \ 1 \} \wedge T$ . Then $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ is a continuous martingale bounded strictly between 1 and $1 + e .$ , and 

$$
d \epsilon (t) = (\epsilon (t) - 1) 1 _ {\{t \leq \tau \}} d W (t), \quad \epsilon (0) = 2.
$$

This is of the form (2.2) with $\nu ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 , \xi ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ , and $\textstyle \rho ( t ) = { \frac { \epsilon ( t ) - 1 } { \epsilon ( t ) } } 1 _ { \{ t \leq \tau \} }$ Condition 2.1(iii) is satisfied. 

Because $\epsilon ( t ) > 1$ for $0 \leq t \leq T$ , almost surely, we have $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \frac { 2 \epsilon ( t ) } { 1 + \epsilon ( t ) } d t > } \end{array}$ T. Choose $\kappa \in ( 0 , 1 )$ to satisfy 

$$
\kappa \cdot E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {2 \epsilon (t)}{1 + \epsilon (t)} d t > T\tag{7.8}
$$

and set $\epsilon _ { 1 } ( t ) = \kappa \epsilon ( t ) , \epsilon _ { 2 } ( t ) = ( 1 - \kappa ) \epsilon ( t )$ , so that Condition 2.1(ii) is also satisfied. Equation (5.17) with k = 1 or 2 reduces to 

$$
\frac {T}{\kappa} = f \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\lambda_ {2}}\right),\tag{7.9}
$$

where 

$$
f (\alpha) \triangleq E \int_ {0} ^ {T} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) <   \alpha \}} d t + \left(1 + \frac {1}{\alpha}\right) \cdot E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {\epsilon (t)}{1 + \epsilon (t)} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha \}} d t.\tag{7.10}
$$

Note that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (\alpha) = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) <   \alpha \}} d t + E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(1 - \frac {1}{1 + \epsilon (t)}\right) 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha \}} d t \\ \quad + \frac {1}{\alpha} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {\epsilon (t)}{1 + \epsilon (t)} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha \}} d t \\ = T + \frac {1}{\alpha} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {(\epsilon (t) - \alpha) ^ {+}}{1 + \epsilon (t)} d t. \end{array}\tag{7.11}
$$

From (7.10) we have $\begin{array} { r } { f ( 1 ) = 2 E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \frac { \epsilon ( t ) } { 1 + \epsilon ( t ) } d t > \frac { T } { \kappa } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { f ( 1 + e ) = T < \frac { T } { \kappa } . } \end{array}$ Because f is continuous, there must exist $\alpha \in ( 1 , 1 + e )$ such that 

$$
f (\alpha) = \frac {T}{\kappa}.\tag{7.12}
$$

Let $\alpha ^ { * }$ be the smallest such α. Because $\alpha ^ { * }$ solves (7.12), (7.11) implies $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } 1 _ { \{ \epsilon ( t ) > \alpha ^ { * } \} } d t > 0 } \end{array}$ , and $f ( \alpha ) < f ( \alpha ^ { * } )$ for all $\alpha > \alpha ^ { * }$ . For $0 < \alpha < 1$ , it is apparent from (7.8) that $\begin{array} { r } { f ( \alpha ) \geq f ( 1 ) > \frac { T } { \kappa } } \end{array}$ . Therefore, $\alpha ^ { * }$ is the unique solution in $( 0 , \infty )$ to (7.12). 

From (7.9) we see that the equilibrium vector $\underset { \sim } { \Lambda } = \left( \lambda _ { 1 } , \lambda _ { 2 } \right)$ must satisfy $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \lambda _ { 1 } } { \lambda _ { 2 } } \ = \ \alpha ^ { * } } \end{array}$ . We determine $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 }$ <sup>˜</sup> individually from the normalization condition 

$$
1 = \mathcal {H} (\epsilon (0); \tilde {\Lambda}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\epsilon (0)}, & \text { if } 0 <   \epsilon (0) <   \alpha^ {*}, \\ \frac {\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}}{1 + \epsilon (0)}, & \text { if } \epsilon (0) \geq \alpha^ {*}. \end{array} \right.
$$

We have already seen that $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } 1 _ { \{ \epsilon ( t ) > \alpha ^ { * } \} } d t > 0 } \end{array}$ . We must also have $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } 1 _ { \{ \epsilon ( t ) \leq \alpha ^ { * } \} } d t > 0 } \end{array}$ , because $P [ \operatorname* { i n f } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \epsilon ( t ) = 1 ] > 0$ by construction. It follows that the process $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ crosses the level $\alpha ^ { * }$ during the interval $[ 0 , T ]$ with positive probability. Being a continuous martingale, $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ is a timechanged Brownian motion (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Section 3.4B), and hence $L _ { t } ( \alpha ^ { * } )$ increases at each t satisfying $\epsilon ( t ) \ = \ \alpha ^ { * }$ (ibid, Problem 6.13(iv)). The equilibrium market coeficient processes (6.20)–(6.22) are 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (t) = - \left[ \frac {1}{\epsilon^ {2} (t)} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) <   \alpha^ {*} \}} + \frac {1}{(1 + \epsilon (t)) ^ {2}} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha^ {*} \}} \right] (\epsilon (t) - 1) ^ {2} 1 _ {\{t \leq \tau \}}, \\ \theta (t) = \left[ \frac {1}{\epsilon (t)} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) <   \alpha^ {*} \}} + \frac {1}{1 + \epsilon (t)} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha^ {*} \}} \right] (\epsilon (t) - 1) 1 _ {\{t \leq \tau \}}, \\ A (t) = - \frac {L _ {t} (\alpha^ {*})}{\alpha^ {*} (1 + \alpha^ {*})}, \end{array}
$$

and $A ( \cdot )$ is nontrivial. According to (6.6) and (7.6), (7.7), the optimal consumption processes are 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {c} _ {1} (t) = \epsilon (t) 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) <   \alpha^ {*} \}} + \frac {\alpha^ {*} (1 + \epsilon (t))}{1 + \alpha^ {*}} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha^ {*} \}}, \\ \hat {c} _ {2} (t) = \frac {\epsilon (t) - \alpha^ {*}}{1 + \alpha^ {*}} 1 _ {\{\epsilon (t) \geq \alpha^ {*} \}}. \end{array}
$$

Example 7.8 (Ergodic aggregate endowment): Let us suppose that each agent k has utility function $U _ { k }$ with $\bar { c } _ { k } = 0$ and $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \infty , \mathtt { s o } \ \bar { c } = 0$ . Let us further suppose that the aggregate endowment process $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ is a timehomogeneous difusion on an interval $\mathcal { T } = \left( \gamma _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 2 } \right)$ with $0 < \gamma _ { 1 } < \gamma _ { 2 } < \infty ;$ i.e., 

$$
d \epsilon (t) = \epsilon (t) \nu (\epsilon (t)) d t + \epsilon (t) \rho (\epsilon (t)) d W (t),
$$

where the functions $\nu : \mathcal { T }  \mathbb { R }$ and $\rho : \mathcal { T } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ are bounded on compact subintervals of . We assume also that $\| \rho ( \cdot ) \|$ is bounded away from zero on compact subintervals of . 

We introduce the scale function 

$$
p (c) = \int_ {\gamma} ^ {c} \exp \left\{- 2 \int_ {\gamma} ^ {y} \frac {\nu (z) d z}{z \| \rho (z) \| ^ {2}} \right\} d y, \quad c \in \mathcal {I},
$$

and the speed measure 

$$
m (d c) = \frac {2 d c}{c ^ {2} \| \rho (c) \| ^ {2} p ^ {\prime} (c)}, \quad c \in \mathcal {I},
$$

where $\gamma$ is a fixed point in $\mathcal { T }$ , and assume that 

$$
p (\gamma_ {1}) = - \infty , \quad p (\gamma_ {2}) = \infty , \quad m (\mathcal {I}) <   \infty .\tag{7.13}
$$

Then the difusion process $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ is ergodic with invariant measure $m ( d c ) / m ( \mathcal { I } )$ (cf. Proposition 5.5.22 and Exercise 5.5.40 in Karatzas and Shreve (1991)). 

Finally, suppose that $\beta ( \cdot ) = \beta$ is constant. Then (6.20)–(6.22) give $A ( \cdot ) \equiv$ 0 and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (t) = \beta - \frac {1}{U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t))} \left[ U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (t)) \epsilon (t) \nu (\epsilon (t)) + \frac {1}{2} U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (\epsilon (t)) \| \rho (\epsilon (t)) \| ^ {2} \epsilon^ {2} (t) \right], \\ \theta (t) = \epsilon (t) \rho (\epsilon (t)) \left(- \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (t))}{U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t))}\right), \end{array}
$$

where $U ( \cdot ) = U ( \cdot ; \Lambda )$ is the representative agent utility function of (5.24). In particular, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (t) + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (t) \| ^ {2} = \beta - \frac {1}{2} \epsilon^ {2} (t) \| \rho (\epsilon (t)) \| ^ {2} \left[ \frac {U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t)) U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (\epsilon (t)) - (U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (t))) ^ {2}}{(U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t))) ^ {2}} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\epsilon (t))}{U ^ {\prime} (\epsilon (t))} \cdot \frac {2 \nu (\epsilon (t))}{\epsilon (t) \| \rho (\epsilon (t)) \| ^ {2}} \right], \end{array} \tag {7.14}
$$

and the maximal growth rate from investment in this market (corresponding to the “optimal logarithmic portfolio” $\hat { \pi } ( \cdot ) = ( \sigma ^ { \prime } ( \cdot ) ) ^ { - 1 } \theta ( \cdot ) \hat { X } ( \cdot )$ of (3.10.2)) is equal to the discount rate $\beta ,$ , as we show below. 

We note first from (3.10.3) that the wealth process ${ \hat { X } } ( \cdot )$ corresponding to the optimal logarithmic portfolio, regardless of the positive initial condition $\hat { X } ( 0 )$ ), satisfies 

$$
\lim _ {T \to \infty} \frac {1}{T} \log \hat {X} (T) = \lim _ {T \to \infty} \frac {1}{T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ r (s) + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (s) \| ^ {2} \right] d s,
$$

because $\theta ( \cdot )$ is bounded, which implies lim $\begin{array} { r } { \stackrel { \triangledown } { \boldsymbol { \cdot } } \infty \stackrel { 1 } { T } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \theta ^ { \prime } ( s ) d W ( s ) = 0 } \end{array}$ . The ergodic property for $\epsilon ( \cdot )$ , in conjunction with (7.13), implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {T \to \infty} \frac {1}{T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ r (s) + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (s) \| ^ {2} \right] d s \\ = \beta - \frac {1}{2 m (\mathcal {I})} \int_ {\gamma_ {1}} ^ {\gamma_ {2}} c ^ {2} \| \rho (c) \| ^ {2} \left[ \frac {U ^ {\prime} (c) U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (c) - (U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)) ^ {2}}{(U ^ {\prime} (c)) ^ {2}} + \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U ^ {\prime} (c)} \right. \\ \left. \cdot \frac {2 \nu (c)}{c \| \rho (c) \| ^ {2}} \right] m (d c) \\ = \beta - \frac {1}{m (\mathcal {I})} \int_ {\gamma_ {1}} ^ {\gamma_ {2}} \left[ \frac {U ^ {\prime} (c) U ^ {\prime \prime \prime} (c) - (U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)) ^ {2}}{(U ^ {\prime} (c)) ^ {2}} - \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U ^ {\prime} (c)} \cdot \frac {p ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{p ^ {\prime} (c)} \right] \frac {d c}{p ^ {\prime} (c)} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = \beta - \frac {1}{m (\mathcal {I})} \int_ {\gamma_ {1}} ^ {\gamma_ {2}} \left[ \left(\frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U ^ {\prime} (c)}\right) ^ {\prime} \cdot \frac {1}{p ^ {\prime} (c)} - \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U ^ {\prime} (c)} \cdot \frac {p ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{(p ^ {\prime} (c)) ^ {2}} \right] d c \\ = \beta - \frac {1}{m (\mathcal {I})} \int_ {\gamma_ {1}} ^ {\gamma_ {2}} \frac {d}{d c} \left(\frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (c)}{U ^ {\prime} (c)} \cdot \frac {1}{p ^ {\prime} (c)}\right) d c \\ = \beta - \frac {1}{m (\mathcal {I})} \left[ \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\gamma_ {2})}{U ^ {\prime} (\gamma_ {2}) p ^ {\prime} (\gamma_ {2} -)} - \frac {U ^ {\prime \prime} (\gamma_ {1})}{U ^ {\prime} (\gamma_ {1}) p ^ {\prime} (\gamma_ {1} +)} \right] = \beta , \end{array}
$$

because $p ^ { \prime } ( \gamma _ { 2 } - ) = p ^ { \prime } ( \gamma _ { 1 } + ) = \infty$ from (7.13). 

## 4.8 Notes

Models of competitive equilibrium, i.e., of the way in which demand for goods determines prices, have occupied economists for more than a century. One of the oldest works on this subject is Walras (1874/77). A mathemat ical treatment of the existence and uniqueness of solutions to Walras’s equations was given by Wald (1936), in whose work can be found an early version of the risk-aversion index condition 6.4 (see also Rothschild and Stiglitz (1971) for another use of this condition). The first complete proof for the existence of equilibrium in an economy with several agents and finitely many commodities was given by Arrow and Debreu (1954). A per spective on this and related work can be obtained from Arrow (1970, 1983), Debreu (1982), and the surveys by Debreu (1959, 1983). 

The classical reference on competitive equilibrium with an infinitedimensional commodity space is Bewley (1972). The commodity space in this work is $L _ { \infty }$ , a space whose positive orthant has nonempty interior, and this fact is necessary for the separating hyperplane argument at the heart of the paper. To remove this interiority condition, Mas-Colell (1986) introduced the concept of “uniform properness” for the preferences of agents. In the context of the model of this chapter, and with $\overline { { c } } _ { k } ~ = ~ 0$ for all $k ,$ uniform properness requires that $U _ { k } ^ { \prime } ( 0 )$ be finite for every k. A survey of equilibrium existence theory in infinite-dimensional spaces is Mas-Colell and Zame (1991). 

The models in the above papers are not explicitly either dynamic or stochastic. Models that are both stochastic and dynamic have the interest ing feature that individuals can achieve equilibrium allocations by trading in securities. This role of securities in spanning uncertainty in a complete market was already recognized by Arrow (1952). Radner (1972) established existence of equilibrium in a discrete-time dynamical market with severa agents who trade with one another. Lucas (1978) set up a discrete-time Markov model in which the optimal consumption/production of a representative agent leads to equilibrium. This work was presaged by LeRoy (1973). Prescott and Mehra (1980) extended the work of Lucas (1978) to a setup with several identical agents. The analysis of a representative agent or several identical agents leads to the consumption-based capital asset pricing model (CCAPM) of Merton (1973b), Breeden (1979), and Cox, Ingersoll, and Ross (1985a); see Remark 6.7. Empirical tests of this model performed by Breeden, Gibbons, and Litzenberger (1989) found partial agreement with data. 

The issue of existence and uniqueness of equilibrium in a continuous-time stochastic model with nonidentical (heterogeneous) agents is inherently infinite-dimensional, because consumption is indexed by both time and by the “state of nature” $\omega \in \Omega$ . Dufie (1986) gave conditions suficient for the existence of such an equilibrium, but CCAPM was not obtained because the analysis required the uniform properness condition of Mas-Colell (1986); see also Dufie and Huang (1987). Dufie and Huang (1985) showed that if a continuous-time stochastic model with heterogeneous agents has an equilibrium, then this equilibrium can be implemented by trading in securities. Huang (1987) provided conditions under which such an equilibrium leads to prices that are functions of a difusion state-process. The missing piece in this puzzle was supplied by Dufie and Zame (1989), and independently by Araujo and Monteiro (1989a,b), who provided functional-analytic proofs of the existence of equilibrium without the uniform properness condition of Mas-Colell (1986). 

The approach to the questions of existence and uniqueness of equilibrium followed in this chapter is taken from the papers Karatzas, Lehoczky, and Shreve (1990, 1991) and Karatzas, Lakner, Lehoczky, and Shreve (1991). The fundamental idea of assigning weights to the diferent agents, and thereby reducing the problem to one of finding the proper weights, was apparently first used by Negishi (1960). Other authors, including Magill (1981) and Constantinides (1982), have used this method. In the model of this chapter the Negishi method turns the infinite-dimensional problem of finding equilibrium consumption processes into the finite-dimensional problem of finding the proper weights. Extensions of this approach permit a study of equilibrium in the presence of several commodities (e.g., Lakne (1989)), of an agent who takes into account the efect ofhis actions on prices (Cuoco and Cvitani´c (1996), Ba¸sak (1996b)), of heterogeneous beliefs or information for agents (cf. Detemple (1986a,b), Detemple and Murthy (1993), Ba¸sak (1996b,c), DeMarzo and Skiadas (1996, 1997), Pikovsky (1998)), of restrictions on stock-market participation (Detemple and Murthy (1996)), Ba¸sak (1996c), Ba¸sak and Cuoco (1998), Cuoco (1997)), of stochastic differential utility (Dufie, Geofard and Skiadas (1994)), and of the efec that portfolio insurers have on the market (Ba¸sak (1993, 1995, 1996a), Grossman and Zhou (1996)). Dana and Pontier (1992) and Dana (1993a,b) have extended some of the results in Karatzas, Lehoczky, and Shreve (1990) and have cast the arguments of this chapter into more traditional economic terms. Dumas (1989) is similar to, but more detailed than, our Example 7.6. Example 7.8 grew out of conversations with Dean Foster. 

When markets are incomplete, equilibrium analysis becomes more difi cult. Hart (1975) provided an example of a discrete-time model in which equilibrium does not exist. Following this, Kreps (1982), McManus (1984), Magill and Shafer (1984), and Dufie and Shafer (1985, 1986) demonstrated that for nearly all discrete-time models, equilibrium does exist.
