and (3.35) follows. 

Finally, let us assume $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y ) \ < \ \infty$ . We define $c _ { \nu } ( t ) ~ = ~ I _ { 1 } ( t , y H _ { \nu } ( t ) )$ $B _ { \nu } = I _ { 2 } ( y H _ { \nu } ( T ) )$ -and consider for each positive integer $n \in \mathbb N$ the process $c _ { \nu } ^ { ( n ) } ( t ) = c _ { \nu } ( t ) 1 _ { \{ c _ { \nu } ( t ) \leq n \} } + 1 _ { \{ c _ { \nu } ( t ) > n \} }$ as well as the random variable $B _ { \nu } ^ { ( n ) } = B _ { \nu } 1 _ { \{ B _ { \nu } \leq n \} } + 1 _ { \{ B _ { \nu } > n \} }$ . $$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \left(E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, c _ {\nu} ^ {(n)} (t)) d t + U _ {2} (B _ {\nu} ^ {(n)}) \right] - x ^ {(n)} y\right) = \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y).\tag{3.36}

From Lemma 3.4.3 we have

$$

The last integrand is bounded from above by $\widetilde { U } _ { 1 } ( t , y H _ { \nu } ( t ) ) + | U _ { 1 } ( t , 1 ) |$ , and because $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y ) < \infty$ and (3.34) holds, $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } [ \widetilde { U } _ { 1 } ( t , y H _ { \nu } ( t ) ) + | U _ { 1 } ( t , 1 ) | ] d t < } \end{array}$ -. The integrand is bounded from below by

\min \left[ 0, \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu} (t)) d t \right] - | U _ {1} (t, 1) | - y H _ {\nu} (t),

A similar analysis shows that

Equation (3.36) is the sum of (3.37) and (3.38). 

Let the initial wealth x be strictly positive. Our strategy now is to find a process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ for which the optimal pair $\left( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } \right)$ of (3.17), (3.21) for the unconstrained Problem 3.2 is also optimal for the constrained Problem 2.6. In other words, we seek a process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ that satisfies

almost surely. Remark 3.3 shows that such a $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ should satisfy the “complementary slackness” condition

almost surely as well, so that $X ^ { x , c , p } ( T ) = X _ { \nu } ^ { x , c , p } ( T )$ almost surely. 

Proposition 3.8: Let $x > 0$ be given, and suppose for some $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ that $( { \mathcal { 3 . 4 0 } } )$ and $\left( 3 . 4 1 \right)$ are satisfied. The necessity of conditions (3.40), (3.41) for optimality in Problem 2.6, and their precise relationship to (3.39) and other equivalent conditions, will be explored in the next section. We shall see there that if we can find $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ that minimizes $V _ { \nu } ( x )$ over $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ , then the corresponding pair $\left( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } \right)$ is indeed optimal for Problem 2.6; in other words, there is no “duality gap.”

## 6.4 Equivalent Optimality Conditions

For a fixed initial capital $x > 0$ , let $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ be a consumption and portfolio proportion process pair in the class $\mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ of Problem 2.6, and denote by $\widehat { X } ( \cdot ) = X ^ { x , \widehat { c } , \widehat { p } } ( \cdot )$ the corresponding wealth process in the market ${ \mathcal { M } } ( K )$ 7Consider the statement that this pair is optimal for Problem 2.6: 

(A) Optimality of $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ : We have 

$$
V (x; K) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t + U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) \right] <   \infty .\tag{4.1}
$$

We shall characterize property (A) in terms of the following conditions $( \mathrm { B } ) { - } ( \mathrm { E } )$ , which concern a given process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ in the class $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ of (3.24). The notation of (3.16)–(3.18) will be used freely in what follows. 

(B) Financeability of $( c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) , B _ { \hat { \nu } } )$ : There exists a portfolio-proportion process $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ such that the pair $( c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) , p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) )$ is in the class $\mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ and the properties 

$$
p _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \in K, \zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) + p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t) = 0 \text { for   Lebesgue - a.e. } t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{4.2}
$$

$$
X ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (\cdot) = X _ {\hat {\nu}} (\cdot)\tag{4.3}
$$

are valid almost surely. 

(C) Minimality of $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ : We have 

$$
V _ {\hat {\nu}} (x) \leq V _ {\nu} (x), \quad \forall \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D}.\tag{4.4}
$$

(D) Dual optimality of $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ : With $y = \mathcal { V } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ , we have 

$$
\widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) \leq \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y), \quad \forall \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D}.\tag{4.5}
$$

(E) Parsimony of $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ : We have 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\nu} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\nu} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \right] \leq x, \quad \forall \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D}.\tag{4.6}
$$

The portfolio-proportion process $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ in (B) is not assumed to be given by (3.21) with $\nu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ ; this follows from (3.22), (4.3), and Remark 3.3 (see (3.13)). 

We have already encountered conditions $( \mathrm { A } ) { - } ( \mathrm { C } )$ in Proposition 3.8 and the preceding discussion. Condition (D) is the “dual” version of (C) in the sense of convex duality. Condition (E) asserts that 

$$
u (\nu) \triangleq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\nu} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\nu} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \right],\tag{4.7}
$$

the “price of the European contingent claim $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { \hat { \nu } } 1 _ { \{ t = T \} } + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( s ) d s , \ 0 \leq } \end{array}$ $t \leq T$ in the market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu } , ^ { \dag }$ attains its maximum over at $\nu \big ( \cdot \big ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ , and 

this maximum value is 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \right] = \mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (\mathcal {Y} _ {\hat {\nu}} (x)) = x.\tag{4.8}
$$

Theorem 4.1: The conditions $( B ) \mathrm { - } ( E )$ are equivalent, and imply con dition (A) with $\left( \hat { p } , \hat { c } \right) \ : = \ : \left( p _ { \hat { \nu } } , c _ { \hat { \nu } } \right)$ . Conversely, condition $( A )$ implies the existence of a process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ that satisfies $( B ) \mathrm { - } ( E )$ with $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) = \hat { p } ( \cdot )$ provided that the utility functions $U _ { 1 }$ and $U _ { 2 }$ satisfy the conditions (3.4.15), (3.6.17). 

Theorem 4.1 is the central result of this chapter. It provides necessary and suficient conditions for optimality in Problem 2.6. Its condition (D) is perhaps the most important, as it will provide the cornerstone for ou general existence theory in Section 5, based on methods from convex duality and martingale theories (Theorem 5.4). Condition (D) also underlies the computations of optimal consumption and portfolio policies in Section 6. Even without such a general existence theory, either condition (C) or (D) is suficient for a complete treatment of logarithmic utilities (see Example 4.2, 7.2, and 7.3), and condition (B) sufices for treating the important case of independent coeficients and utilities of power type (Example 7.4). The convex-duality approach also allows us to make connections with the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman theory of stochastic control in Section 6. 

The important special case of incomplete markets receives special treatment in Section 7. 

Proof of Theorem 4.1: We first prove that $( \mathrm { B } ) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { E } )$ . Assume (B) and let $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ be given. From Remark 3.3, we have 

$$
X _ {\nu} ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (t) \geq X ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (t) = X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t), 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

Condition (E) now follows from Remark 5.5.4 (recalling (2.6)) and the equality $X _ { \hat { \nu } } ( T ) = B _ { \hat { \nu } }$ 

We next prove $\left( \mathrm { E } \right) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { D } )$ . To begin, we note that (3.4.13), (3.4.14) imply 

$$
\widetilde {U} _ {2} (U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi)) + \xi U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi) = U _ {2} (\xi) \leq \widetilde {U} _ {2} (\eta) + \xi \eta , \quad \forall \xi > 0, \forall \eta > 0.\tag{4.9}
$$

Assume that $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ satisfies (E), and let $y = \mathcal { y } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ . Let $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ be given. Take $\xi = B _ { \hat { \nu } } = I _ { 2 } ( y H _ { \hat { \nu } } ( T ) )$ so that $U _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \xi ) = y H _ { \hat { \nu } } ( T )$ , and take $\eta = y H _ { \nu } ( T )$ in (4.9), which becomes 

$$
\widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) + y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \leq \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (T)) + y H _ {\nu} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}}.
$$

Similarly, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) + y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \right] d t \\ \leq \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu} (t)) + y H _ {\nu} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \right] d t. \end{array}
$$

Summing these two inequalities and taking expectations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) + y E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \right] \\ \leq \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) + y E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\nu} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\nu} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \right]. \end{array}
$$

By assumption, 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t) c _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\tilde {\nu}} (T) B _ {\tilde {\nu}} \right] \geq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\nu} (t) c _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\nu} (T) B _ {\tilde {\nu}} \right],
$$

and we conclude that (4.5) holds. 

The implications $\mathrm { ( B ) { \Rightarrow } ( A ) }$ and $\mathrm { ( B ) { \Rightarrow } ( C ) }$ are consequences of Proposition 3.8. 

$\mathrm { ( C ) } { \Rightarrow } \mathrm { ( D ) }$ : With $y = \mathcal { y } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) = V _ {\hat {\nu}} (\mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y)) - y \mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) = V _ {\hat {\nu}} (x) - x y \\ \leq V _ {\nu} (x) - x y \leq \sup _ {\xi > 0} [ V _ {\nu} (\xi) - \xi y ] \leq \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) \end{array}
$$

from (3.25), (3.27), and Proposition 3.7. 

$\mathrm { ( D ) \Rightarrow ( B ) }$ : Assume (D), and let $c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) , p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ be given by (3.17) and (3.21), respectively. The corresponding wealth process $X _ { \hat { \nu } } ^ { x , c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } } ( \cdot )$ in the market $\mathcal { M } _ { \hat { \nu } }$ is defined by the equivalent equations $( 3 . 1 ) \mathrm { - } ( 3 . 3 )$ , where we replace $c ( \cdot )$ by $c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ and $p ( \cdot )$ by $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ . In light of (3.22), we have 

$$
X _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (\cdot) = X _ {\hat {\nu}} (\cdot),\tag{4.10}
$$

where the latter is given by (3.18) with $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ replacing $\nu ( \cdot )$ . We divide the remainder of the proof into six steps. 

Step 1. For any $\boldsymbol { \mu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ and any $\epsilon \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , 1 )$ , the convex combination $( 1 - \epsilon ) \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) + \epsilon \mu ( \cdot )$ is in $\mathcal { D } ,$ , because of the convexity of $\widetilde { K }$ and the positive homogeneity and subadditivity of $\zeta ( \cdot )$ -(see (5.4.3), (5.4.4)), which guarantee that $( 1 - \epsilon ) \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) + \epsilon \mu ( \cdot )$ satisfies (5.5.2). We shall be interested in two particular choices of $\mu ( \cdot )$ . The first is $\mu ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ , which is an element of $\mathcal { D }$ because $0 \in \tilde { K }$ and $\zeta ( 0 ) = 0$ . The other is $\mu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) + \lambda ( \cdot )$ for some $\lambda ( \cdot ) \in { \mathcal { D } }$ -; this process $\mu ( \cdot )$ is in $\mathcal { D }$ because $\widetilde { K }$ is a convex cone and thus closed under addition, and $\zeta ( \cdot )$ -is subadditive. 

Let $\{ \tau _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a nondecreasing sequence of stopping times converging up to $T _ { : }$ , and consider the small random perturbation of $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \nu_ {\epsilon , n} (t) \stackrel {{\Delta}} {{=}} \hat {\nu} (t) + \epsilon (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) 1 _ {\{t \leq \tau_ {n} \}} \\ = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (t) + \epsilon \mu (t), & 0 \leq t \leq \tau_ {n}, \\ \hat {\nu} (t), & \tau_ {n} <   t \leq T. \end{array} \right. \end{array}
$$

Because $\nu _ { \epsilon , n } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ and $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ minimizes $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y )$ over $\mathcal { D }$ , we must have 

$$
0 \leq E Y _ {\epsilon , n} = \frac {\widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (y) - \widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y)}{\epsilon y}, \quad \forall \epsilon \in (0, 1), n = 1, 2, \dots ,\tag{4.11}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {\epsilon , n} \triangleq \frac {1}{\epsilon y} \left[ \left\{\widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (T)) - \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) \right\} \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left\{\widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (t)) - \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) \right\} d t \right]. \end{array}\tag{4.12}
$$

Step 2. A straightforward computation using (5.5.7) and (5.5.10)–(5.5.12) shows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Lambda_ {\epsilon , n} (t) \triangleq \frac {H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (t)}{H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)} \\ = \exp \left[ - \epsilon N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) - \frac {\epsilon^ {2}}{2} \langle N \rangle (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) \right. \\ \left. - \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}} \big (\zeta ((1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (s) + \epsilon \mu (s)) - \zeta (\hat {\nu} (s)) \big) d s \right], \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{c} N (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \big (\sigma^ {- 1} (s) (\mu (s) - \hat {\nu} (s)) \big) ^ {\prime} d W _ {\hat {\nu}} (s), \\ \langle N \rangle (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \sigma^ {- 1} (s) (\mu (s) - \hat {\nu} (s)) \| ^ {2} d s. \end{array}
$$

In the case $\mu ( \cdot ) = 0$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \zeta \left((1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (s) + \epsilon \mu (s)\right) - \zeta \left(\hat {\nu} (s)\right) = \zeta ((1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (s)) - \zeta (\hat {\nu} (s)) \\ = - \epsilon \zeta (\hat {\nu} (s)), \end{array}
$$

whereas in the case $\mu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) + \lambda ( \cdot )$ for some $\lambda ( \cdot ) \in { \mathcal { D } }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \zeta \left((1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (s) + \epsilon \mu (s)\right) - \zeta \left(\hat {\nu} (s)\right) = \zeta \left(\hat {\nu} (s) + \epsilon \lambda (s)\right) - \zeta \left(\hat {\nu} (s)\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \epsilon \zeta (\lambda (s)). \end{array}
$$

If we define 

$$
\xi (s) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - \zeta (\hat {\nu} (s)), & \text { if } \mu (\cdot) = 0, \\ \zeta (\lambda (s)), & \text { if } \mu (\cdot) = \hat {\nu} (\cdot) + \lambda (\cdot) \text { for some } \lambda (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D}, \end{array} \right.
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { L ( t ) \triangleq \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \xi ( s ) d s } \end{array}$ , we obtain the lower bound 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Lambda_ {\epsilon , n} (t) \geq Q _ {\epsilon , n} (t) \\ \stackrel {{\Delta}} {{=}} \exp \left\{- \epsilon (N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) + L (t \wedge \tau_ {n})) - \frac {\epsilon^ {2}}{2} \langle N \rangle (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) \right\}. \end{array}\tag{4.13}
$$

Step 3. For each positive integer n, we introduce the stopping time 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {n} \triangleq \inf \left\{t \in [ 0, T ]; | N (t) | + \langle N \rangle (t) + | L (t) | \geq n \right. \\ \quad \text {or} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \theta_ {\hat {\nu}} (s) \| ^ {2}   d s \geq n \\ \quad \text {or} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(\frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (s)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (s)}\right) ^ {2} \| \sigma^ {- 1} (s) (\mu (s) - \hat {\nu} (s)) \| ^ {2}   d s \geq n \\ \quad \text {or} \int_ {0} ^ {t} (L (s) + N (s)) ^ {2} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (s) p _ {\hat {\nu}} (s) \| ^ {2}   d s \geq n \Bigg \} \wedge T. \end{array}
$$

Clearly, $\tau _ { n } \uparrow T$ almost surely as $n  \infty$ . According to the Girsanov and Novikov theorems (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), 3.5), the process 

$$
W _ {\hat {\nu}, n} (t) \triangleq W (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}} \theta_ {\hat {\nu}} (s) d s, 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

is Brownian motion under the probability measure 

$$
P _ {\hat {\nu}, n} (A) \triangleq E [ Z _ {\hat {\nu}} (\tau_ {n}) 1 _ {A} ], A \in \mathcal {F} (T).
$$

With this choice of $\tau _ { n }$ , the process $Q _ { \epsilon , n } ( \cdot )$ of (4.13) admits the lower bound 

$$
Q _ {\epsilon , n} (t) \geq e ^ {- \epsilon n}, 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

and consequently, 

$$
\frac {1}{\epsilon} \left(1 - \frac {H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (t)}{H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}\right) = \frac {1 - \Lambda_ {\epsilon , n} (t)}{\epsilon} \leq K _ {n}, 0 \leq t \leq T\tag{4.14}
$$

holds almost surely, where $\begin{array} { r } { K _ { n } \stackrel { \Delta } { = } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 < \epsilon < 1 } \frac { 1 } { \epsilon } ( 1 - e ^ { - \epsilon n } ) } \end{array}$ is finite. Furthermore, 

$$
\varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1 - \Lambda_ {\epsilon , n} (t)}{\epsilon} \leq N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) + L (t \wedge \tau_ {n}).
$$

Step 4. The functions $- \widetilde { U } _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ and $- \widetilde { U } _ { 1 } ( t , \cdot )$ have derivatives $I _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ and $I _ { 1 } ( t , \cdot )$ - -, respectively, and these derivatives are nonincreasing functions (Section 3.4). For $U _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ we have the inequality 

$$
\widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (T)) - \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) \leq y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) I _ {2} (y e ^ {- n} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) (1 - \Lambda_ {\epsilon , n} (T)) ^ {+}.
$$

From (4.14), we see that 

$$
\frac {1}{\epsilon} [ \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (T)) - \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) ] \leq Y _ {n, 2} \stackrel {\Delta} {=} K _ {n} y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) I _ {2} (y e ^ {- n} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T))
$$

and also that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1}{\epsilon} [ \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (T)) - \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) ] & = y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) I _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) [ N (\tau_ {n}) + L (\tau_ {n}) ] \\ & \leq y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} [ N (\tau_ {n}) + L (\tau_ {n}) ]. \end{array} \tag {4.15}
$$

Because $E Y _ { n , 2 } \leq K _ { n } y \mathcal { X } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( y e ^ { - n } )$ , which is finite by the assumption $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in$ $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ , we may apply Fatou’s lemma in (4.15) to conclude that 

$$
\varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} E \frac {1}{\epsilon} [ \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {\epsilon , n}} (T)) - \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) ] \leq y E \left\{H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} [ N (\tau_ {n}) + L (\tau_ {n}) ] \right\}.\tag{4.16}
$$

We proceed similarly with the diference 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu} _ {\epsilon , n}} (t)) - \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) \right] d t
$$

to obtain in the end, by analogy with (4.16), that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1}{\epsilon} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} [ \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu} _ {\epsilon , n}} (t)) - \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) ] d t \\ \qquad \leq y E \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) + L (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) ]   d t \right\}. \end{array}\tag{4.17}
$$

Finally, from (4.11) and (4.12) we have 

$$
E \left\{H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} [ N (\tau_ {n}) + L (\tau_ {n}) ] + \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) + L (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) ] d t \right\}\tag{4.18}
$$

Step 5. We next prove that 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) + \xi (t) ] d t \geq 0, n = 1, 2, \dots .\tag{4.19}
$$

To see this, we first recall from (4.10) and (3.1) that 

$$
d \left(\frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)}\right) + \frac {c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} = \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \sigma (t) d W _ {\hat {\nu}} (t),
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \left(\frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} (L (t) + N (t))\right) \\ = \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} (d L (t) + d N (t)) + (L (t) + N (t)) d \left(\frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)}\right) \\ + \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) d t. \end{array}
$$

Integration of this equation yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (\tau_ {n})}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (\tau_ {n})} (L (\tau_ {n}) + N (\tau_ {n})) + \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} \frac {L (t) + N (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)   d t \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) + \xi (t) ]   d t \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} \frac {X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)} [ \sigma^ {- 1} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) \\ \qquad + (L (t) + N (t)) \sigma^ {\prime} (t) p _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) ] ^ {\prime}   d W _ {\hat {\nu}} (t). \end{array}
$$

By the choice of $\tau _ { n }$ , the integrand of the Itˆo integral in this last expression is square-integrable, and thus has expectation zero under $P _ { \hat { \nu } , n }$ . Taking expectations under this probability measure, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) + \xi (t) ] d t \\ = E \left[ (L (\tau_ {n}) + N (\tau_ {n})) H _ {\hat {\nu}} (\tau_ {n}) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (\tau_ {n}) + \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) (L (t) + N (t)) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t \right]. \end{array} \tag {4.20}
$$

An application of the optional sampling theorem to the martingale of (3.19) shows that (3.18) is still valid if we replace t in that equation by the stopping time $\tau _ { n }$ . Using this fact, we rewrite (4.20) as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) (\mu (t) - \hat {\nu} (t)) + \xi (t) ] d t \\ = E \left[ (L (\tau_ {n}) + N (\tau_ {n})) \left(H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} + \int_ {\tau_ {n}} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t\right) \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) (L (t) + N (t)) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t \right], \end{array}
$$

which is the left-hand side of (4.18), hence a nonnegative quantity. Thi completes the proof of (4.19). 

Step 6. We invoke Lemma 5.4.2 to obtain a process $\lambda ( \cdot ) \in { \mathcal { D } }$ satisfying (5.4.8) with $p ( \cdot ) = p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ , and take $\mu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) + \lambda ( \cdot )$ so that $\xi ( \cdot ) = \zeta ( \lambda ( \cdot ) )$ The inequality (4.19) becomes 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \lambda (t) + \zeta (\lambda (t)) ] d t \geq 0, n = 1, 2, \dots ,
$$

which, together with (5.4.8), implies 

$$
p _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \in K \text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{4.21}
$$

almost surely. From (5.4.5) we have also that 

$$
\zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) + p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t) \geq 0 \text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ]
$$

almost surely. We next take $\mu ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ , so that $\xi ( \cdot ) = - \zeta ( \hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) )$ , and (4.19) becomes 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) [ p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t) + \zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) ] d t \leq 0, n = 1, 2, \dots ,
$$

which proves 

$$

## 6.5 Duality and Existence

We now turn to the dual optimization problem associated with the “primal” constrained Problem 2.6. The dual problem is, for fixed $y > 0$ , to minimize $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y )$ over $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ , and its value function is defined by 

$$
\widetilde {V} (y) \triangleq \inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {D}} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y), 0 <   y <   \infty ,\tag{5.1}
$$

in the notation of (3.27), (3.33). This problem is suggested by condition (D) preceding Theorem 4.1, which amounts to $\widetilde V ( y ) = \widetilde V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( y )$ for some $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ and $y = \mathcal { y } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ - -. The terminology “dual” comes from the fact that, as we shall show in Propositions 5.1 and 5.2 below, the value function $\widetilde V ( \cdot )$ of (5.1) is the convex dual of the concave function $V ( \cdot ; K )$ -of (2.16), in the sense of Definition 3.4.2. 

We shall assume throughout this section that 

$$
\widetilde {V} (y) <   \infty , 0 <   y <   \infty .\tag{5.2}
$$

Our plan in this section is to show that under reasonable conditions, for any given $y > 0$ , the dual problem (5.1) has a minimizer $\nu _ { y } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 } ; \mathrm { i . e . }$ , 

$$
\forall y \in (0, \infty), \exists \nu_ {y} (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D} _ {0} \text { such   that } \widetilde {V} (y) = \widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {y}} (y)\tag{5.3}
$$

(see Theorem 5.3, whose proof occupies a good part of this section). We can then argue that in conjunction with Theorem 4.1, this solution implies the existence of an optimal consumption and portfolio-proportion pair for the “primal” Problem 2.6 (see Theorem 5.4). 

Proposition 5.1 (Weak Duality): Suppose $( 5 . 2 )$ and $( 5 . 3 )$ hold. Then, for any given $y \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and with $x = \mathcal { X } _ { \nu _ { y } } ( y )$ 

(i) there exists an optimal consumption and portfolio-proportion process pair $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ for Problem 2.6, and 

(ii) we have 

$$

$$

Now fix $y \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , let $x = \mathcal { X } _ { \nu _ { y } } ( y )$ , and note that the assumption $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu _ { y } } ( y ) \leq$ $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y )$ for all $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ of (5.3) amounts to (4.5) with $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) = \nu _ { y } ( \cdot )$ . By (3.17), (3.22), (3.18), and (3.16),

Theorem 5.3 (Existence in the dual problem): Suppose that (5.2) holds, and that the utility functions $U _ { 1 } ( t , \cdot ) , U _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ satisfy

Theorem 5.4 (Existence in the primal problem): Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.3 we have $V ( x ; K ) < \infty$ for every $x \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , and there exists an optimal pair $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ for Problem ${ \it 2 . 6 } .$ . The conditions (5.11), (5.12) exclude logarithmic utility functions; for these, however, we have the direct arguments and explicit computations presented in Example 4.2, and thus need not appeal to general existence results.

For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { H }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) \geq E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- \log \frac {1}{Z _ {\nu} (t)} \right\}\right) d t \\ \qquad + E \widetilde {U} _ {2} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- \log \frac {1}{Z _ {\nu} (T)} \right\}\right) \\ \geq \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- E \log \frac {1}{Z _ {\nu} (t)} \right\}\right) d t \\ \qquad + \widetilde {U} _ {2} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- E \log \frac {1}{Z _ {\nu} (T)} \right\}\right) \\ \geq \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2} E \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \theta_ {\nu} (s) \| ^ {2}   d s \right\}\right) d t \\ \qquad + \widetilde {U} _ {2} \left(\frac {y}{s _ {0}} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \theta_ {\nu} (s) \| ^ {2}   d s \right\}\right). \end{array}
$$

As $[ \nu ] \to \infty$ , condition (5.2.4) implies that $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \theta _ { \nu } ( s ) \| ^ { 2 } d s \to \infty } \end{array}$ . But $\widetilde { U } _ { 2 } ( 0 + ) = U _ { 2 } ( \infty ) = \infty$ , and (5.17) follows. 

Finally, let $\{ \nu _ { n } ( \cdot ) \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence in $\mathcal { H }$ converging to a limit $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { H }$ in the norm of Definition 5.5.1. We may extract a subsequence $\{ \nu _ { n _ { k } } ( \cdot ) \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ for which 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (y) = \underline {{\lim}} _ {n \to \infty} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {n}} (y),
$$

and we seek to show that 

$$
\widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) \leq \lim _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (y).\tag{5.19}
$$

Consider the martingales 

$$
M _ {\nu_ {n}} (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \theta_ {\nu_ {n}} (s) d W (s), 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

According to the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Theorem 3.3.28), 

$$
E \left[ \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} | M _ {\nu_ {n}} (t) - M _ {\nu} (t) | ^ {2} \right] \leq \kappa E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \theta_ {\nu_ {n}} (s) - \theta_ {\nu (s)} \| ^ {2} d s
$$

for some constant κ, and the right-hand side approaches zero as $n  \infty$ Therefore, we may choose a further subsequence, also labeled $\{ \nu _ { n _ { k } } ( \cdot ) \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ along which we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \nu_ {n _ {k}} (t) = \nu (t) \text {for Lebesgue - a.e.} t \in [ 0, T ], \\ \lim _ {k \to \infty} \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} | Z _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t) - Z _ {\nu} (t) | = 0 \end{array}
$$

almost surely. These equalities and the lower semicontinuity of $\zeta ( \cdot )$ imply 

$$
\overline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t) \leq H _ {\nu} (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

almost surely. Because $\widetilde { U } _ { 1 } ( t , \cdot )$ and $\widetilde { U } _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ are nondecreasing and continuous on $( 0 , \infty )$ - -, we have the almost sure inequalities 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t)) \geq \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu} (t)), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,} \\ & {\underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (T)) \geq \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (T)).} \end{array}
$$

Moreover, (5.14), (5.15), and Fatou’s lemma give us 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (y) \\ = \lim _ {k \to \infty} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t))   d t + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (T)) \right] \\ \geq \underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t))   d t + \underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} E \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (T)) \\ \geq E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (t))   d t + E \left[ \underline {{\lim}} _ {k \to \infty} \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu_ {n _ {k}}} (T)) \right] \\ \geq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\nu} (t))   d t + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (T)) \right] = \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y). \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 5.3: Let $y > 0$ be given. From Lemma 5.6 and Proposition 2.12 in Ekeland and Temam (1976), the convex, coercive, and lower-semicontinuous functional $\mathcal { H } \ni \nu \mapsto \widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( y ) \in ( - \infty , \infty ]$ attains its infimum on the Hilbert space $\mathcal { H } \colon$ 

$$
\inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {H}} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) = \widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) \text { for some} \hat {\nu} (\cdot) \in \mathcal {H}.
$$

According to Remark 5.5 and (5.2), $\widetilde V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( y ) = \widetilde V ( y ) < \infty$ , so $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ must be in . It remains to show that $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ - -actually belongs to the class $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ of (3.24). 

The finiteness of $\widetilde { V } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( y )$ and the inequality (3.35) show that $V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x ) < \infty$ for all $x > 0$ -. It remains to check that 

$$
\mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (\eta) <   \infty , \forall \eta > 0.\tag{5.20}
$$

From the decrease of $\widetilde { U }$ , (3.4.12), the decrease of I, and (3.6.17) (in particular, $( 3 . 4 . 1 6 ^ { \prime \prime } ) )$ -, we have

\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {U} (\eta) - \widetilde {U} (\infty) \geq \widetilde {U} (\eta) - \widetilde {U} \left(\frac {\eta}{\beta}\right) = \int_ {\eta} ^ {\frac {\eta}{\beta}} I (u) d u} \\ & {\qquad \geq \left(\frac {\eta}{\beta} - \eta\right) I \left(\frac {\eta}{\beta}\right)} \\ & {\qquad \geq \frac {1 - \beta}{\beta \gamma} \eta I (\eta), 0 <   \eta <   \infty ,} \end{array}
$$

where $\beta \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , 1 )$ and $\gamma \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 1 , \infty )$ are as in $\left( 3 . 4 . 1 6 ^ { \prime \prime } \right)$ , and $\widetilde U ( \cdot )$ stands generically for $\tilde { U } ( t , \cdot )$ and $ { \widetilde { U } } _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ . Consequently, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} y \mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) I _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t))   d t + y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) I _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) \right] \\ \leq \frac {\beta \gamma}{1 - \beta} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t))   d t + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) \right. \\ \left. - \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, \infty) + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (\infty)\right) \right] \\ \leq \frac {\beta \gamma}{1 - \beta} \left[ \widetilde {V} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y) - \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, 0)   d t + U _ {2} (0)\right) \right] <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality is a consequence of (5.14) and (5.15). This proves (5.20) for $\eta = y$ (but not for all $\eta > 0$ , because $\hat { \nu }$ depends on $y )$ . Assumption $( 3 . 6 . 1 7 ^ { \prime \prime } )$ (see the sentence following that assumption) now implies that (5.20) holds for all $\eta > 0$ ␀ 

Remark 5.7: It can be checked rather easily that utility functions of the form 

$$
U _ {1} (t, x) = \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {- \alpha t} x ^ {\beta}, U _ {2} (x) = \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {- \alpha T} x ^ {\beta}, 0 \leq t \leq T, x > 0,
$$

where $\alpha \geq 0$ and $0 < \beta < 1$ , satisfy all the conditions of Theorems 5.3 and 5.4. 

Remark 5.8: The theory of Sections 2–5 goes through without change if one sets formally $U _ { 1 } \equiv 0$ and admits only the identically zero con sumption process throughout. This leads to the problem of maximizing the expected utility from terminal wealth only. On the other hand, the condition $U _ { 2 } ( \infty ) = \infty$ was used extensively in this section. The situation with regard to existence of optimal solutions when $U _ { 2 } \equiv 0$ is not well understood. 

## 6.6 Deterministic Coeficients, Cone Constraints

In this section, we consider Problem 2.6 and its dual under the assumption that $r ( \cdot ) , \theta ( \cdot )$ , and $\sigma ( \cdot )$ are continuous, deterministic functions; $A ( \cdot ) \equiv 0 ;$ and the constraint set K is a cone. The analysis proceeds through a study of the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equations, and for this we use the conditions placed on utility functions in Section 3.8 rather than conditions (3.4.15), (3.6.17) used in the previous section of this chapter. In particular, all functions $U ^ { ( \beta ) } ( x )$ given by (3.4.4), (3.4.5) are included, not just those for which $0 < \beta < 1$ . (We use $\beta$ for the exponent in place of $p$ throughout this chapter, reserving the symbol $p ( \cdot )$ for portfolio-proportion processes.) 

More specifically, we assume in this section that Assumptions 3.8.1, 3.8.2 hold, and, in addition, the following condition is satisfied. 

Assumption 6.1: The process $\sigma ( \cdot )$ is nonrandom, $\sigma ( t )$ is nonsingular for every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , and $\sigma ( \cdot )$ is H¨older-continuous, i.e., for some $\kappa > 0$ and $\rho \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , we have 

$$
\left\| \sigma \left(t _ {1}\right) - \sigma \left(t _ {2}\right) \right\| \leq \kappa \left| t _ {1} - t _ {2} \right| ^ {\rho}, \forall t _ {1}, t _ {2} \in [ 0, T ].
$$

In particular, $\sigma ( \cdot )$ and $\sigma ^ { - 1 } ( \cdot )$ are both bounded, and $\sigma ^ { - 1 } ( \cdot )$ is also H¨oldercontinuous. 

Assumption 6.2: The constraint set K is a nonempty closed convex cone. 

From Assumption 6.2 we see that $\widetilde { K }$ is the polar cone of $- K$ , which is necessarily closed. $\mathrm { O n } \ : \widetilde { K }$ -, the support function $\zeta ( \cdot )$ is identically zero (Rock--afellar (1970), Theorem 14.1). From Assumption 3.8.1 we have the validity of (2.4) and (2.5). Conditions (2.13) and (2.14) are assumed throughout this chapter, including in the present section. 

Our aim is to study the time-dependent generalization of Problem 2.6 via the time-dependent generalization of Problem 3.2. Toward that end, for $0 \leq$ $t \leq T , x \geq 0$ and with $( c ( \cdot ) , p ( \cdot ) )$ a consumption and portfolio-proportion process pair, we define the corresponding wealth process $X ^ { t , x , c , p } ( s ) , t \leq$ $s \leq T$ , by 

$$
\frac {X ^ {t , x , c , p} (s)}{S _ {0} (s)} + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \frac {c (u) d u}{S _ {0} (u)} = x + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \frac {X ^ {t , x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u)
$$

(cf. (2.7)). The process $X ^ { t , x , c , p } ( \cdot )$ reaches zero no later than the stopping time 

$$
\tau_ {t, p} \triangleq \inf \left\{s \in [ t, T ]; \int_ {t} ^ {s} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (u) p (u) \| ^ {2} d u = \infty \right\}
$$

(cf.(2.9)). We set 

$$
\tau_ {t, 0} \stackrel {\Delta} {=} \inf \left\{s \in [ t, T ]; X ^ {t, x, c, p} (s) = 0 \right\},
$$

and define $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A } } ( t , \boldsymbol { x } ; K )$ to be the set of all consumption and portfolio-process pairs $( c ( \cdot ) , p ( \cdot ) )$ that satisfy the almost sure conditions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} c (s) = 0, \text {   Lebesgue - a.e.   } s \in [ \tau_ {t, 0}, T ], \\ p (s) \in K, \text {   Lebesgue - a.e.   } s \in [ t, T ]. \end{array}
$$

Following (2.15), (2.16), we set 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {A} _ {3} (t, x; K) \triangleq \left\{(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} _ {3} (t, x; K); E \int_ {t} ^ {T} \min [ 0, U _ {1} (s, c (s)) ] d s > - \infty , \right. \\ \left. E \left(\min [ 0, U _ {2} (X ^ {t, x, c, p} (T)) ]\right) > - \infty \right\} \end{array}
$$

and define the time-dependent value function 

$$
V (t, x; K) \triangleq \sup _ {(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} (t, x; K)} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} U _ {1} (s, c (s)) d s + U _ {2} (X ^ {t, x, c, p} (T)) \right].\tag{6.1}
$$

We show below that the function $V ( \cdot , \cdot ; K ) \ : \ [ 0 , T ] \times ( 0 , \infty ) \ \to \ \mathbb { R }$ of (6.1) is continuous and satisfies the constrained Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation (see Theorem 3.8.11 for the unconstrained case) 

$$
\begin{array}{l}V_{t}(t,x;K) + \max_{\substack{0\leq c <   \infty \\ p\in K}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{2}\| \sigma^{\prime}(t)p\|^{2}x^{2}V_{xx}(t,x;K)\\ \\ \qquad + (r(t)x - c + xp^{\prime}\sigma (t)\theta (t))  V_{x}(t,x;K) + U_{1}(t,c)\Bigg] = 0 \end{array}\tag{6.2}
$$

for $0 \leq t \leq T , x > 0$ . By definition, $V ( \cdot , \cdot ; K )$ satisfies the boundary conditions 

$$
V (t, x; K) = U _ {2} (x), \quad x > 0,\tag{6.3}
$$

$$
V (t, 0; K) = \int_ {t} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, 0) d t + U _ {2} (0), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{6.4}
$$

We approach the constrained HJB equation through the dual problem. For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } , t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , and $x \geq 0$ , we determine $X _ { \nu } ^ { t , x , c , p } ( \cdot )$ by the equation (cf. (3.1)) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {X _ {\nu} ^ {t , x , c , p} (s)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\nu)} (s)} + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \frac {c (u) d u}{S _ {0} ^ {(\nu)} (u)} = x + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \frac {X _ {\nu} ^ {t , x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\nu)} (u)} p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {\nu} (u), \\ t \leq s \leq T, \end{array}
$$

or its equivalent variations similar to (3.2) and (3.3). We define $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A } } _ { \nu } ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ to be the set of all consumption and portfolio-process pairs $( c , p )$ for which 

$$
c (s) = 0, \mathrm{Lebesgue-a.e.} s \in [ \tau_ {t, \nu}, T ]
$$

almost surely, where 

$$
\tau_ {t, \nu} = \inf \left\{s \in [ t, T ]; X _ {\nu} ^ {t, x, c, p} (s) = 0 \right\}.
$$

Following (3.5), (3.6), we set 

$$
\mathcal {A} _ {3} ^ {(\nu)} (t, x) \triangleq \left\{(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} _ {\nu} (t, x); E \int_ {t} ^ {T} \min [ 0, U _ {1} (s, c (s)) ] d s > - \infty , \right.
$$

$$
\left. E \left(\min [ 0, U _ {2} (X _ {\nu} ^ {t, x, c, p} (T)) ]\right) > - \infty \right\},
$$

$$
V _ {\nu} (t, x) \triangleq \sup _ {(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} _ {3} ^ {(\nu)} (t, x)} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} U _ {1} (s, c (s)) d s + U _ {2} (X _ {\nu} ^ {t, x, c, p} (T)) \right].\tag{6.5}
$$

For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ and $t ~ \in ~ [ 0 , T ]$ , we introduce the processes with time parameter $s \in [ t , T ]$ , 

$$
Z _ {\nu} (t, s) \triangleq \frac {Z _ {\nu} (s)}{Z _ {\nu} (t)} = \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {s} \theta_ {\nu} ^ {\prime} (u) d W (u) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {s} \| \theta_ {\nu} (u) \| ^ {2} d u \right\},
$$

$$
H _ {\nu} (t, s) \triangleq \frac {H _ {\nu} (s)}{H _ {\nu} (t)} = \exp \left\{- \int_ {t} ^ {s} r (u) \right\} Z _ {\nu} (t, s).
$$

The nonnegative function 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (t, y) \triangleq E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} H _ {\nu} (t, s) I _ {1} (s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s)) d s + H _ {\nu} (t, T) I _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (t, T)) \right], \\ 0 \leq t \leq T, y > 0, \end{array} \tag {6.}\tag{6.6}
$$

is finite if $\nu ( \cdot )$ is in the set $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ of $( 3 . 2 4 )$ . In this case, $\textstyle { \mathcal { X } } _ { \nu } ( t , \cdot )$ is a strictly de creasing function mapping $( 0 , \infty ) \ o n t o \ ( 0 , \infty )$ and has a strictly decreasing inverse $y _ { \nu } ( t , \cdot )$ , likewise mapping $( 0 , \infty )$ onto $( 0 , \infty )$ 

For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ we have, just as in Remark 3.6, that 

$$
V _ {\nu} (t, x) = G _ {\nu} (t, \mathcal {Y} _ {\nu} (t, x)), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, x > 0,\tag{6.7}
$$

where 

$$
G _ {\nu} (t, y) \triangleq E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} U _ {1} \left(I _ {1} \left(s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s)\right)\right) d s + U _ {2} \left(I _ {2} \left(y H _ {\nu} (t, T)\right)\right) \right].\tag{6.8}
$$

Furthermore, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (t, y) \triangleq \sup _ {x > 0} [ V _ {\nu} (t, x) - x y ] \\ \quad = G _ {\nu} (t, y) - y \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (t, y) \\ \quad = E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s)) d s + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (t, T)) \right] \\ <   \infty , \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, y > 0 \end{array}\tag{6.9}
$$

(cf. (3.27)), and for $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } \setminus \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ , we follow (3.33) and define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (t, y) \triangleq E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} \widetilde {U} _ {1} (s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s))   d s + \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (t, T)) \right], \\ y > 0, \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D} \setminus \mathcal {D} _ {0}. \end{array}\tag{6.10}
$$

Proposition 3.7 can be adapted to the time-dependent case to ensure that 

$$
E \int_ {t} ^ {T} \min [ 0, \widetilde {U} _ {1} (s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s)) ] d s > - \infty , E (\min [ 0, \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (t, T)) ]) > - \infty ,
$$

and hence 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} | \widetilde {U} _ {1} (s, y H _ {\nu} (t, s)) | d s + | \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (t, T)) | \right] <   \infty\tag{6.11}
$$

if $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( t , y ) < \infty$ . Also, as in (3.35), $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( t , y ) < \infty$ implies 

$$
\sup _ {x > 0} [ V _ {\nu} (t, x) - x y ] = \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y).\tag{6.12}
$$

From the theory of Section 6.5—in particular, from (5.4)—we expect 

$$
\widetilde {V} (t, y) \triangleq \inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {D}} \widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (t, y)\tag{6.13}
$$

to be the convex dual of the function $V ( t , \cdot ; K )$ in (6.1), i.e., 

$$
\widetilde {V} (t, y) = \sup _ {\xi > 0} [ V (t, \xi ; K) - \xi y ], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, y > 0.\tag{6.14}
$$

From Theorem 3.8.12, we also expect $\widetilde { V }$ to satisfy a linear partial diferential -equation, which turns out to be (cf. (3.8.44)) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {V} _ {t} (t, y) + \frac {1}{2} \min _ {\nu \in \widetilde {K}} \| \theta (t) + \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \nu \| ^ {2} y ^ {2} \widetilde {V} _ {y y} (t, y) - r (t) y \widetilde {V} _ {y} (t, y) + \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y) \\ = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, y > 0, \end{array} \tag {6.1}\tag{6.15}
$$

as well as the terminal condition 

$$
\widetilde {V} (T, y) = \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y), y > 0.\tag{6.16}
$$

Our program then is to construct $\widetilde { V }$ via (6.15), (6.16) and in the process to obtain the minimizer $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ -in (6.13). Then, just as in Theorem 4.1, we discover that when $\nu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ in (6.5), the maximizing $( c , p ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ^ { ( \hat { \nu } ) } ( t , x )$ is optimal in (6.1). Finally, we prove (6.14), (6.2) and obtain the optimal $( c , p )$ for Problem 2.6 in feedback form. 

We begin this program with a study of the minimization appearing in (6.15). Given $\epsilon > 0$ , let $L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ denote the set of $N \times N$ nonsingular matrices $\sigma$ whose operator norm 

$$
\| \sigma \| \stackrel {\Delta} {=} \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}, \| x \| = 1} \| \sigma x \|
$$

satisfies $\| \sigma \| \geq \epsilon$ . Then $\| \sigma ^ { - 1 } \| \leq \frac { 1 } { \epsilon }$ for every $\sigma \in L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ . Recall from (5.2.4) that we have assumed $\sigma ( \mathsf { \bar { t } } ) \in L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ for all $0 \leq t \leq T$ for suficiently small $\epsilon > 0$ . Define the function 

$$
h (\theta , \sigma) \stackrel {\Delta} {=} \inf _ {\nu \in \widetilde {K}} \| \theta + \sigma^ {- 1} \nu \|
$$

mapping R ${ \mathbf { \mathbb { N } } \times L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ) }$ to $[ 0 , \infty )$ . Lemma 6.3: The function $h \colon \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \times L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ) \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is locally Lipschitz continuous. 

Proof. For $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $\sigma _ { 1 } , \sigma _ { 2 } \in L _ { \epsilon } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| \Upsilon (\theta , \sigma) \| \leq \| \sigma \theta + \Upsilon (\theta , \sigma) \| + \| - \sigma \theta \|} \\ & {\quad \leq \| \sigma \| \| \theta + \sigma^ {- 1} \Upsilon (\theta , \sigma) \| + \| \sigma \| \| \theta \|} \\ & {\quad = \| \sigma \| (h (\theta , \sigma) + \| \theta \|)} \\ & {\quad \leq 2 \| \sigma \| \| \theta \|.} \end{array}

$$

and reversing the roles of $\theta _ { 1 } , \sigma _ { 1 }$ with $\theta _ { 2 } , \sigma _ { 2 }$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | h (\theta_ {1}, \sigma_ {1}) - h (\theta_ {2}, \sigma_ {2}) | \leq \| \theta_ {1} - \theta_ {2} \| \\ \qquad + \frac {2}{\epsilon^ {2}} \max \{\| \sigma_ {1} \| \| \theta_ {1} \|, \| \sigma_ {2} \| \| \theta_ {2} \| \} \cdot \| \sigma_ {1} - \sigma_ {2} \|. \end{array}
$$

Lemma 6.5: $M ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , be a positive, continuous, local martingale, and let $\varphi \colon ( 0 , \infty ) \to \mathbb { R }$ be a convex nonincreasing function satisfying $E | \varphi ( M ( t ) ) | < \infty$ for every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . Then $\varphi ( M ( t ) ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , is a submartingale. 

Proof. Let $\{ \tau _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a nondecreasing sequence of stopping times with $\tau _ { n } \uparrow T$ almost surely and such that $M ( t \wedge \tau _ { n } ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , is a martingale for every n. For $\epsilon > 0$ and $\kappa > 0$ , we introduce the function 

$$
\varphi_ {\epsilon , \kappa} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \varphi (\epsilon) + (x - \epsilon) D ^ {+} \varphi (\epsilon), & 0 <   x <   \epsilon , \\ \max \{\varphi (x), \varphi (\epsilon + \kappa) \}, & x \geq \epsilon , \end{array} \right.\tag{6.30}
$$

where $D ^ { + } \varphi$ denotes the right-hand derivative of $\varphi$ . Note that $\varphi _ { \epsilon , \kappa }$ is bounded, convex, and nonincreasing. Jensen’s inequality implies that $\varphi _ { \epsilon , \kappa } ( M ( t \wedge \tau _ { n } ) ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , is a bounded submartingale. In other words, for $0 \leq s \leq t \leq T$ and $A \in { \mathcal { F } } ( s )$ 

$$
\int_ {A} \varphi_ {\epsilon , \kappa} (M (s \wedge \tau_ {n})) d P \leq \int_ {A} \varphi_ {\epsilon , \kappa} (M (t \wedge \tau_ {n})) d P.
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ , we obtain 

$$
\int_ {A} \varphi_ {\epsilon , \kappa} (M (s)) d P \leq \int_ {A} \varphi_ {\epsilon , \kappa} (M (t)) d P
$$

by the bounded convergence theorem. Letting first $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ and then $\kappa  \infty$ , we obtain from two applications of the monotone convergence theorem tha 

$$
\int_ {A} \varphi (M (s)) d P \leq \int_ {A} \varphi (M (t)) d P.
$$

## 6.7 Incomplete Markets

We return to the general model of a complete, standard financial market set up in Section 6.2. There are N stocks driven by an N-dimensional Brownian motion, as described by (2.3). We simplify the notation by assuming that $\delta ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ . We choose an integer $M \in \{ 1 , \ldots , N - 1 \}$ , let $L = N - M$ , and consider the case that only the first M stocks are available for investment. This corresponds to 

$$
K = \{p \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}; p _ {M - 1} = \dots = p _ {N} = 0 \}\tag{7.1}
$$

as in Example 5.4.1(iii). Thus, in place of (2.2), (2.3), the relevant equations are 

$$
d S _ {0} (t) = S _ {0} (t) [ r (t) d t + d A (t) ],\tag{7.2}
$$

$$
d S _ {n} (t) = S _ {n} (t) \left[ b _ {n} (t) d t + d A (t) + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {N} \sigma_ {n d} (t) d W ^ {(d)} (t) \right],\tag{7.3}
$$

$$
n = 1, \dots , M.
$$

We denote by $\tilde { b } ( t )$ the M-dimensional column vector $( b _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , b _ { M } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime }$ , and by $\tilde { \sigma } ( t )$ the bounded $M \times N$ matrix $( \sigma _ { n d } ( t ) ) _ { n = 1 , \dots , M }$ . By assumption, $\tilde { \sigma } ( t )$ has full row rank for Lebesgue-almost-every t, almost surely. In the market $\widetilde { \mathcal { M } }$ consisting of the money market and the first M stocks, the :market price of risk process (1.4.9) is the N-dimensional vector process 

$$
\tilde {\theta} (t) \triangleq \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ \tilde {b} (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {M} ].\tag{7.4}
$$

Although in this section investment in stocks $M + 1 , \dots , N$ is not permit ted in the constrained Problem 2.6, it is useful to create the unconstrained Problem 3.2 in which such investment is permitted. We may fashion stocks $M + 1 , \ldots ,$ N however we like, provided that we respect the assumptions of Section 6.2. It is convenient to assume that the rows of the $L \times N$ matrix $\rho ( t ) = ( \sigma _ { n d } ( t ) ) _ { n = M + 1 , \dots , N }$ are orthonormal vectors spanning the kernel of $\tilde { \sigma } ( t ) ; \mathrm { i . e . , } \qquad d { = } 1 , { \ldots } , \qquad $ 

$$
\rho (t) \rho^ {\prime} (t) = I _ {L}, \quad \tilde {\sigma} (t) \rho^ {\prime} (t) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{7.5}
$$

almost surely, where $I _ { L }$ is the $L \times L$ identity matrix. It is then easily verified that 

$$
\sigma^ {- 1} (t) = [ \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} \quad | \quad \rho^ {\prime} (t) ].\tag{7.6}
$$

The boundedness of $\sigma ( t )$ and $\sigma ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ follows from the assumption of boundedness of $\tilde { \sigma } ( t )$ and $( \tilde { \sigma } ( t ) \tilde { \sigma } ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) ^ { - 1 }$ , conditions that we impose throughout. 

To simplify later notation, we denote by $a ( t )$ the L-dimensional vecto $( b _ { M + 1 } ( t ) , \dots , b _ { N } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime }$ of mean rates of return for the unavailable stocks. 

With K given by (7.1) we have 

$$
\widetilde {K} = \{\nu \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}; \nu_ {1} = \dots = \nu_ {M} = 0 \},
$$

and the class of Definition 5.5.1 consists of all process of the form 

$$
\nu (\cdot) = \left[ \frac {0 _ {M}}{\xi (\cdot)} \right],\tag{7.7}
$$

where $\stackrel { 0 } { \sim } M$ is the M-dimensional zero vector and $\xi ( \cdot )$ is any $\mathbb { R } ^ { L }$ -valued <sup>˜</sup>progressively measurable process satisfying 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \xi (t) \| ^ {2} d t <   \infty .\tag{7.8}
$$

The evolution of prices in the auxiliary market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ is given by (7.2), (7.3), and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d S _ {n} ^ {(\nu)} (t) = S _ {n} ^ {(\nu)} (t) \left[ \left(a _ {n - M} (t) + \xi_ {n - M} (t)\right) d t + d A (t) \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {N} \rho_ {n - M, d} (t)   d W ^ {(d)} (t) \Bigg ], n = M + 1, \ldots , N. \end{array}\tag{7.9}
$$

We say that $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ is a fictitious completion of $\widetilde { \mathcal { M } }$ . The theory of this chapter is about choosing the process $\xi ( \cdot )$ :so that an agent permitted to invest in the stocks $M + 1 , \dots , N$ chooses not to. 

Remark 7.1: Using (7.4), (7.6), we see that the market price of risk process $\theta _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ for $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\theta_ {\nu} (t) = \sigma^ {- 1} (t) [ b (t) + \nu (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \tilde {\theta} (t) + \rho^ {\prime} (t) [ a (t) + \xi (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {L} ].} \end{array}\tag{7.10}
$$

Note that $\rho ^ { \prime } ( t ) [ a ( t ) + \xi ( t ) - r ( t ) \underline { { 1 } } _ { L } ]$ is orthogonal to $\tilde { { \boldsymbol { \theta } } } ( t )$ , because of (7.5). 

Example 7.2 (Logarithmic utility, incomplete market): $\begin{array} { r l } { U _ { 1 } ( t , x ) } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $U _ { 2 } ( x ) = \log x$ for every $( t , x ) \in [ 0 , T ] \times ( 0 , \infty )$ 

This is Example 4.2, specialized to the case of an incomplete market; i.e., $K$ given by (7.1). The expression in (4.23) to be minimized over $\boldsymbol { \xi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { L }$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {1}{2} \| \tilde {\theta} (t) + \rho^ {\prime} (t) (a (t) + \xi - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {L}) \| ^ {2} = \frac {1}{2} \| \tilde {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {1}{2} \| \rho^ {\prime} (t) (a (t) + \xi - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {L}) \| ^ {2},} \end{array}
$$

and this is minimized by $\hat { \xi } ( t ) = r ( t ) \mathbb { 1 } _ { L } - a ( t )$ . In other words, $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ satisfying <sup>˜</sup>the equivalent conditions of Theorem 4.1 is

\hat {\nu} (t) = \left[ \frac {0 _ {M}}{r (t) \widetilde {1} _ {L} - a (t)} \right]

and $\theta _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) = \tilde { \theta } ( \cdot )$ . This corresponds to choosing the fictitious completion for which $\frac { S _ { n } ^ { ( \nu ) } ( \cdot ) } { S _ { 0 } ( \cdot ) }$ is a martingale, $n = M + 1 , \ldots , N$ . The formula for the optimal portfolio-proportion process in Example 4.2 becomes

Example 7.3 (Logarithmic utility, incomplete market, short-selling prohibited): $U _ { 1 } ( t , x ) = U _ { 2 } ( x ) = \log x$ for every $( t , x ) \in [ 0 , T ] \times ( 0 , \infty )$ In contrast to Example 7.2, we now take

$$

as in Example $5 . 4 . 1 ( \mathrm { i v } )$ . Because $\widetilde { K } = \{ \nu \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \nu _ { 1 } \ge 0 , \dots , \nu _ { M } \ge 0 \}$ , the expression in (4.23) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {1}{2} \| \sigma^ {- 1} (t) (b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N}) + \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \nu \| ^ {2}} \\ & {= \frac {1}{2} \left\| \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) [ (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} (t)) ^ {- 1} | \rho^ {\prime} (t) ] \left[ \frac {b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {M}}{a (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {L}} \right] \right.} \\ & {\qquad + [ \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} | \rho^ {\prime} (t) ] \left[ \frac {\eta}{\xi} \right] \Bigg \| ^ {2}} \\ & {= \frac {1}{2} \| \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} (b (t) + \eta - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {M})} \\ & {\qquad + \rho^ {\prime} (t) (a (t) + \xi - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {L}) \| ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r} = \frac {1}{2} \| \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t) (\tilde {\sigma} (t) \tilde {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} (b (t) + \eta - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {M}) \| \\ + \frac {1}{2} \| \rho^ {\prime} (t) (a (t) + \xi - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {L}) \| ^ {2}, \end{array}
$$

and this is to be minimized over $[ \eta ^ { \prime } | \xi ^ { \prime } ] ^ { \prime } \in \widetilde { K }$ . As in the previous example, the minimizing $\xi$ is $\hat { \xi } ( t ) = r ( t ) \mathbb { 1 } _ { L } - a ( t )$ -. The minimizing $\eta \geq 0$ can be <sup>˜</sup>solved from the Kuhn–Tucker conditions
