Example 7.4 (“Totally unhedgeable” coeficients, utility of power type): We take again 

$$
K = \{p \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}; p _ {M + 1} = \dots = p _ {N} = 0 \}.\tag{7.12}
$$

Suppose now that the M N-matrix-valued process $\tilde { \sigma } ( t ) = ( \sigma _ { n d } ( t ) ) _ { n = 1 , \dots , M }$ is of the form 

$$
\tilde {\sigma} (t) = \left[ \stackrel {\circ} {\sigma} (\cdot) \Big | 0 _ {M \times L} \right],\tag{7.13}
$$

where $\overset { \circ } { \sigma } \left( \cdot \right)$ is an $M \times M$ nonsingular matrix. Suppose further that 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} r (\cdot), b (\cdot), \sigma (\cdot) \text {   are adapted   to   the   filtration } \\ \check {\mathcal {F}} (t) \triangleq \sigma (\check {W} (s), 0 \leq s \leq t), 0 \leq t \leq T, \\ \text { generated   by   the   L -dimensional   Brownian   motion } \\ \check {W} (\cdot) = (W _ {M + 1} (\cdot), \ldots , W _ {N} (\cdot)) ^ {\prime} \end{array} \right.\tag{7.14}
$$

and 

$$
A (\cdot) \equiv 0.\tag{7.15}
$$

Then the market $\widetilde { \mathcal { M } }$ of (7.2), (7.3) takes the form 

$$
d S _ {0} (t) = r (t) S _ {0} (t) d t,\tag{7.16}
$$

$$
d S _ {n} (t) = S _ {n} (t) \left[ b _ {n} (t) d t + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {M} \stackrel {\circ} {\sigma} _ {n d} (t) d \stackrel {\circ} {W} ^ {(d)} (t) \right], n = 1, \dots , M;\tag{7.17}
$$

it consists of the money market and of M stocks, driven by the M-dimensional Brownian motion 

$$
\stackrel {\circ} {W} (t) = \left(W _ {1} (\cdot), \dots , W _ {M} (\cdot)\right) ^ {\prime}.
$$

But the driving Brownian motion $\overset { \circ } { W } \left( \cdot \right)$ in (7.17) is independent of $\check { W } ( \cdot )$ to whose natural filtration $\{ \check { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) \}$ the coeficients $r ( \cdot ) , b _ { n } ( \cdot )$ , and ${ \overset { \circ } { \sigma } } _ { n d } \left( \cdot \right)$ appearing in (7.16), (7.17) are adapted. We refer to this situation as one of totally unhedgeable coeficients. 

The risk inherent in the coeficient processes is undiversifiable, and economic intuition suggests that an investor should simply “ignore” it. While it is by no means obvious how to implement this maxim in general, in the case 

$$
U _ {1} (t, x) = 0, U _ {2} (x) = \frac {1}{\beta} x ^ {\beta}, \forall 0 \leq t \leq T, x > 0,\tag{7.18}
$$

for some $\beta < 1 , \beta \neq 0$ , one might expect the optimal portfolio-proportion process to be given by 

$$
\stackrel {\circ} {p} (t) = \frac {1}{1 - \beta} (\stackrel {\circ} {\sigma} (t) \stackrel {\circ} {\sigma} ^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ \tilde {b} (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {M} ],\tag{7.19}
$$

which is the same formula as in a complete market with deterministic coef ficients (see (3.6.16) in Example 3.6.7). Formula (7.19) directs investment in stocks $1 , \ldots , M ;$ ; the corresponding portfolio-proportion process in the constrained market $\mathcal M ( K )$ is 

$$
\hat {p} (t) = \left[ \frac {\stackrel {\circ} {p} (t)}{\underset {\sim} {0} _ {L}} \right].\tag{7.20}
$$

The remainder of this example is a proof that (7.19), (7.20) indeed do provide the optimal portfolio-proportion process under the assumptions (7.12)–(7.15), provided that 

$$
E \left[ \exp \left\{\beta \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(r (t) + \frac {1}{2 (1 - \beta)} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2}\right) d t \right\} \right] <   \infty ,\tag{7.21}
$$

where 

$$
\stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \triangleq (\stackrel {\circ} {\sigma} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ \tilde {b} (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {M} ],
$$

and provided that either $\beta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ or else $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } r ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \parallel \overset { \circ } { \theta } ( t ) \parallel ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ dt are bounded. 

We begin by choosing $a ( t ) = r ( t ) \textbar { ‰}$ and $\rho ( t ) = ( \sigma _ { n d } ( t ) ) _ { n = M + 1 , \ldots , N }$ to be of the form $\rho ( t ) \ = \ \left[ \operatorname * { Q } _ { \sim \ / L \times M } | \breve { \rho } ( t ) \right]$ , where the $M \times M$ matrix $\check { \rho } ( t )$ is orthonormal: $\check { \rho } ( t ) \check { \rho } ^ { \prime } ( t ) = \check { I } _ { L }$ . Then $\sigma ( t )$ has the block form 

$$
\sigma (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \stackrel {{\circ}} {{\sigma}} (t) & | \underset {\sim L \times M} {0} _ {M \times L} \\ \hline 0 _ {L \times M} & | \check {\rho} (t) \end{array} \right],
$$

and the market price of risk for $\mathcal M ( K )$ is 

$$
\theta (t) = \sigma^ {- 1} (t) [ b (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} ] = \left[ \frac {\stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t)}{\mathbb {0} _ {M}} \right].
$$

Processes in are of the form (7.7), where (7.8) holds, and for such a process $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ we have 

$$
\theta_ {\nu} (t) = \left[ \frac {\stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t)}{\check {\nu} (t)} \right],
$$

where 

$$
\check {\nu} (t) \triangleq \check {\rho} ^ {\prime} (t) \xi (t).\tag{7.22}
$$

It follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} H _ {\nu} (T) = \exp \Bigg \{- \int_ {0} ^ {T} \stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} ^ {\prime} (t) d \stackrel {{\circ}} {W} (t) - \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t) d \check {W} (t) \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(r (t) + \frac {1}{2} \| \stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2}\right) d t \Bigg \} \end{array}\tag{7.23}
$$

and 

$$
(H _ {\nu} (T)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} = m _ {\nu} (T) \stackrel {\circ} {\Lambda} (T) \check {\Lambda} _ {\nu} (T),\tag{7.24}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} m _ {\nu} (T) \triangleq \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (t) d t \right. \\ \left. + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t\right) \right\}, \end{array} \tag {7.2}\tag{7.25}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r} \stackrel {\circ} {\Lambda} (T) = \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} ^ {\prime} (t) d \stackrel {\circ} {W} (t) \right. \\ \left. - \frac {1}{2} \left(\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}\right) ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t \right\}, \end{array}\tag{7.26}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \check {\Lambda} _ {\nu} (T) \triangleq \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t)   d \check {W} (t) \right. \\ \left. - \frac {1}{2} \left(\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}\right) ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2}   d t \right\}. \end{array}\tag{7.27}
$$

The implication $\mathrm { ( B ) { \Rightarrow } ( A ) }$ in Theorem 4.1 and Remark 5.8 show that in order to prove optimality of $\hat { p } ( \cdot )$ in (7.20), it sufices to find a process 

$\boldsymbol \nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ such that 

$$
X ^ {x, 0, \hat {p}} (T) = I _ {2} (\mathcal {Y} _ {\nu} (x) H _ {\nu} (T)).\tag{7.28}
$$

With $\hat { p } ( \cdot )$ given by (7.19), (7.20), we have 

$$
\sigma^ {\prime} (t) \hat {p} (t) = \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \left[ \frac {\stackrel {o} {\theta} (t)}{\underset {\sim L} {0}} \right],
$$

and the left-hand side of (7.28) is easily computed from (2.7) in the form 

$$
d \left(\frac {X ^ {x , 0 , \hat {p}} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)}\right) = \frac {X ^ {x , 0 , \hat {p}} (t)}{(1 - \beta) S _ {0} (t)} \stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} ^ {\prime} (t) (\stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} (t) d t + d \stackrel {{\circ}} {W} (t)).
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} X ^ {x, 0, \hat {p}} (T) = x \cdot \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(r (t) + \frac {1 - 2 \beta}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \|\right) d t \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \stackrel {o} {\theta} ^ {\prime} (t) d W (t) \right\}. \end{array}\tag{7.29}
$$

To compute the right-hand side of (7.28) we observe that $I _ { 2 } ( y ) = y ^ { \frac { 1 } { \beta - 1 } }$ ， so that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (y) & = E \left[ H _ {\nu} (T) I _ {2} (y H _ {\nu} (T)) \right] \\ & = y ^ {\frac {1}{\beta - 1}} E \left[ \bigl (H _ {\nu} (T) \bigr) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} \right] \\ & = y ^ {\frac {1}{\beta - 1}} \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1). \end{array}\tag{7.30}
$$

Consequently, $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { V } _ { \nu } ( x ) = \Big ( \frac { x } { \mathcal { X } _ { \nu } ( 1 ) } \Big ) ^ { \beta - 1 } } \end{array}$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {2} (\mathcal {Y} _ {\nu} (x) H _ {\nu} (T)) \\ = \frac {x}{\mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1)} \exp \left\{\frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} ^ {\prime} (t) d \stackrel {{\circ}} {W} (t) + \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t) d \check {W} (t) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(r (t) + \frac {1}{2} \| \stackrel {{\circ}} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2}\right) d t \right\}. \end{array}\tag{7.31}
$$

Comparing (7.29) and (7.31), we see that it sufices to construct a process $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1) = \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (t) d t + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2 (1 - \beta)} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t + \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t) d \check {W} (t) \right\} \end{array} \tag {7.32}
$$

almost surely. 

Consider now the $\{ \check { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) \}$ -martingale 

$$
Q (t) \triangleq E \left[ \exp \left\{\beta \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (u) d u + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta)} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (u) \| ^ {2} d u \right\} \Bigg | \check {\mathcal {F}} (t) \right],\tag{7.33}
$$

defined for $0 \leq t \leq T$ and taking values in $[ \gamma , \infty )$ , where $\gamma$ is a positive constant. Indeed, if $\beta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , then we may take $\gamma = s _ { 0 } ^ { \beta }$ , whereas we use the assumed boundedness of $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } r ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \stackrel { \circ } { \theta } ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t } \end{array}$ to construct $\gamma$ if $\beta < 0$ . According to the martingale representation theorem, 

$$
Q (t) = Q (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \psi^ {\prime} (u) d \check {W} (u), 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

for some $\{ \check { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) \} _ { - \mathrm { p r o g r e s s i v e l y } }$ measurable $\psi ( \cdot ) \colon [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { L }$ satisfying $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \lVert \psi ( u ) \rVert ^ { 2 } d u < } \end{array}$ almost surely. We set $\begin{array} { r } { \check { \nu } ( t ) = - \frac { 1 } { Q ( t ) } \psi ( t ) } \end{array}$ . Since $Q ( \cdot )$ is bounded away from zero, we have $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \check { \nu } ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely and 

$$
Q (t) = Q (0) \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (u) d \check {W} (u) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \check {\nu} (u) \| ^ {2} d u \right\}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{7.34}
$$

With $\begin{array} { r } { \tau _ { n } \stackrel { \Delta } { = } \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \in [ 0 , T ) ; \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \Vert \tilde { \nu } ( u ) \Vert ^ { 2 } d u = n \} \wedge T } \end{array}$ , we obtain from (7.34) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{2} E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t = \log Q (0) - E \log Q (\tau_ {n}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \log Q (0) - \log \gamma <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Letting $n  \infty$ , we conclude from the monotone convergence theorem that E $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \check { \nu } ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ . Now set $\xi ( t ) = \check { \rho } ( t ) \check { \nu } ( t )$ and $\nu ( t ) = \Big [ \frac { \mathrm { { 0 } } _ { M } } { \xi ( t ) } \Big ]$ , in accordance with (7.22) and $( 7 . 7 )$ , and observe that $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ because $\check { \rho } ( \cdot )$ is bounded. From (7.33), (7.34) we also have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \exp \left\{\beta \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (t) d t + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta)} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t \right\} \\ = Q (0) \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t)   d \check {W} (t) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2}   d t \right\}, \end{array}
$$

or equivalently, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (t) d t + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2 (1 - \beta)} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t + \frac {1}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t) d \check {W} (t) \right\} = (Q (0)) ^ {\frac {1}{1 - \beta}}. \end{array} \tag {7.35}
$$

To prove (7.32), it sufices to show that 

$$
\mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1) = (Q (0)) ^ {\frac {1}{1 - \beta}}.\tag{7.36}
$$

From (7.30), (7.24), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1) = E \left[ (H _ {\nu} (T)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} \right]} \\ & {\quad = E \left[ m _ {\nu} (T) \stackrel {\circ} {\Lambda} (T) \check {\Lambda} _ {\nu} (T) \right]} \\ & {\quad = E \left[ m _ {\nu} (T) \check {\Lambda} _ {\nu} (T) E \left(\stackrel {\circ} {\Lambda} (T) \Big | \check {\mathcal {F}} (T)\right) \right],} \end{array}
$$

where we have used the <sup>ˇ</sup>(T)-measurability of $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ . Because $\overset { \circ } { \theta } ( \cdot ) \mathrm { i s } \{ \check { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) \} -$ progressively measurable and $\overset { \circ } { W } \left( \cdot \right)$ is independent of $\check { \mathcal { F } } ( T )$ , we see that $E [ \stackrel { \circ } { \Lambda } ( T ) | \check { \mathcal { F } } ( T ) ] = 1$ , just as would be the case if $\overset { \circ } { \theta } ( \cdot )$ were nonrandom. We conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {X} _ {\nu} (1) = E \left[ m _ {\nu} (T) \check {\Lambda} _ {\nu} (T) \right] \\ \qquad = E \left[ \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} r (t) d t + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \stackrel {\circ} {\theta} (t) \| ^ {2} d t \right. \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \left. + \frac {\beta}{2 (1 - \beta)} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \check {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t + \frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \check {\nu} ^ {\prime} (t) d \check {W} (t) \right\} \\ \qquad = E \left[ (Q (T)) ^ {\frac {1}{1 - \beta}} \left(\frac {Q (0)}{Q (T)}\right) ^ {\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}} \right], \end{array}
$$

where we have used (7.33) to evaluate $( Q ( T ) ) ^ { \frac { 1 } { 1 - \beta } }$ and (7.34) to evaluate $\left( { \frac { Q ( 0 ) } { Q ( T ) } } \right) ^ { \frac { \beta } { 1 - \beta } }$ . But 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E \left[ (Q (T)) ^ {\frac {1}{1 - \beta}} \left(\frac {Q (0)}{Q (T)}\right) ^ {\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}} \right] & = (Q (0)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}} E Q (T) \\ & = (Q (0)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta}} Q (0) = (Q (0)) ^ {\frac {1}{1 - \beta}}, \end{array}
$$

and (7.36) follows. 

## 6.8 Higher Interest Rate for Borrowing Than for Investing

In this section we modify the optimal consumption and investment Problem 3.5.4 to allow the interest rate for borrowing to exceed the interest rate for investing. The solution of this problem can be obtained via a dual problem in the spirit of Theorem 4.1, although not as a direct application of that theorem. We indicate below how to make the appropriate modifications to the arguments in Sections 2–5. 

As in Section 2 we begin with a complete, standard financial market with asset prices governed by (2.2), (2.3); we assume that (2.4), (2.5), and (5.2.4) hold, and that $Z _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is a martingale, so the standard martingale measure $P _ { 0 }$ is defined. Consumption processes and portfolio-proportion processes are as in Definitions 2.1 and 2.2, respectively. 

The process $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ records the value of investment in the money market. Borrowing, on the other hand, can occur only at a premium $R ( \cdot ) { - } r ( \cdot )$ above the money-market rate. More specifically, there is a bounded, nonnegative, progressively measurable process $R ( \cdot ) \geq r ( \cdot )$ such that for initial wealth $x \geq 0$ , consumption process $c ( \cdot )$ , and portfolio-proportion process $p ( \cdot )$ , the corresponding wealth process $X ^ { x , c , p } ( \cdot ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , satisfies (cf. (2.7)), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {c (u) d u}{S _ {0} (u)} = x + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} (R (u) - r (u)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) 1 _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} d u. \end{array} \tag {8.1}
$$

The last integral in (8.1) accounts for the higher interest paid when the fraction of total wealth borrowed, 

$$
(p ^ {\prime} (u) \underset {N} {1} - 1) ^ {+} = \max \left\{0, \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} p _ {n} (u) - 1 \right\},
$$

is strictly positive. Equation (8.1) is equivalent to 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d X ^ {x, c, p} (t) = - c (t) d t + (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) ^ {+} X ^ {x, c, p} (t) (r (t) d t + d A (t)) \\ \quad - (p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} X ^ {x, c, p} (t) (R (t) d t + d A (t)) \\ \quad + X ^ {x, c, p} (t) p ^ {\prime} (t) [ b (t) d t + \delta (t) d t + \underline {{1}} _ {N} d A (t) + \sigma (t) d W (t) ]. \end{array} \tag {8.2}
$$

The solution of (8.1), or equivalently, (8.2), is constructed as follows. Define $\tau _ { p }$ by (2.9) and $I _ { p } ( t ) , 0 \le t < \tau _ { p }$ , by (2.8), so (2.10) holds. Set 

$$
K _ {p} (t) \triangleq I _ {p} (t) \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} (R (u) - r (u)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) 1 _ {\sim N} - 1) ^ {+} d u \right\},
$$

and then define $X ^ { x , c , p } ( t )$ for $0 \leq t < \tau _ { p }$ by 

$$
\frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} = K _ {p} (t) \left[ x - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {c (u) d u}{S _ {p} (u) K _ {p} (u)} \right];\tag{8.3}
$$

it is easily verified that (8.1) holds. With $\tau _ { 0 } \stackrel { \Delta } { = } \operatorname* { i n f } \big \{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; X ^ { x , c , p } ( t ) = 0 \big \}$ we have $\tau _ { 0 } \leq \tau _ { p }$ almost surely. As in Definition 2.4 we say that $( c , p )$ is admissible at x in the market with higher interest rate for borrowing than for investing, and write $( c , p ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x )$ , if (2.11) holds. For $( c , p ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x )$ the process $X ^ { x , c , p } ( t )$ defined by (8.3) for $0 \leq t < \tau _ { 0 }$ and set equal to 0 fo $\tau _ { 0 } \leq t \leq T$ , solves (8.1), or equivalently (8.2). 

Here is the problem that we shall study in this section. 

Problem 8.1: Given $x \geq 0$ , find a pair $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ in the class 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {A} _ {3} (x) \triangleq \Bigg \{(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} (x); \quad E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \min [ 0, U _ {1} (t, c (t)) ]   d t > - \infty , \\ E \left(\min [ 0, U _ {2} (X ^ {x, c, p} (T)) ]\right) > - \infty \Bigg \} \end{array}
$$

that attains 

$$
V (x) \triangleq \sup _ {(c, p) \in \mathcal {A} _ {3} (x)} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, c (t)) d t + U _ {2} (X ^ {x, c, p} (T)) \right],
$$

the maximal expected utility from both consumption and terminal wealth in the market with higher interest rate for borrowing than for investing. 

We define the random, set-valued process 

$$
\widetilde {K} (t) \stackrel {\Delta} {=} \left\{\nu \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}; - (R (t) - r (t)) \leq \nu_ {1} = \nu_ {2} = \dots = \nu_ {N} \leq 0 \right\}.
$$

As in Definition 5.5.1, we denote by $\mathcal { H }$ the Hilbert space of $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} \mathrm { - p r o g r e s - }$ sively measurable processes $\nu ( \cdot ) \colon [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \nu ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ and by $\mathcal { D }$ the closed subset of $\mathcal { H }$ consisting of processes $\nu ( \cdot )$ that satis $\mathrm { f y }$ the almost sure condition 

$$
\nu (t) \in \widetilde {K} (t), \text {   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ].
$$

For $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ and $\boldsymbol \nu \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , we define the nonnegative random variable 

$$
\zeta (t, \nu) \triangleq \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - \nu_ {1}, & \text {if} \nu \in \widetilde {K} (t), \\ \infty , & \text {if} \nu \notin \widetilde {K} (t). \end{array} \right.
$$

For each $\nu , \zeta ( \cdot , \nu )$ is $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \}$ -progressively measurable. For each $( t , \omega )$ , the mapping $\nu \mapsto \zeta ( t , \nu )$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. 

These definitions of and $\zeta$ are in the spirit of Definition 5.5.1, except that $\widetilde { K }$ depends now on $( t , \omega )$ and is not a cone. There is no convex set $K$ -corresponding to $\widetilde { K }$ via (5.4.1), (5.4.2). 

For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ -, we form the auxiliary market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ described in Section 5.5.2. In $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ there is a single interest rate for investing and borrowing, namely 

$$
r _ {\nu} (t) \triangleq r (t) + \zeta (t, \nu (t))
$$

(cf. (5.5.3)). Note that 

$$
0 \leq \zeta (t, \nu (t)) \leq R (t) - r (t), \text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{8.4}
$$

holds almost surely, so $r ( t ) \leq r _ { \nu } ( t ) \leq R ( t )$ . The money market in $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ has price process 

$$
S _ {0} ^ {(\nu)} (t) = S _ {0} (t) \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \zeta (s, \nu (s)) d s \right\},\tag{8.5}
$$

while the stock prices are given by 

$$
S _ {n} ^ {(\nu)} (t) = S _ {n} (t), n = 1, \ldots , N\tag{8.6}
$$

(see (5.5.7) and (5.5.8)). The market price of risk in the market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ is 

$$
\theta_ {\nu} (t) \stackrel {{\Delta}} {{=}} \theta (t) + \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \nu (t) = \sigma^ {- 1} (t) [ b (t) + \delta (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} + \nu_ {1} (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} ].\tag{8.7}
$$

Given $x \ge 0$ and a consumption and portfolio-proportion process pair $( c , p )$ , we define the corresponding wealth process $X _ { \nu } ^ { x , c , p } ( \cdot )$ in $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ by the equivalent equations (3.1)–(3.3). Note that in the case at hand, (3.2) may be written as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {X _ {\nu} ^ {x , c , p} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {c (u) d u}{S _ {0} (u)} = x + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {X _ {\nu} ^ {x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} \zeta (u, \nu (u)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (u) 1 _ {\sim N}) d u. \end{array} \tag {8.8}
$$

We say that $( c , p )$ is admissible at x in the unconstrained market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ , and write $( c , p ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { \nu } ( x )$ , if (3.4) holds. We define $A _ { 3 } ^ { ( \nu ) } ( x )$ and $V _ { \nu } ( x )$ as in Problem 3.2. 

Remark 8.2: Suppose $( c , p ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x )$ , so that $X ^ { x , c , p } ( \cdot )$ is defined. If we choose $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ , then $X _ { \nu } ^ { x , c , p } ( \cdot )$ is also defined, and we have 

$$
X _ {\nu} ^ {x, c, p} (t) \geq X ^ {x, c, p} (t), 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{3.8}
$$

as we show below. In particular, 

$$
\mathcal {A} _ {3} (x) \subset \mathcal {A} _ {3} ^ {(\nu)} (x), \text { for } x \geq 0, \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D},\tag{8.9}
$$

and 

$$
V (x) \leq V _ {\nu} (x), \text { for } x \geq 0, \nu (\cdot) \in \mathcal {D}.\tag{8.10}
$$

To derive (3.8), we first note that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \zeta (t, \nu (t)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) + (R (t) - r (t)) (p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} \\ = \zeta (t, \nu (t)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) ^ {+} + (R (t) - r (t) - \zeta (t, \nu (t))) (p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} \\ \geq 0. \end{array} \tag {8.}\tag{8.11}
$$

Subtraction of (8.1) from (8.8) shows that the process 

$$
\Delta (t) \triangleq \frac {X _ {\nu} ^ {x , c , p} (t) - X ^ {x , c , p} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

satisfies 

$$
\Delta (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Delta (u) p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Delta (u) \zeta (u, \nu (u)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (u) 1 _ {N}) d u
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {X ^ {x , c , p} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} \left[ \zeta (u, \nu (u)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) \right. \\ \left. + (R (u) - r (u)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} \right] d u. \end{array}
$$

Setting 

$$
\begin{array}{c} J (t) = \exp \bigg \{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} p ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (u) p (u) \| ^ {2}   d u \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \zeta (u, \nu (u)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N})   d u \bigg \}, \end{array}
$$

we compute 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d (\Delta (t) J (t)) = \frac {J (t) X ^ {x , c , p} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} \Big [ \zeta (t, \nu (t)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) \\ + (R (t) - r (t)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} \Big ] d t. \end{array}
$$

We integrate this equation, using (8.11) and the fact that $\Delta ( 0 ) = 0$ , to conclude that (3.8) holds. Note also that if we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \zeta (t, \nu (t)) (1 - p ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) + (R (t) - r (t)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} = 0, \\ \text { for   Lebesgue - a.e. } t \in [ 0, T ] \end{array}\tag{8.12}
$$

almost surely, then 

$$
X _ {\nu} ^ {x, c, p} (t) = X ^ {x, c, p} (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T\tag{8.13}
$$

holds almost surely. 

The unconstrained market $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ satisfies (3.14), and hence Assumption 3.2.3. We define $\mathcal { X } _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ and $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ by (3.15) and (3.24), respectively, and for $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ satisfying $\mathcal { X } _ { \nu } ( y ) < \infty$ for all $y > 0$ , we denote by $\mathcal { D } _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ the inverse of $\mathcal { X } _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ . We define $c _ { \nu } ( \cdot ) , X _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ , and $p _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ by $( 3 . 1 6 ) \ – ( 3 . 2 1 )$ ; then (3.22) holds and $\left( c _ { \nu } , p _ { \nu } \right)$ attains the supremum in (3.6). Remarks 3.4, 3.5, and 3.6 apply to $\mathcal { M } _ { \nu }$ . For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ we define $\widetilde { V } _ { \nu } ( \cdot )$ by (3.27). We extend this definition to $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } \setminus \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ -by (3.33), and Proposition 3.7 holds. 

Let the initial wealth x be strictly positive. Just as in Section 3, our strategy is to find a process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ for which the optimal pair $( c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) , p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) )$ for the market $\mathcal { M } _ { \hat { \nu } }$ is also optimal for Problem 8.1. In other words, we seek $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ that satisfies 

$$
V (x) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, c _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t)) d t + U _ {2} (B _ {\tilde {\nu}}) \right] = V _ {\tilde {\nu}} (x).\tag{8.14}
$$

Remark 8.2 shows that such a $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ should satisfy almost surely the complementary slackness condition 

$$
\zeta (t, \hat {\nu} (t)) (1 - \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N}) + (R (t) - r (t)) (p ^ {\prime} (u) \mathbb {1} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} = 0,\tag{8.15}
$$

$$
\text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ].
$$

Proposition 8.3: Let $x > 0$ be given, and suppose that $( 8 . 1 5 )$ is satisfied for some process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) ~ \in ~ \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ . Then the pair $\left( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } \right)$ of (3.17), (3.21) is optimal for Problem 8.1, and $V ( x ) = V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ . Furthermore, $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ minimizes $V _ { \nu } ( x )$ over $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ 

Proof. From Remark 8.2 we see that (8.15) implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V (x) \geq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t))   d t + U _ {2} (X ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (T)) \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t))   d t + U _ {2} (X _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (T)) \right] \\ = V _ {\hat {\nu}} (x). \end{array}\tag{8.16}
$$

Remark 8.2 also gives $V ( x ) \leq V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ for every $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ . Hence equality holds in (8.16), $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ minimizes $V _ { \nu } ( x )$ over $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ , and $\left( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } \right)$ is optimal for Problem 8.1. ␀ 

We alter slightly two of the optimality conditions of Section 6.4. For a fixed initial capital $x \ > \ 0$ , let $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ be a consumption and portfolio proportion process pair in the class $ { \mathcal { A } } _ { 3 } ( x )$ of Problem 8.1, and denote by $\widehat { X } ( \cdot ) = X ^ { x , \widehat { c } , \widehat { p } } ( \cdot )$ the corresponding wealth process of (8.1). Consider the 7statement that this pair is optimal for Problem 8.1: 

(A) Optimality of $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ : We have 

$$
V (x) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t + U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) \right] <   \infty .
$$

Now let $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ be a process in $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ . In the next condition, we use the notation $( 3 . 1 6 ) \ – ( 3 . 1 8 )$ 

(B) Financeability of $( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , B _ { \hat { \nu } } )$ : There exists a portfolio-proportion process $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ such that $( c _ { \hat { \nu } } , p _ { \hat { \nu } } ) \in \mathcal A _ { 3 } ( x )$ and 

$$
\zeta (t, \hat {\nu} (t)) (1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} 1 _ {N}) + (R (t) - r (t)) (p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) 1 _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} = 0,\tag{8.17}
$$

for Lebesgue-a.e. $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ • 

$$
X ^ {x, c _ {\hat {\nu}}, p _ {\hat {\nu}}} (\cdot) = X _ {\hat {\nu}} (\cdot)\tag{8.18}
$$

hold almost surely. 

As in Section 4.1, the portfolio-proportion process $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ in $\mathrm { ( B ^ { \prime } ) }$ is not assumed to be given by (3.21) with $\nu ( \cdot ) = \hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ ; this follows from (8.17), (8.18), and Remark 8.2 (see (8.13)). 

For the present purpose, the other three optimality conditions in Section 6.4 are suitable exactly as stated there. We have the following counterpart to the first assertion in Theorem 4.1. 

Theorem 8.4: The condition (B) and the conditions (C), (D) and (E) of Section $6 . 4$ are equivalent, and they imply condition $\left( \mathrm { A } ^ { \prime } \right)$ with $( { \hat { p } } , { \hat { c } } ) =$ $( p _ { \hat { \nu } } , c _ { \hat { \nu } } )$ 

Proof. The implications $( \mathrm { B } ^ { \prime } ) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { E } ) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { D } ) , ( \mathrm { B } ^ { \prime } ) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { A } ^ { \prime } )$ , and $\mathrm { ( B ^ { \prime } ) } \mathrm { \Rightarrow \left( C \right) } \mathrm { \Rightarrow }$ (D) are proved as in Theorem 4.1. It remains to prove $\mathrm { ( D ) { \Rightarrow } ( B ^ { \prime } ) }$ 

We assume (D), define $\mu ( t ) = ( \mu _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , \mu _ { 1 } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { D }$ by 

$$
\mu_ {1} (t) = \dots = \mu_ {N} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text {if} 1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \mathbb {1} _ {\widetilde {N}} \geq 0, \\ - (R (t) - r (t)), & \text {if} 1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \mathbb {1} _ {\widetilde {N}} <   0, \end{array} \right.
$$

and proceed through the proof of the implication $\mathrm { ( D ) \{ \Rightarrow ( B ) } $ in Theorem 4.1, taking 

$$
\xi (s) = \frac {1}{\epsilon} [ \zeta (s, (1 - \epsilon) \hat {\nu} (s) + \epsilon \mu (s)) - \zeta (s, \hat {\nu} (s)) ] = \hat {\nu} _ {1} (s) - \mu_ {1} (s),
$$

so that (4.19) becomes 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) X _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \left[ (\hat {\nu} _ {1} (t) - \mu_ {1} (t)) (1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) \right] d t \geq 0, n = 1, 2, \dots .
$$

Because $- ( R ( t ) - r ( t ) ) \leq \hat { \nu } _ { 1 } ( t ) \leq 0$ , the integrand is negative unless $\hat { \nu } _ { 1 } ( t ) =$ $\mu _ { 1 } ( t ) \mathrm { o r } 1 - p _ { \hat { \nu } } ^ { \prime } ( t ) { \bf 1 } _ { N } = 0$ . Because $\tau _ { n } \uparrow T$ almost surely as $n \to \infty$ , we must have 

$$
(\hat {\nu} (t) - \mu (t)) (1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) 1 _ {N}) = 0, \text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ]
$$

almost surely. It follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \zeta (t, \hat {\nu} (t)) (1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) ^ {+} + (R (t) - r (t) - \zeta (t, \hat {\nu} (t))) (p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+} \\ = \zeta (t, \hat {\nu} (t)) (1 - p _ {\hat {\nu}} ^ {\prime} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}) + (R (t) - r (t)) (p _ {\hat {\nu} (t)} ^ {\prime} \underline {{1}} _ {N} - 1) ^ {+}, \\ \text { for   Lebesgue - a.e. } t \in [ 0, T ] \end{array}
$$

almost surely. 

The existence theory for the dual problem captured by condition (D) goes through just as in Section 6.5. In particular, Theorem 5.3 holds, and under the assumptions of that theorem, for every $x > 0$ , we have $V ( x ) < \infty$ and there exists an optimal pair $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x )$ for Problem 8.1. 

Example 8.5 (Logarithmic utilities, general coeficients): In the special case $U _ { 1 } ( t , x ) = U _ { 2 } ( x ) = \log x , 0 \leq t \leq T , x > 0$ , we have $\widetilde { U } _ { 1 } ( t , y ) = \widetilde { U } _ { 2 } ( y ) =$ $- ( 1 + \log y ) , y > 0$ (see Example 4.2), and 

$$
\widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) = - (T + 1) (1 + \log y) - \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ \log H _ {\nu} (t) ] d t - E [ \log H _ {\nu} (T) ].
$$

For $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - E [ \log H _ {\nu} (t) ] \\ = E A (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} E \left[ r (u) + \zeta (u, \nu) + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (u) + \sigma^ {- 1} \nu (u) \| ^ {2} \right] d u. \end{array}
$$

The optimal dual process is thus $\hat { \nu } ( t ) = \hat { \nu } _ { 1 } ( t ) ! _ { \sim N }$ , where $\hat { \nu } _ { 1 } ( t )$ minimizes 

$$
- \nu_ {1} + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (t) + \nu_ {1} \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} \| ^ {2} \quad \text { over } \nu_ {1} \in [ - (R (t) - r (t)), 0 ].
$$

With 

$$
B (t) \triangleq \theta^ {\prime} (t) \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N}, C (t) \triangleq \underline {{1}} _ {N} ^ {\prime} (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} \underline {{1}} _ {N},\tag{8.19}
$$

this minimization is achieved as follows: 

$$
\hat {\nu} _ {1} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text {if} B (t) - 1 \leq 0, \\ \frac {1 - B (t)}{C (t)}, & \text {if} 0 <   B (t) - 1 <   C (t) (R (t) - r (t)), \\ r (t) - R (t), & \text {if} B (t) - 1 \geq C (t) (R (t) - r (t)). \end{array} \right.
$$

Example 3.6.6 applied to the market $\mathcal { M } _ { \hat { \nu } }$ shows that the optimal portfolioproportion process is $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( t ) = ( \sigma ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) ^ { - 1 } \theta _ { \hat { \nu } } ( t )$ ; i.e., 

$$
p _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ b (t) + \delta (t) - r (t) \mathbb {1} _ {N} ], & \text {if} B (t) - 1 \leq 0, \\ (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} \Big [ b (t) + \delta (t) - r (t) + \frac {1 - B (t)}{C (t)} \mathbb {1} _ {N} \Big ], \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {if} 0 <   B (t) - 1 <   C (t) (R (t) - r (t)), \\ (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ b (t) + \delta (t) - R (t) ], \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {if} B (t) - 1 \geq C (t) (R (t) - r (t)). \end{array} \right.
$$

Example 8.6 (Utilities of power type, deterministic coeficients): As sume that $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { 1 } ( t , x ) = U _ { 2 } ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { \beta } x ^ { \beta } , 0 \le t \le T , x > 0 } \end{array}$ , for some $\beta < 0$ , $\beta \neq 0$ . Assume further that $r ( \cdot ) , R ( \cdot ) , \sigma ( \cdot )$ , and $\theta ( \cdot )$ are deterministic. We have 

$$
\widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y) = \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y) = \frac {1 - \beta}{\beta} y ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}}, y > 0,
$$

and 

$$
\widetilde {V} _ {\nu} (y) = \frac {1 - \beta}{\beta} y ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(H _ {\nu} (t)\right) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} d t + \left(H _ {\nu} (T)\right) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} \right].
$$

We take $\hat { \nu } _ { 1 } ( t )$ to be the (nonrandom) minimizer of 

$$
- (1 - \beta) \nu_ {1} + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (t) + \nu_ {1} \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} \| ^ {2} \text {over} \nu_ {1} \in [ - (R (t) - r (t)), 0 ],
$$

i.e., 

$$
\nu_ {1} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text { if } B (t) + \beta - 1 \leq 0, \\ \frac {1 - \beta - B (t)}{C (t)}, & \text { if } 0 <   B (t) + \beta - 1 <   C (t) (R (t) - r (t)), \\ r (t) - R (t), & \text { if } B (t) + \beta - 1 \geq C (t) (R (t) - r (t)), \end{array} \right.
$$

where $B ( t )$ and C(t) are given by (8.19). From Example 3.6.7, we have for all $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ that $( H _ { \nu } ( t ) ) ^ { \frac { \beta } { \beta - 1 } } = m _ { \nu } ( t ) \Lambda _ { \nu } ( t )$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} m _ {\nu} (t) \triangleq \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \left[ A (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} r (u) d u \right] \right. \\ \quad \quad \quad + \frac {\beta}{(1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left[ - (1 - \beta) \nu_ {1} (u) \right. \\ \quad \quad \quad \left. + \frac {1}{2} \| \theta (u) + \nu_ {1} (u) \sigma^ {- 1} (u) 1 _ {N} \| ^ {2} \right] d u \Bigg \}, \end{array}
$$

$$
\Lambda_ {\nu} (t) \triangleq \exp \left\{\frac {\beta}{1 - \beta} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \theta_ {\nu} ^ {\prime} (u) d W (u) - \frac {\beta^ {2}}{2 (1 - \beta) ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \theta_ {\nu} (u) \| ^ {2} d u \right\}.
$$

If $0 < \beta < 1$ , then 

$$
E (H _ {\nu} (t)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} = E [ m _ {\nu} (t) \Lambda_ {\nu} (t) ] \geq m _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) E \Lambda_ {\nu} (t) = m _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) = E (H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}},
$$

but if $\beta < 0$ , then 

$$
E (H _ {\nu} (t)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}} \leq m _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) = E (H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) ^ {\frac {\beta}{\beta - 1}}.
$$

In either case, we see that $V _ { \hat { \nu } } ( y ) \leq V _ { \nu } ( y )$ holds for all $\nu ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D }$ . Having thus solved the dual problem, we appeal to (3.6.16) to obtain the optimal portfolio process in the form $\begin{array} { r } { p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( t ) = \frac { 1 } { 1 - \beta } ( \sigma ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) ^ { - 1 } \theta _ { \hat { \nu } } ( t ) ; \mathrm { i . e . } } \end{array}$ , 

$$
p _ {\tilde {\nu}} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{1 - \beta} (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ b (t) + \delta (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}} _ {N} ], \qquad \text {if} B (t) + \beta - 1 \leq 0, \\ \frac {1}{1 - \beta} (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} \left[ b (t) + \delta (t) - r (t) + \frac {1 - \beta - B (t)}{C (t)} \right], \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {if} 0 <   B (t) + \beta - 1 <   C (t) (R (t) - r (t)), \\ \frac {1}{1 - \beta} (\sigma (t) \sigma^ {\prime} (t)) ^ {- 1} [ b (t) + \delta (t) - R (t) ], \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {if} B (t) + \beta - 1 \geq C (t) (R (t) - r (t)). \end{array} \right.
$$

## 6.9 Notes

The stochastic duality theory of Bismut (1973) was apparently first employed to study constrained portfolio optimization problems in the doctoral dissertation of Xu (1990) (see also Shreve and Xu (1992)), who consid ered the special case $K \stackrel { \cdot } { = } [ 0 , \infty ) ^ { N }$ of Example 5.4.1(iii) corresponding to prohibiting the short-sale of stocks. Xu formulated a dual problem in the spirit of this chapter, whose solution could be shown to exist and to be useful in constructing and characterizing the solution to the original, constrained optimization problem. His methodology was then applied to the more traditional incomplete market model of Section 7 by Karatzas, Lehoczky, Shreve, and Xu (1991). He and Pearson (1991b) also dealt with the same problem in a discrete-time, finite-probability-space framework, where they proposed finding the pairs of optimal consumption processes and terminal wealth levels corresponding to each member in a family of equivalent martingale measures and then searching over those pairs for a policy that yields minimal expected utility; they used separating hyper plane theorems to show that the total utility obtained by this two-step “minimax” procedure leads to the value of the optimization problem in the incomplete market. Using techniques of Xu (1990), He and Pearson (1991a) extended He and Pearson (1991b) to continuous time. For earlier work on these matters with Markovian price processes, see also Pag`es (1989), who deals with the case of incomplete markets using probabilistic tools, and $\mathrm { Z a - }$ riphopoulou (1989), who discusses constraints using methods from partial diferential equations. 

For the generality of the model presented in this chapter the reader is referred to the paper by Cvitani´c and Karatzas (1992), whose exposition we have followed rather closely. For other expositions, see the lectures by Cvitani´c (1997), El Karoui and Quenez (1997), Karatzas (1996). Pliska (1997) has a presentation of these techniques and results in the much simpler setting of a discrete-time model. Work related to the problem of Section 8 (consumption/investment optimization in the presence of a higher interest rate for borrowing than for investing) includes the pa pers by Brennan (1971) in an equilibrium setting, as well as Fleming and Zariphopoulou (1991), who deal with an infinite-horizon model with discounting, $d = 1$ and constant $R > r , \ b _ { 1 } , \ \sigma _ { 1 1 }$ and obtain explicit formulae for power-type utility functions. We also refer the reader to Foldes (1992) for related work on infinite-horizon models; to He and Pag`es (1993), Browne (1995), Cuoco (1997), El Karoui and Jeanblanc-Picqu´e (1997) and the references therein, as well as Dufie, Fleming, Soner, and Zariphopoulou (1997), for utility maximization and/or equilibrium problems under various constraints and random endowment streams; and to Cuoco and Cvitani´c (1996) for generalizations in the context of a “large investor” model. In particular, Cuoco (1997) establishes directly the existence of optimal con sumption/investment strategies for fairly general price dynamics and utility functions; his model allows for a random endowment stream and for port folio constraints that include short sale, borrowing, and incompleteness restrictions, and he characterizes equilibrium risk premia when these exist. 

In another very interesting development, Schweizer (1992b) considers an incomplete market with $r ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ and one stock, with price-per-share process 

$$
d S (t) = S (t) \left[ b (t) d t + \sigma_ {1} (t) d W _ {1} (t) + \sigma_ {2} (t) d W _ {2} (t) \right]\tag{9.1}
$$

driven by a two-dimensional Brownian motion $W ( \cdot ) = ( W _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , W _ { 2 } ( \cdot ) )$ that generates the filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ . The coeficients $b ( \cdot ) , \sigma _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \sigma _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ are bounded and adapted to this filtration, and $\sigma ( \cdot ) \ \triangleq \ \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } ( \cdot ) + \sigma _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } ( \cdot ) }$ is bounded away from zero. One considers portfolio processes $\pi : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega $ R in the Hilbert space of measurable, $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \}$ -adapted processes with $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \pi ^ { 2 } ( t ) d t < \infty } \end{array}$ , and tries to “hedge” with such portfolios a given contingent claim $B \in L ^ { p } ( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } _ { T } , P )$ for some $p > 2$ . Since exact duplication in such a setting is typically not possible, Schweizer considers the minimization 

$$
\inf _ {\pi (\cdot) \in \mathcal {H}} E (B - X ^ {x, \pi} (T)) ^ {2}\tag{9.2}
$$

of expected quadratic loss for a given initial capital $x \in \mathbb { R }$ ; see also Richard son (1989), Dufie and Richardson (1991) for earlier results in this vein. Of course, if the market were complete and $x = E _ { 0 } ( B )$ , then the infimum in (9.2) would be zero, since one could employ the hedging porfolio $\hat { \pi } ( \cdot )$ of Section 2.2 and achieve the exact hedging $X ^ { x , \hat { \pi } } ( T ) = B$ almost surely. In our present setting, such exact duplication is not possible even for $x = E _ { 0 } ( B )$ ), and (9.2) merely attempts to minimize the $L ^ { 2 } \mathrm { - n o r m }$ of the discrepancy in the hedge at time $t = T$ (or equivalently, to find the “best approximation in $L ^ { 2 }$ of the random variable B by a stochastic integral”). 

In the notation of Chapter 1, we have here $X ^ { x , \pi } ( t ) ~ = ~ x + G ^ { \pi } ( t )$ for the gains process $\begin{array} { r } { G ^ { \pi } ( t ) \ = \ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \pi ( s ) \sigma ( s ) d W _ { 0 } ( s ) } \end{array}$ , where we set $\theta ( \cdot ) \ { \stackrel { \Delta } { = } }$ $b ( \cdot ) / \sigma ( \cdot ) , \ \rho ( \cdot ) \stackrel { \Delta } { = } \sigma _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) / \sigma ( \cdot )$ , as well as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & W (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (u) d W _ {1} (u) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2} (u)} \cdot d W _ {2} (u), \\ & N (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2} (u)} \cdot d W _ {2} (u) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (u) d W _ {2} (u), \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
W _ {0} (t) \triangleq W (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \theta (s) d s.
$$

One notices that $W ( \cdot ) , N ( \cdot )$ are Brownian motions with $\langle W , N \rangle \equiv 0 ;$ ; and that $W _ { 0 } ( \cdot ) , N ( \cdot )$ are Brownian motions with $\langle W _ { 0 } , N \rangle \equiv 0$ under the socalled minimal equivalent martingale measure 

$$
P _ {0} (A) \triangleq E \left[ \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {T} \theta (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \theta^ {2} (s) d s \right\} \cdot 1 _ {A} \right]
$$

on $\mathcal { F } ( T )$ , introduced by F¨ollmer and Schweizer (1991). On the other hand, elementary Hilbert-space arguments show that the portfolio $\pi ^ { * } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { H }$ which attains the infimum in (9.2) satisfies 

$$
E \left[ \left(B - x - G ^ {\pi^ {*}} (T)\right) \cdot G ^ {\pi} (T) \right] = 0, \quad \forall \pi (\cdot) \in \mathcal {H}.\tag{9.3}
$$

In order to find this optimal portfolio $\pi ^ { * } ( \cdot )$ , one introduces the “intrinsic value process” $V ( t ) \ { \stackrel { \Delta } { = } } \ E _ { 0 } [ B | { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ] , \ 0 \ \leq \ t \ \leq T$ ; from the martingale representation theorem, this process can be written in the form 

$$
V (t) = E _ {0} (B) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \xi (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \eta (u) d N (u)
$$

for suitable processes $\xi ( \cdot ) , \eta ( \cdot )$ in ${ \mathcal { H } } ,$ and (9.3) is implied by the equality 

$$
E \left[ (V (t) - x - G ^ {\pi^ {*}} (T)) \cdot G ^ {\pi} (T) \right] = 0, \quad \forall \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{9.4}
$$

Using tools from stochastic analysis, Schweizer (1992b) then produces the optimal portfolio $\pi ^ { * } ( \cdot )$ in the form 

$$
\pi^ {*} (t) = \xi (t) + \frac {b (t)}{\sigma^ {2} (t)} \left(V (t) - x - G ^ {*} (t)\right),\tag{9.5}
$$

under the assumption that the ratio 

$$
\frac {b (\cdot)}{\sigma (\cdot)} \text { is   deterministic },\tag{9.6}
$$

where $G ^ { * } ( \cdot )$ is the solution of the linear stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d G ^ {*} (t) = \left[ \sigma (t) \xi (t) + \frac {b (t)}{\sigma (t)} \bigl (V (t) - x - G ^ {*} (t) \bigr) \right] d W _ {0} (t), G ^ {*} (0) = 0.\tag{9.7}
$$

This result is further extended to a much more general framework in Schweizer (1994); this paper should also be consulted for the study of additional quadratic-optimization problems such as the optimal choice of both initial capital and hedging strategy, the determination of varianceminimizing strategies and of the “mean-variance frontier,” and the approximation of a riskless asset. See also Pham, Rheinl¨ander and Schweizer (1998). For the related notion of “variance-optimal martingale measure,” see Schweizer (1996).

# Appendix A Essential Supremum of a Family of Random Variables

The essential infimum of a family of nonnegative random variables is defined and constructed by Dunford and Schwartz (1957). We modify this material to suit our purposes. 

Definition A.1: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal { X }$ be a nonempty family of nonnegative random variables defined on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ The essential supremum of $\mathcal { X }$ , denoted by ess sup $\mathcal { X }$ , is a random variable $X ^ { * }$ satisfying: 

(i) $\forall X \in { \mathcal { X } } , X \leq X ^ { * } { \mathrm { ~ a . s . , ~ a n d } }$ 

(ii) if Y is a random variable satisfying $X \le Y \mathrm { ~ a . s ~ }$ . for all $X \in { \mathcal { X } }$ , then $X ^ { * } \leq Y \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ 

Because random variables are defined only up to P-almost sure equivalence, it is in general not meaningful to speak of an $^ { 6 6 } \omega$ by $\omega ^ { \ast }$ supremum $\operatorname* { s u p } \{ X ( \omega ) ; X \in \mathcal { X } \}$ . The essential supremum substitutes for this concept. 

It is apparent from Definition A.1 that if the essential supremum of $\mathcal { X }$ exists, then it is unique. The purpose of this appendix is to establish its existence and a few basic properties. 

Given $\mathcal { X }$ as in Definition A.1 and given $A \in { \mathcal { F } } .$ , we will say that $\pi =$ $( K ; A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { K } ; X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { K } )$ is an -partition of A, provided that: 

(i) K is a positive integer, 

(ii) $A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { K }$ are disjoint sets in $\mathcal { F }$ whose union is $A ,$ and (iii) $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { K }$ are random variables in $\mathcal { X }$ 

For $\lambda \in ( 0 , \infty ]$ we define 

$$
\mu_ {\pi} ^ {\lambda} (A) \triangleq E \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \left(X _ {k} \wedge \lambda\right) \cdot 1 _ {A _ {k}},\tag{A.1}
$$

$$
\mu^ {\lambda} (A) \triangleq \sup \{\mu_ {\pi} ^ {\lambda} (A); \pi \text {is an} \mathcal {X} \text {-partition of} A \}.\tag{A.2}
$$

Then $\mu ^ { \lambda }$ is a nonnegative set function defined on ${ \mathcal F }$ , and is easily seen to be finitely additive. By the monotone convergence theorem, 

$$
\mu^ {\infty} (A) = \sup _ {\pi} \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \mu_ {\pi} ^ {\lambda} (A) = \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \sup _ {\pi} \mu_ {\pi} ^ {\lambda} (A) = \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \mu^ {\lambda} (A).\tag{A.3}
$$

Lemma A.2: For $\lambda \in ( 0 , \infty ] , \mu ^ { \lambda }$ is countably additive. 

Proof. We first consider the case $\lambda < \infty$ . Let $\{ A _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be an increasing sequence of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ with $A = \textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { j }$ . Then ${ \dot { \mu ^ { \lambda } } } ( A ) = \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A _ { j } ) +$ $\mu ^ { \lambda } ( A \backslash A _ { j } ) \geq \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A _ { j } )$ , so lim ${ \mathfrak { i } } _ { j \to \infty } \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A _ { j } ) \leq \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A )$ . Given $\varepsilon > 0$ , choose $j$ such that $P ( A \backslash A _ { j } ) < \varepsilon$ . From (A.1), (A.2), we have $\mu ^ { \lambda } ( A \backslash A _ { j } ) \leq \lambda \varepsilon$ , and thus $\mu ^ { \lambda } ( A ) \geq \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A _ { j } ) - \varepsilon$ . It follows that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { j  \infty } \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A _ { j } ) \geq \mu ^ { \lambda } ( A ) } \end{array}$ 

We finally consider the case $\lambda = \infty$ . We have from (A.3) that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {j \to \infty} \mu^ {\infty} (A _ {j}) = \sup _ {j} \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \mu^ {\lambda} (A _ {j}) = \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \sup _ {j} \mu^ {\lambda} (A _ {j}) \\ = \sup _ {\lambda \in (0, \infty)} \mu^ {\lambda} (A) = \mu^ {\infty} (A). \end{array}
$$

Theorem A.3: Let be a nonempty family of nonnegative random variables. Then $X ^ { * } = \mathrm { e s s }$ sup $\mathcal { X }$ exists. Furthermore, if $\mathcal { X }$ is closed under pairwise maximization, $i . e . , X , Y \in \mathcal { X }$ implies $X \vee Y \ \in \ \mathcal { X }$ , then there is a nondecreasing sequence $\{ Z _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ of random variables in satisfying $X ^ { * } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } Z _ { n }$ almost surely. 

Proof. Note first that $\mu ^ { \infty }$ defined by (A.1), (A.2) is absolutely continuous with respect to P. Define

For all $X \in { \mathcal { X } }$ and $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , we have $E ( 1 _ { A } X ) \leq \mu ^ { \infty } ( A ) = E ( 1 _ { A } X ^ { * } )$ , so condition (i) of Definition A.1 is satisfied. If $Y$ is as in condition (ii) of Definition A.1, then

Then $Y _ { n } \triangleq X _ { 1 } ^ { ( n ) } \vee \cdots \vee X _ { K ^ { ( n ) } } ^ { ( n ) }$ is in and $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ^ { n } ( \Omega ) \leq E Y _ { n } + \frac { 1 } { n } } \end{array}$ . Likewise, $Z _ { n } \overset { \triangle } { = } Y _ { 1 } \lor \cdots \lor Y _ { n }$ is in $\mathcal { X }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ^ { n } ( \Omega ) \leq E Z _ { n } + \frac { 1 } { n } } \end{array}$ . Letting $n \to \infty$ in this inequality, we obtain

E X ^ {*} = \mu^ {\infty} (\Omega) \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} E Z _ {n} = E (\lim _ {n \to \infty} Z _ {n}).

Because $Z _ { n } ~ \in ~ { \mathcal { X } }$ for each n, we have $Z ^ { n } \leq X ^ { * }$ and $\smash { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } Z _ { n } \leq X ^ { * } }$ almost surely. Hence, $X ^ { * } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } Z _ { n }$ almost surely. ␀

# Appendix B On the Model of Section 1.1.

In this appendix we return to the market model of Section 1.1. Recall that $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ is a complete probability space; $W ( t ) = ( W ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) , \ldots , W ^ { ( D ) } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime } .$ $0 \leq t \leq T$ , is a standard D-dimensional Brownian motion on this space; and $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is the augmentation by P-null sets of the filtration generated by $W ( \cdot )$ . The purpose of this appendix is to verify two assertions made in Section 1.1. We first show that if S( ) is a strictly positive and continuous semimartingale with respect to $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ , then $S ( \cdot )$ has the form 

$$
d S (t) = S (t) \left[ \beta (t) d t + d \alpha (t) + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {D} \rho_ {d} (t) d W ^ {(d)} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{B.1}
$$

where $\alpha ( \cdot )$ is singularly continuous. Applying this result to each one of the stock-price processes $S _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , S _ { N } ( \cdot )$ of Section 1.1, we conclude that $S _ { n } ( \cdot )$ has the form 

$$
d S _ {n} (t) = S _ {n} (t) \left[ b _ {n} (t) d t + d A _ {n} (t) + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {D} \sigma_ {n d} (t) d W ^ {(d)} (t) \right]\tag{B.2}
$$

for each $n = 1 , \ldots , N$ . Our second result is that each process $A _ { n } ( \cdot )$ of this representation (B.2) must agree with $A ( \cdot )$ , the process appearing in the representation 

$$
d S _ {0} (t) = S _ {0} (t) [ r (t) d t + d A (t) ]\tag{B.3}
$$

of the money-market price process $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ as in (1.1.6). If this were not the case, the model would admit arbitrage opportunities. 

Proposition B.1: Let $S : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega \to ( 0 , \infty )$ be an $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T ^ { - } }$ semimartingale with continuous paths. Then $( B . 1 )$ holds, where $\beta ( \cdot )$ and $\rho _ { d } ( \cdot ) , d = 1 , \ldots , D$ are suitable (t) <sub>t T</sub>-progressively measurable processes with $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } [ | \beta ( t ) | + \sum _ { d = 1 } ^ { D } ( \rho _ { d } ( t ) ) ^ { 2 } ] d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely, and $\alpha ( \cdot )$ is an (t) <sub>t T</sub>-progressively measurable process with paths that are continuous but singular with respect to Lebesgue measure; i.e., dα $( t ) / d t = 0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely, and with $\alpha ( 0 ) = 0$ 

Proof. By the definition of a semimartingale, S( ) can be written as $S ( t ) = S ( 0 ) + B ( t ) + M ( t ) , \quad 0 \leq t \leq T$ , where $B ( \cdot )$ is an $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T ^ { - } }$ adapted process with RCLL paths of finite variation on $[ 0 , T ] , M ( \cdot )$ is an $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } .$ -local martingale, and $B ( 0 ) ~ = ~ M ( 0 ) ~ = ~ 0 .$ . From the martingale representation theorem for the augmented Brownian filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ (e.g. Karatzas and Shreve (1991), pp. 182–184), we have the integral representation $\begin{array} { r } { M ( t ) = \sum _ { d = 1 } ^ { D } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \psi _ { d } ( s ) d W ^ { ( d ) } ( s ) , 0 \leq t \leq T } \end{array}$ , for suitable $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T ^ { - } } \mathrm { p r o g n }$ essively measurable processes $\psi _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \psi _ { D } ( \cdot )$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { d = 1 } ^ { D } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } ( \psi _ { d } ( s ) ) ^ { 2 } d s < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely. In particular, $M ( \cdot )$ has continuous paths, and since this is true for $S ( \cdot )$ , it is also true for $B ( \cdot )$ . We can then decompose $B ( \cdot )$ into its absolutely continuous part $\begin{array} { r } { B ^ { a c } ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \frac { d } { d s } B ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds and its singularly continuous part $B ^ { s } ( t ) = B ( t ) - B ^ { a c } ( t )$ . Noting that each path of the continuous, positive process $S ( \cdot )$ must be bounded away from zero, we obtain the desired representation, with 

$$
\beta (t) = \frac {1}{S (t)} \cdot \frac {d B (t)}{d t}, \alpha (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {1}{S (u)} d B ^ {s} (u), \rho_ {d} (t) = \frac {\psi_ {d} (t)}{S (t)}, d = 1, \ldots , D.
$$

Consider now a financial market , consisting in part of a money market with price per share $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ governed by (B.3), where $r ( \cdot )$ and $A ( \cdot )$ are (t) -progressively measurable, $A ( \cdot )$ is singularly continuous with $A ( 0 ) = 0$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } | r ( t ) | d t < \infty } \end{array}$ holds almost surely. The remainder of consists of N stocks with prices per share $S _ { n } ( \cdot )$ that are continuous, strictly positive $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ -semimartingales, $n = 1 , \ldots , N$ . According to Proposition B.1 these prices admit the representation (B.2), where all the processes $b _ { n } ( \cdot ) , A _ { n } ( \cdot ) , \sigma _ { n d } ( \cdot )$ appearing in (B.2) are $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T ^ { - } }$ progressively measurable, $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { N } [ | b _ { n } ( t ) | + \sum _ { d = 1 } ^ { D } ( \sigma _ { n d } ( t ) ) ^ { 2 } ] d t < \infty } \end{array}$ holds almost surely, each $A _ { n } ( \cdot )$ is singularly continuous, and $A _ { n } ( 0 ) = 0$ . This is the model of Definition 1.3.1, except that here we permit the diferent stocks to have singularly continuous parts that difer from $A ( \cdot )$ , and for the sake of simplicity we are setting $\delta _ { n } ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ for all $n = 1 , \ldots , N$ . As in Definition 1.3.1, we set $S _ { 0 } ( 0 ) = 1$ , but allow $S _ { 1 } ( 0 ) , \ldots , S _ { N } ( 0 )$ to be arbitrary positive constants. 

Following Definition 1.2.1, we define the gains process $G ^ { \pi } ( \cdot )$ correspond ing to a self-financed portfolio $\pi ( \cdot ) = ( \pi _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \pi _ { N } ( \cdot ) ) ^ { \prime }$ to be the solution to the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d G ^ {\pi} (t) = \left(G ^ {\pi} (t) - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \pi_ {n} (t)\right) \frac {d S _ {0} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \pi_ {n} (t) \frac {d S _ {n} (t)}{S _ {n} (t)} \\ \qquad = G ^ {\pi} (t) [ r (t)   d t + d A (t) ] + \pi^ {\prime} (t) [ (b (t) - r (t) \underline {{1}})   d t + d B (t) \\ \qquad + \sigma (t)   d W (t) ] \end{array}\tag{B.4}
$$

with the initial condition $G ^ { \pi } ( 0 ) = 0$ , where 

$$
B _ {n} (\cdot) \triangleq A _ {n} (\cdot) - A (\cdot), \quad B (\cdot) \triangleq (B _ {1} (\cdot), \ldots , B _ {N} (\cdot)) ^ {\prime}.\tag{B.5}
$$

By analogy with Definitions 1.2.4 and 1.4.1, a self-financed portfolio $\pi ( \cdot )$ is called 

(i) tame if the process $G _ { \pi } ( \cdot ) / S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is almost surely bounded from below; (ii) an arbitrage opportunity if it is tame and satisfies 

$$
P [ G ^ {\pi} (T) \geq 0 ] = 1, \quad P [ G ^ {\pi} (T) > 0 ] > 0.\tag{B.6}
$$

Theorem B.2: In order to exclude arbitrage opportunities from the model of (B.2), it is necessary that 

$$
A _ {n} (\cdot) = A (\cdot), \quad \forall n = 1, \dots , N,\tag{B.7}
$$

The proof of Theorem B.2, which occupies the remainder of this section, uses a random time change. To set up the notation, we rewrite (B.4) in the more compact form

But $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \dot { A } } _ { n , k } = { \dot { \Omega } }$ and we see that $X ( \tau ( s , \omega ) , \omega )$ is a $B ( [ 0 , r - \epsilon ] ) \otimes \mathcal { H } ( r ) / \mathcal { B } ( \mathbb { R } ) \ – \mathrm { m } \ /$ easurable mapping from $[ 0 , r - \epsilon ] \times \Omega$ to R. Since $\epsilon \in [ 0 , r )$ is arbitrary, the mapping $( s , \omega ) \mapsto X ( \tau ( s , \omega ) , \omega )$ is $ { \mathcal { B } ( [ 0 , r ) ) \otimes }  { \mathcal { H } ( r ) / B (  { \mathbb { R } } ) }$ -measurable on $[ 0 , r ) \times \Omega$ . We have already shown that $\omega \mapsto X ( \tau ( r , \omega ) , \omega )$ is $\mathcal { H } ( r ) / B ( [ 0 , r ] )$ )-measurable, and we conclude that $\tilde { X } ( \cdot , \cdot ) \mid _ { [ 0 , r ] \times \Omega }$ is $B ( [ 0 , r ] ) \otimes \mathcal { H } ( r ) / B ( \mathbb { R } )$ )-measurable. This is the requirement of progressive measurability. 

To prove (iv), we note that (B.10) gives, almost surely, 

$$
C (t _ {2}) - C (t _ {1}) = (t _ {2} - t _ {1}) + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} (\check {F} _ {n} (t _ {2}) - \check {F} _ {n} (t _ {1})), \quad 0 \leq t _ {1} \leq t _ {2} \leq T,
$$

whence also 

$$
\begin{array}{l} s _ {2} - s _ {1} \geq C (\tau (s _ {2})) - C (\tau (s _ {1})) \\ \qquad = \tau (s _ {2}) - \tau (s _ {1}) + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} (\check {F} _ {n} (\tau (s _ {2})) - \check {F} _ {n} (\tau (s _ {1}))) \\ \qquad \geq \tau (s _ {2}) - \tau (s _ {1}) + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} | H _ {n} (s _ {2}) - H _ {n} (s _ {1}) |, \quad 0 \leq s _ {1} \leq s _ {2} <   \infty . \end{array}

This proves the Lipschitz continuity of $\tau ( \cdot )$ and $H _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , H _ { N } ( \cdot )$ , with Lipschitz constant equal to 1. ␀ 

We note that for proving Theorem B.2, it is enough to show that the process 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{c} B _ {n} (\cdot) = A _ {n} (\cdot) - A (\cdot) \text {   of   (B.5)   is   absolutely } \\ \text { continuous   with   respect   to   Lebesgue   measure } \\ \text { almost   surely,   for   every   } n = 1, \ldots , N. \end{array} \right\}\tag{B.15}
$$

Proof of Theorem B.2. Following the notation of Lemma B.3 (iii), whenever the process $\{ X ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ is $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ -progressively mea surable, we denote by $\{ { \tilde { X } } ( s ) = X ( \tau ( s ) ) ; 0 \leq s < \infty \}$ the corresponding time-changed process. (The sole exception to this convention is the use of $H _ { n } ( \cdot )$ to denote the time-change of $F _ { n } ( \cdot )$ ; see (B.12).) With this notation, equation (B.8) becomes (cf. Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Problem 3.4.5(vi) and Proposition 3.4.8) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {\tilde {G} ^ {\pi} (s)}{\tilde {S} _ {0} (s)} = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \int_ {0} ^ {s} \frac {1}{\tilde {S} _ {0} (v)} \tilde {\pi} _ {n} (v) \left[ \dot {H} _ {n} (v) d v + \sum_ {d = 1} ^ {D} \tilde {\sigma} _ {n d} (v) d \tilde {W} ^ {(d)} (v) \right], \\ 0 \leq s \leq C (T), \end{array}\tag{B.16}
$$

in view of (B.14). Each component of the D-dimensional process $\{ \tilde { W } ( s ) \stackrel { \triangle } { = }$ $W ( \tau ( s ) ) , 0 \leq s < \infty \}$ is an $\{ \mathcal { H } ( s ) \} _ { 0 \leq s < \infty ^ { - } }$ martingale, with 

$$
\langle \tilde {W} ^ {(k)}, \tilde {W} ^ {(l)} \rangle (s) = \delta_ {k l} \cdot \tau (s) = \delta_ {k l} \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {s} \dot {\tau} (v) d v,\tag{B.17}
$$

from (B.13). Therefore, there exists a D-dimensional Brownian motion $\tilde { B } ( \cdot )$ on the probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ (possibly extended to accommodate ad ditional independent Brownian motions; see Karatzas and Shreve (1991), pp. 170–173), such that 

$$
\tilde {W} ^ {(d)} (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {s} \sqrt {\dot {\tau} (v)} d \tilde {B} ^ {(d)} (v), 0 \leq s <   \infty , d = 1, \ldots , D,\tag{B.18}
$$

almost surely. 

Now consider the self-financed portfolio process $\pi ( \cdot )$ given as 

$$
\pi_ {n} (t) = \tilde {\pi} _ {n} (C (t)), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, \quad n = 1, \ldots , N,\tag{B.19}
$$

where 

$$
\tilde {\pi} _ {n} (s) \stackrel {\triangle} {=} \operatorname{sgn} (\dot {H} _ {n} (s)) \cdot 1 _ {\{\dot {\tau} (s) = 0 \}}, \quad 0 \leq s <   \infty , \quad n = 1, \ldots , N.\tag{B.20}
$$

In light of (B.16), (B.18) we have then 

$$
\frac {\tilde {G} ^ {\pi} (s)}{\tilde {S} _ {0} (s)} = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \int_ {0} ^ {s} \frac {1}{\tilde {S} _ {0} (v)} | \dot {H} _ {n} (v) | \cdot 1 _ {\{\dot {\tau} (v) = 0 \}} d v, \quad 0 \leq s \leq C (T),
$$

or equivalently, inverting the time change, 

$$
\frac {G ^ {\pi} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} \int_ {0} ^ {C (t)} \frac {1}{\tilde {S} _ {0} (v)} | \dot {H} _ {n} (v) | \cdot 1 _ {\{\dot {\tau} (v) = 0 \}} d v \geq 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{B.21}
$$

In particular, the self-financed portfolio $\pi ( \cdot )$ is tame. Suppose now that 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{c} \text {for some n = 1,\ldots,N and for some \Omega_{o} \in\mathcal {F} with} \\ P (\Omega_ {o}) > 0, \text {we have for every \omega\in\Omega_{o}}, \\ \text {meas} \{s \in [ 0, C (T, \omega) ]; \dot {H} _ {n} (s, \omega) \neq 0, \dot {\tau} (s, \omega) = 0 \} > 0. \end{array} \right\}\tag{B.22}
$$

Then from (B.21), (B.22), the random variable $G ^ { \pi } ( T )$ is almost surely nonnegative, and is positive with positive probability (i.e., satisfies the conditions (B.6)); consequently, the tame portfolio $\pi ( \cdot )$ of (B.19), (B.20) is an arbitrage opportunity in $\mathcal { M }$ . It follows that viability for , that is, absence of arbitrage opportunities, implies the negation of (B.22), namely, 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text { meas } \{s \in [ 0, C (T, \omega) ]; \dot {H} _ {n} (s, \omega) \neq 0,   \dot {\tau} (s, \omega) = 0 \} = 0 \\ \quad \text { holds   for   all } n = 1, \ldots , N, \forall \omega \in \Omega^ {*}, \\ \quad \text { for   some   event } \Omega^ {*} \in \mathcal {F} \text { with } P (\Omega^ {*}) = 1. \end{array} \right\}\tag{B.23}
$$

The following result then completes the proof of Theorem B.2. 

Lemma B.4: Condition (B.23) implies (B.15). 

Proof. Assume (B.23); from (B.9) it sufices to show that for each $n =$ $1 , \ldots , N$ and $\omega \in \Omega ^ { * }$ , we have 

$$
F _ {n} (\cdot , \omega) \text {   is   absolutely   continuous   on   } [ 0, T ]\tag{B.24}
$$

with respect to Lebesgue measure. Fix $n = 1 , \dots , N , \ \omega \in \Omega ^ { * } , \ \epsilon > 0$ , and choose $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} [ C ^ {a c} (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega) - C ^ {a c} (t _ {j}, \omega) ] <   \epsilon
$$

holds for every finite collection $\left\{ ( t _ { j } , t _ { j } ^ { \prime } ) \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { m }$ of nonoverlapping intervals in $[ 0 , T ]$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { m } ( t _ { j } ^ { \prime } - t _ { j } ) < \delta } \end{array}$ . Here $C ^ { a c } ( \cdot , \omega )$ is the absolutely continuous part of the continuous function $C ( \cdot , \omega )$ of (B.10). For every $n = 1 , \ldots , N $ , it follows from Lemma B.3(iv), (B.12), and (B.23) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} | F _ {n} (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega) - F _ {n} (t _ {j}, \omega) | = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} | H _ {n} (C (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega), \omega) - H _ {n} (C (t _ {j}, \omega), \omega) | \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \int_ {C (t _ {j}, \omega)} ^ {C (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega)} | \dot {H} _ {n} (v, \omega) |   d v \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \int_ {C (t _ {j}, \omega)} ^ {C (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega)} | \dot {H} _ {n} (v, \omega) | \cdot 1 _ {\{\dot {\tau} (v, \omega) > 0 \}}   d v \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \int_ {C (t _ {j}, \omega)} ^ {C (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega)} \dot {C} (\tau (v, \omega), \omega) \dot {\tau} (v, \omega)   d v \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \int_ {t _ {j}} ^ {t _ {j} ^ {\prime}} \dot {C} (\theta , \omega)   d \theta \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} [ C ^ {a c} (t _ {j} ^ {\prime}, \omega) - C ^ {a c} (t _ {j}, \omega) ] <   \epsilon . \end{array}
$$

# Appendix C On Theorem 6.4.1

The purpose of this appendix is to establish the implication $\mathrm { ( A ) { \Rightarrow } ( B ) }$ , and thereby complete the proof of Theorem 6.4.1. For this we assume throughout this appendix the conditions (3.4.15), (3.6.17) as well as (6.2.13) and (6.2.14), which are in force throughout Chapter 6. We assume also tha there exists a pair $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ that is optimal for the consump tion/investment Problem 6.2.6 in the constrained market $\mathcal M ( K )$ , and tha $V ( x ; K ) < \infty$ . We denote by $\widehat { X } ( \cdot ) = X ^ { x , \widehat { c } , \widehat { p } } ( \cdot )$ the corresponding wealth process, which satisfies 

$$
\frac {\widehat {X} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\hat {c} (u) d u}{S _ {0} (u)} = x + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\widehat {X} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{C.1}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} H _ {0} (t) \widehat {X} (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} H _ {0} (u) \widehat {c} (u)   d u = x + \int_ {0} ^ {t} H _ {0} (u) \widehat {X} (u) \lambda^ {\prime} (u)   d W (u), \\ 0 \leq t \leq T, \end{array}\tag{C.2}
$$

according to (6.3.1), (6.3.2), and (6.3.3), with 

$$
\lambda (t) \triangleq \sigma^ {\prime} (t) \hat {p} (t) - \theta (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{C.3}
$$

Our program is as follows. We shall construct a process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ for which the positive process ${ \widehat { X } } ( \cdot )$ can be represented as 

$$
\widehat {X} (t) = \frac {1}{H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (u) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (u) d u + H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) B _ {\hat {\nu}} \Bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{C.4}
$$

and the requirements 

$$
\hat {c} (t) = c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t), \text {   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{C.5}
$$

$$
\zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) + \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t) = 0, \mathrm{Lebesgue-a.e.} t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{C.6}
$$

hold almost surely. Then we shall have $X _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) = { \widehat X } ( \cdot ) = X ^ { x , { \hat { c } } , { \hat { p } } } ( \cdot )$ from 7(6.3.18), (C.4), and Remark 6.3.3. We may also then take $p _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot ) = \hat { p } ( \cdot )$ ), and (B) will be established. We prove the above facts in a series of lemmas. 

Lemma C.1: Suppose that for every $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , there is a consumption and portfolio-proportion process pair $( c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x ; K )$ satisfying 

$$
c _ {\epsilon} (t) \geq \alpha (\epsilon) \hat {c} (t), L e b e s g u e - a. e. t \in [ 0, T ] a n d X ^ {x, c _ {\epsilon}, p _ {\epsilon}} (T) \geq \beta (\epsilon) \widehat {X} (T)\tag{C.7}
$$

almost surely, where $\alpha ( \epsilon ) > 0$ and $\beta ( \epsilon ) > 0$ satisfy 

$$
0 <   \lim _ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1 - \alpha (\epsilon)}{\epsilon} <   \infty , \quad 0 <   \lim _ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1 - \beta (\epsilon)}{\epsilon} <   \infty .
$$

Then we have $( c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ for each $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {U _ {1} (t , \hat {c} (t)) - U _ {1} (t , c _ {\epsilon} (t))}{\epsilon}   d t \\ \qquad + \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) - U _ {2} (X ^ {x , c _ {\epsilon} , p _ {\epsilon}} (T))}{\epsilon} \bigg ] \geq 0. \end{array}\tag{C.8}
$$

Proof. The convexity of $U _ { 2 }$ implies the inequality 

$$
U _ {2} (\xi_ {2}) - U _ {2} (\xi_ {1}) \leq (\xi_ {2} - \xi_ {1}) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi_ {1})\tag{C.9}
$$

for all $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } > 0$ . Taking $\xi _ { 1 } = \xi \ge 1$ and $\xi _ { 2 } = 1$ , we obtain 

$$
\xi U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi) \leq U _ {2} (\xi) - U _ {2} (1) + U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi) \leq U _ {2} (\xi) - U _ {2} (1) + U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (1), \quad \xi \geq 1.
$$

On the other hand, 

$$
\xi U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\xi) \leq U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (1), \quad 0 <   \xi \leq 1,
$$

follows from (3.4.15). Similarly, for all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ ， 

$$
\xi U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \xi) \leq \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} U _ {1} (t, \xi) - U _ {1} (t, 1) + U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, 1), & \xi \geq 1, \\ U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, 1), & 0 <   \xi \leq 1. \end{array} \right.
$$

These inequalities and the finiteness of $V ( x ; K )$ imply 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \hat {c} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) 1 _ {\{\hat {c} (t) > 0 \}} d t + \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) 1 _ {\{\widehat {X} (T) > 0 \}} \right] \\ \leq \kappa + E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) 1 _ {\{\hat {c} (t) \geq 1 \}} d t + U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) 1 _ {\{\widehat {X} (T) \geq 1 \}} \right] <   \infty \end{array}\tag{C.10}
$$

for some real constant $\kappa .$ 

For suficiently small $\epsilon > 0$ , we have $0 < \beta ( \epsilon ) < 1$ . From (C.9), the monotonicity of $U _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$ , and (3.4.15), we have also 

$$
\begin{array}{l} U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) - U _ {2} (X ^ {x, c _ {\epsilon}, p _ {\epsilon}} (T)) \leq (\widehat {X} (T) - X ^ {x, c _ {\epsilon}, p _ {\epsilon}} (T)) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (X ^ {x, c _ {\epsilon}, p _ {\epsilon}} (T)) \\ \leq \frac {1 - \beta (\epsilon)}{\beta (\epsilon)} \beta (\epsilon) \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\beta (\epsilon) \widehat {X} (T)) \\ \leq \frac {1 - \beta (\epsilon)}{\beta (\epsilon)} \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)). \end{array} \tag {C.}\tag{C.11}
$$

The finiteness of $V ( x ; K )$ implies $E | U _ { 2 } ( \widehat { X } ( T ) ) | < \infty$ , which, in conjunction with (C.10) and (C.11), leads to 

$$
E \left(\min [ 0, U _ {2} (X ^ {x, c _ {\epsilon}, p _ {\epsilon}} (T)) ]\right) > - \infty .
$$

A similar argument shows that 

$$
U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) - U _ {1} (t, c _ {\epsilon} (t)) \leq \frac {1 - \alpha (\epsilon)}{\alpha (\epsilon)} \hat {c} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)),\tag{C.12}
$$

from which we conclude 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \min [ 0, U _ {1} (t, c _ {\epsilon} (t)) ] d t > - \infty .
$$

Hence, $( c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } ) \in \mathcal { A } _ { 3 } ( x ; K )$ for all suficiently small $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

Finally, the optimality of $( \hat { c } , \hat { p } )$ implies 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \frac {U _ {1} (t , \hat {c} (t)) - U _ {1} (t , c _ {\epsilon} (t))}{\epsilon} d t + \frac {U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) - U _ {2} (X ^ {x , c _ {\epsilon} , p _ {\epsilon}} (T))}{\epsilon} \right] \geq 0.
$$

The bounds (C.10), (C.11), and (C.12) permit us to use Fatou’s lemma to obtain (C.8). ␀ 

Lemma C.2: We have the almost sure inequalities 

$$
\hat {c} (t) > 0, \text {   for   Lebesgue - a.e.   } t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{C.13}
$$

$$
\widehat {X} (t) > 0, \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{C.14}

Proof. We set 

$$
c _ {1} (t) = \frac {x}{2 T} S _ {0} (t), \quad p _ {1} (t) = 0 \quad \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq T,

In particular, $( c _ { 1 } , p _ { 1 } ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x ; K )$ . For $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ we define 

$$
c _ {\epsilon} (t) \triangleq \epsilon c _ {1} (t) + (1 - \epsilon) \hat {c} (t), \quad p _ {\epsilon} (t) \triangleq \frac {(1 - \epsilon) \widehat {X} (t) \hat {p} (t)}{\epsilon X _ {1} (t) + (1 - \epsilon) \widehat {X} (t)}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,

\begin{array}{l} x - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {c _ {\epsilon} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} d u + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {X _ {\epsilon} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} p _ {\epsilon} ^ {\prime} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) \\ \qquad = \epsilon \left[ x - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {c _ {1} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} d u \right] \\ \qquad + (1 - \epsilon) \left[ x - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\hat {c} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} d u + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\widehat {X} (u)}{S _ {0} (u)} \hat {p} (u) \sigma (u) d W _ {0} (u) \right] \\ \qquad = \frac {X _ {\epsilon} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)}, \end{array}\tag{C.15}
