so that $X _ { \epsilon } ( \cdot ) = X ^ { x , c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } } ( \cdot )$ . Thus, we have the situation described in Lemma C.1 with $\alpha ( \epsilon ) = \beta ( \epsilon ) = 1 - \epsilon$ , and this implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {U _ {1} (t , \hat {c} (t)) - U _ {1} (t , c _ {\epsilon} (t))}{\epsilon} d t + \varliminf_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {U _ {2} (\widehat {X} (T)) - U _ {2} (X _ {\epsilon} (T))}{\epsilon} \right] \\ \leq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} (\hat {c} (t) - c _ {1} (t)) U _ {1} (t, c _ {\epsilon} (t)) d t \right. \\ \quad \left. + \varlimsup_ {\epsilon \downarrow 0} (\widehat {X} (T) - X _ {1} (T)) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (X _ {\epsilon} (T)) \right] \\ \leq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \hat {c} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) 1 _ {\{\hat {c} (t) > 0 \}} d t + \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) 1 _ {\{\widehat {X} (T) > 0 \}} \right. \\ \quad \left. - \int_ {0} ^ {T} c _ {1} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t - X _ {1} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) \right] \end{array}

in conjunction with (C.9). Since $X _ { 1 } ( T ) > 0$ and $c _ { 1 } ( t ) > 0$ for all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely, (C.10) and (6.2.14) imply (C.13) and 

$$

The left-hand side of (C.2) is nonnegative, and the right-hand side is a local martingale under $P$ and thus also a supermartingale. Solving (C.2) for

We introduce the continuous, nondecreasing process 

$$
A (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \hat {c} (s) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (s, \hat {c} (s)) d s, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{C.17}

and the continuous martingale 

$$
\begin{array}{l} M (t) \triangleq E [ A (T) + \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] \\ = E M (T) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \psi^ {\prime} (s)   d W (s), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T. \end{array}\tag{C.18}
$$

Here $E A ( T ) \leq E M ( T ) < \infty$ from (C.10), and the progressively measurable process $\psi : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \psi ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely, is uniquely determined from (C.18) by the martingale representation theorem. 

Lemma C.3: The consumption rate process $\hat { c } ( \cdot )$ is given by 

$$
\hat {c} (t) = I _ {1} \left(t, \frac {M (t) - A (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)}\right), f o r L e b e s g u e - a. e. t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{C.19}
$$

almost surely. 

Proof. From (C.1) we see that 

$$
d \left(\frac {\widehat {X} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)}\right) = - \frac {\hat {c} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} + \frac {\widehat {X} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \sigma (t) d W _ {0} (t),
$$

and the solution to this stochastic diferential equation with initial condition ${ \widehat { X } } ( 0 ) = x$ is given by 

$$
\frac {\widehat {X} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} = x \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(f (s) + \frac {1}{2} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (s) \hat {p} (s) \| ^ {2}\right) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (s) \sigma (s) d W _ {0} (s) \right\},\tag{C.20}
$$

where 

$$
f (t) \triangleq \frac {\hat {c} (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)} > 0 \quad \text { for   Lebesgue - a.e. } t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{C.21}
$$

almost surely. We introduce a small random perturbation of the process $f ( \cdot )$ as follows: 

$$
f _ {\epsilon} (t) \stackrel {\triangle} {=} f (t) + \epsilon \rho (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

where $\rho \colon [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega $ R is an arbitrary but fixed progressively measurable process with $| \rho ( t ) | \leq 1 \land f ( t )$ and $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . We further define 

$$
X _ {\epsilon} (t) \triangleq \widehat {X} (t) e ^ {- \epsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (s) d s};
$$

$$
c _ {\epsilon} (t) \stackrel {{\triangle}} {{=}} X _ {\epsilon} (t) f _ {\epsilon} (t) = \left[ \hat {c} (t) + \epsilon \rho (t) \widehat {X} (t) \right] e ^ {- \epsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (s) d s}.
$$

Clearly, $X ^ { x , c _ { \epsilon } , \hat { p } } ( t ) = X _ { \epsilon } ( t ) > 0$ , and thus $( c _ { \epsilon } , \hat { p } ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x ; K )$ 

We are now in the situation described by Lemma C.1 with $\alpha ( \epsilon ) = \beta ( \epsilon ) =$ $e ^ { - \epsilon T }$ , and conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) \left[ \hat {c} (t) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (s)   d s - \rho (t) \widehat {X} (t) \right]   d t \\ + E \left[ U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) \widehat {X} (T) \int_ {0} ^ {T} \rho (t)   d t \right] \geq 0. \end{array}\tag{C.22}
$$

We examine further the terms appearing in (C.22). Note first that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \left[ U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) \hat {c} (t) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (s) d s \right] d t \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \rho (s) d s d A (t) = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {s} ^ {T} d A (t) \rho (s) d s \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} [ A (T) - A (s) ] \rho (s) d s = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} [ A (T) - A (t) ] \rho (t) d t. \end{array}\tag{C.23}
$$

Furthermore, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left[ U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) \widehat {X} (T) \int_ {0} ^ {T} \rho (t) d t \right] \\ = E \left[ (M (T) - A (T)) \int_ {0} ^ {T} \rho (t) d t \right] \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ E [ M (T) \rho (t) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] ] d t - \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ A (T) \rho (t) ] d t \\ = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} [ M (t) - A (T) ] \rho (t) d t. \end{array}\tag{C.24}
$$

Substitution of (C.23) and (C.24) into (C.22) yields 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \rho (t) \left[ M (t) - A (t) - \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) \right] d t \geq 0.\tag{C.25}
$$

But except for the condition $| \rho ( t ) | \leq 1 \land f ( t )$ , the process $\rho ( \cdot )$ is arbitrary. Because $f ( t )$ is strictly positive (see (C.21)), the expression 

$$
M (t) - A (t) - \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t))
$$

must be zero for Lebesgue-amost-every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely; otherwise, we could choose $\rho ( t )$ such that (C.25) is violated. This leads immediately to (C.19). ␀ 

Lemma C.4: With $\lambda ( \cdot )$ and $\psi ( \cdot )$ defined by (C.3) and (C.18), respectively, the process 

$$
\hat {\nu} (t) \triangleq \sigma (t) \left[ \lambda (t) - \frac {\psi (t)}{M (t) - A (t)} \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{C.26}
$$

satisfies (C.6) and 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \left(\zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) + \| \hat {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2}\right) d t <   \infty ,\tag{C.27}
$$

$$
\hat {\nu} (t) \in \widetilde {K}, f o r L e b e s g u e - a. e. t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{C.28}
$$

almost surely. 

Proof. Here again the idea is to start with the expression (C.20) for ${ \widehat { X } } ( \cdot )$ and introduce a small random perturbation. This time we perturb 7the optimal portfolio-proportion process $\hat { p } ( \cdot )$ by defining 

$$
p _ {\epsilon} (t) \triangleq \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (1 - \epsilon) \hat {p} (t) + \epsilon \eta (t), & 0 \leq t \leq \tau_ {n}, \\ \hat {p} (t), & \tau_ {n} <   t \leq T \end{array} \right.
$$

for some arbitrary but fixed progressively measurable process $\eta \colon [ 0 , T ] \times$ $\Omega \to K$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \eta ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely. Here $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , and $\{ \tau _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ to be chosen later, is a nondecreasing sequence of stopping times satisfying $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \tau _ { n } = T$ almost surely. Clearly, $p _ { \epsilon } ( \cdot )$ takes values in $K$ . With $f ( t ) \stackrel { \triangle } { = }$ $\frac { \hat { c } ( t ) } { \widehat { X } ( t ) }$ as in (C.21), we introduce 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {X _ {\epsilon} (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} \triangleq x \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(f (s) + \frac {1}{2} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (s) p _ {\epsilon} (s) \| ^ {2}\right) d s \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} p _ {\epsilon} ^ {\prime} (s) \sigma (s)   d W _ {0} (s) \Bigg \}, \\ c _ {\epsilon} (t) \triangleq f (t) X _ {\epsilon} (t), \end{array}
$$

and notice that $X ^ { x , c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } } ( t ) = X _ { \epsilon } ( t ) > 0$ , so that $( c _ { \epsilon } , p _ { \epsilon } ) \in \mathcal { A } ( x ; K )$ . The processes $p _ { \epsilon } ( \cdot ) , c _ { \epsilon } ( \cdot )$ and $X _ { \epsilon } ( \cdot )$ depend on $n _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , although we do not indicate this explicitly. We write 

$$
X _ {\epsilon} (t) = \widehat {X} (t) \exp \left[ \epsilon N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) - \frac {1}{2} \epsilon^ {2} \langle N \rangle (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) \right],
$$

where 

$$
N (t) \triangleq \int_ {0} ^ {t} (\eta (s) - \hat {p} (s)) ^ {\prime} \sigma (s) \widehat {W} (s),
$$

$$
\langle N \rangle (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (s) (\eta (s) - \hat {p} (s)) \| ^ {2} d s,
$$

$$
\widehat {W} (t) \triangleq W (t) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \lambda (s) d s.
$$

We can define now the nondecreasing sequence of stopping times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {n} \triangleq \inf \left\{t \in [ 0, T ]; \quad | N (t) | + \langle N \rangle (t) + A (t) + | M (t) | \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \| \psi (s) \| ^ {2} d s \geq n \right\} \wedge T, \quad n = 1, 2, \ldots , \end{array}
$$

and observe that $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \tau _ { n } = T$ almost surely, as well as 

$$
\frac {c _ {\epsilon} (t)}{\hat {c} (t)} = \frac {X _ {\epsilon} (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)} \geq e ^ {- \frac {3}{2} \epsilon n}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

Thus, for each fixed $n ,$ we are in the situation described by Lemma C.1 with $\alpha ( \epsilon ) = \beta ( \epsilon ) = e ^ { - \frac { 3 } { 2 } \epsilon n }$ . The conclusion of that lemma is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \geq E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} N (t \wedge \tau_ {n}) \hat {c} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t \right. \\ \quad \left. + N (T \wedge \tau_ {n}) \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} N _ {n} (t) d A (t) + N _ {n} (T) (M (T) - A (T)) \right], \end{array}\tag{C.29}
$$

in the notation (C.17), (C.18) and with ${ N } _ { n } ( t ) = N ( t \wedge \tau _ { n } )$ . The product rule of stochastic calculus gives now 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \big (M (T) N _ {n} (T) \big) = E \big (M (\tau_ {n}) N (\tau_ {n}) \big) \\ \qquad = E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} \big (\eta (t) - \hat {p} (t) \big) ^ {\prime} \sigma (t) \big (\psi (t) - M (t) \lambda (t) \big) d t, \\ E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} N _ {n} (t) d A (t) - A (T) N _ {n} (T) \right] \\ \qquad = - E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} A (t) d N _ {n} (t) \right] \\ \qquad = E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} A (t) \big (\eta (t) - \hat {p} (t) \big) ^ {\prime} \sigma (t) \big (- d W (t) + \lambda (t) d t \big) \\ \qquad = E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} A (t) \big (\eta (t) - \hat {p} (t) \big) ^ {\prime} \sigma (t) \lambda (t) d t. \end{array}
$$

Substituting back into (C.29), we obtain 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {n}} (M (t) - A (t)) (\eta (t) - \hat {p} (t)) ^ {\prime} \hat {\nu} (t) d t \geq 0,\tag{C.30}
$$

where $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ is defined by (C.26). 

The process $M ( t ) - A ( t ) = \widehat { X } ( t ) U _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( t , \widehat { c } ( t ) )$ (see (C.19)) is continuous in 7t and strictly positive almost surely. Letting $p$ be a fixed vector in K and substituting the process $\eta ( t ) \ \stackrel { \angle } { = } \ p 1 _ { \{ ( p - \hat { p } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime } \hat { \nu } ( t ) < 0 \} } + \hat { p } ( t ) 1 _ { \{ ( p - \hat { p } ( t ) ) ^ { \prime } \hat { \nu } ( t ) \geq 0 \} }$ into (C.30), we see that the set 

$$
F _ {p} \stackrel {\triangle} {=} \{(t, \omega) \in [ 0, T ] \times \Omega ; (p - \hat {p} (t)) ^ {\prime} \hat {\nu} (t) <   0 \}
$$

has Lebesgue P-measure zero. Likewise, the set $F \triangleq \cup _ { p \in K \cap \mathbb { Q } ^ { N } } F _ { p }$ has product measure zero. (Here $\mathbb { Q } ^ { N }$ denotes the set of vectors in $\mathbf { \mathbb { R } } ^ { N }$ with rational coordinates.) We have 

$$
p ^ {\prime} \hat {\nu} (t, \omega) \geq \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t, \omega) \hat {\nu} (t, \omega), \text {   for   all   } (t, \omega) \notin F.\tag{C.31}
$$

For $( t , \omega ) \not \in F$ , (C.31) implies 

$$
\zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) = \sup _ {p \in K} \big (- p ^ {\prime} \hat {\nu} (t) \big) \leq - \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t),
$$

and since $\hat { p } ^ { \prime } ( t ) \in K$ , we in fact have $\zeta ( \hat { \nu } ( t ) ) = - \hat { p } ^ { \prime } ( t ) \hat { \nu } ( t )$ for Lebesguealmost-every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely. This is (C.6). 

From (C.6) it follows that $\zeta ( \hat { \nu } ( t ) ) < \infty$ , and hence $\hat { \nu } ( t ) \in \widetilde { K }$ for Lebesguealmost-every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely. This is (C.28). 

We next note that $\widehat { X } ( T ) > 0$ implies $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \hat { p } ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely 7(Definition 6.2.4). The uniform boundedness assumed for $\sigma ( \cdot )$ implies that $\lambda ( \cdot )$ defined by (C.3) satisfies $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \lambda ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely. For fixed $\omega ,$ , the positive continuous process $M ( \cdot ) - A ( \cdot )$ is bounded away from zero uniformly in $t ,$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \psi ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ holds almost surely. It follows from these facts that $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ defined by (C.26) satisfies $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \| \hat { \nu } ( t ) \| ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ almost surely. Furthermore, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) d t \leq \int_ {0} ^ {T} | \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t) | d t \leq \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \hat {p} (t) \| ^ {2} d t\right) ^ {\frac {1}{2}} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} \| \hat {\nu} (t) \| ^ {2} d t\right) ^ {\frac {1}{2}},
$$

which is almost surely finite. Condition (C.27) is satisfied, and the lemma is established. ␀ 

It remains to prove that $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ and (C.4), (C.5) are satisfied. We first prove (C.4), (C.5). 

## Lemma C.5: Equations (C.4) and (C.5) hold.

Proof. Before beginning the computations, we recall the equations 

$$
\lambda (t) = \sigma^ {\prime} (t) \hat {p} (t) - \theta (t),\tag{C.3}
$$

$$
\zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) = - \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \hat {\nu} (t),\tag{C.6}
$$

$$
A (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \hat {c} (s) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (s, \hat {c} (s)) d s,\tag{C.17}
$$

$$
M (t) = E [ A (T) + \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) | \mathcal {F} (t) ]
$$

$$
= E M (T) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \psi^ {\prime} (s) d W (s),\tag{C.18}
$$

$$
f (t) = \frac {\hat {c} (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)},\tag{C.21}
$$

$$
\hat {\nu} (t) = \sigma (t) \left[ \lambda (t) - \frac {\psi (t)}{M (t) - A (t)} \right],\tag{C.26}
$$

$$
S ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t) = S _ {0} (t) \exp \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {t} \zeta (\hat {\nu} (s)) d s \right],\tag{5.5.7}
$$

$$
\theta_ {\hat {\nu}} (t) = \theta (t) + \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \hat {\nu} (t).\tag{5.5.9}
$$

We note also that the conclusion of Lemma C.3 can be written as 

$$
M (t) - A (t) = \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)).\tag{C.32}
$$

It follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & d \Big (\widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) \Big) \\ & \quad = d M (t) - d A (t) \\ & \quad = \psi^ {\prime} (t) d W (t) - \hat {c} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t \\ & \quad = (M (t) - A (t)) (\lambda (t) - \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \hat {\nu} (t)) ^ {\prime} d W (t) \\ & \quad \quad - f (t) \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d t \\ & \quad = \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) [ (\lambda (t) - \sigma^ {- 1} (t) \hat {\nu} (t)) ^ {\prime} d W (t) - f (t) d t ]. \end{array}
$$

From (C.20) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {\widehat {X} (t)}{S _ {0} ^ {(\widehat {\nu})} (t)} = x \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \bigg (f (s) + \zeta (\widehat {\nu} (s)) + \frac {1}{2} \| \sigma^ {\prime} (s) \widehat {p} (s) \| ^ {2} \bigg) d s \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \widehat {p} ^ {\prime} (s) \sigma (s)   d W _ {0} (s) \right\}, \end{array}
$$

which yields the diferential formula 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d \left(\frac {S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)}\right) = \frac {S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t)}{\widehat {X} (t)} \left[ \big (f (t) + \zeta (\hat {\nu} (t)) + \| \sigma^ {\prime} (t) \hat {p} (t) \| ^ {2}\right) d t \\ - \hat {p} ^ {\prime} (t) \sigma (t)   d W _ {0} (t) ]. \end{array}
$$

The product rule for stochastic integration and the above formulas give 

$$
d \left(S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t) U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t))\right) = - \theta_ {\hat {\nu}} (t) S _ {0} ^ {(\hat {\nu})} (t) U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) d W (t),
$$

and hence $S _ { 0 } ^ { ( \hat { \nu } ) } ( t ) U _ { 1 } ( t , \hat { c } ( t ) ) = y _ { * } Z _ { \hat { \nu } } ( t )$ (see (5.5.10)), for some $y _ { * } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ In other words, 

$$
U _ {1} (t, \hat {c} (t)) = y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \quad \text { for   Lebesgue - a.e. } t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{C.33}
$$

almost surely. Without loss of generality, we can modify $\hat { c } ( t )$ as necessary so that (C.33) holds for every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ almost surely. Using (C.33), (C.32), (C.17), and (C.18), we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} y _ {*} \widehat {X} (t) H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (t)) = \widehat {X} (t) U _ {1} ^ {\prime} (t, \hat {c} (t)) \\ \qquad = M (t) - A (t) \\ \qquad = E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} y _ {*} H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (s) \hat {c} (s)   d s + \widehat {X} (T) U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)) \bigg |   \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \end{array}
$$

for $0 \leq t \leq T$ . Evaluating this equation at $t = T$ , we see that 

$$
y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) = U _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\widehat {X} (T)),\tag{C.34}
$$

and hence 

$$
\widehat {X} (t) = \frac {1}{H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (t)} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {T} H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (s) \widehat {c} (s) d s + H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (T) \widehat {X} (T) \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right].\tag{C.35}
$$

From (C.33), (C.34), we have 

$$
\hat {c} (t) = I _ {1} (t, y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)), \quad \widehat {X} (T) = I _ {2} (y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)),\tag{C.36}
$$

and substitution into (C.35), evaluated at $t = 0$ , yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} x = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (s) I _ {1} (s, y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (s))   d s + H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) I _ {2} (y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T)) \right] \\ = \mathcal {X} _ {\hat {\nu}} (y _ {*}), \end{array}\tag{C.37}
$$

which is thus seen to be finite. Therefore, $y _ { * } = \ y _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ , and $\boldsymbol { B } _ { \hat { \nu } }$ defined by (6.3.16) is ${ \widehat { X } } ( T )$ , while $c _ { \hat { \nu } } ( \cdot )$ defined by (6.3.17) is $\hat { c } ( \cdot )$ . Thus, equation (C.5) 7holds. Equation (C.4) now follows from (C.35). ␀ 

The following lemma concludes the proof of Theorem 6.4.1. 

Lemma C.6: The process $\hat { \nu } ( \cdot )$ defined by $\left( C . \mathcal { Z } 6 \right)$ is in the set $\mathcal { D } _ { 0 }$ of $( 6 . 3 . \mathcal { Z } 4 )$ 

Proof. We note first from (6.2.1) and (6.2.4) that 

$$
E H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \leq \frac {1}{s _ {0}} E Z _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) \leq \frac {1}{s _ {0}} e ^ {\zeta_ {0} t},
$$

and hence 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) d t + H _ {\hat {\nu}} (T) \right] <   \infty .
$$

With $y _ { * } = \mathcal { V } _ { \hat { \nu } } ( x )$ as in (C.37), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} U _ {1} (t, c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) - y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) c _ {\hat {\nu}} (t) = \widetilde {U} _ {1} (t, y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t)) \\ \geq U _ {1} (t, 1) - y _ {*} H _ {\hat {\nu}} (t), \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} U _ {2} (t, \widehat {X} (T)) - y _ {*} H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (T) \widehat {X} (T) = \widetilde {U} _ {2} (y _ {*} H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (T)) \\ \geq U _ {2} (1) - y _ {*} H _ {\widehat {\nu}} (T) \end{array}
$$

from the definition of convex dual functions and (C.36). It follows that 

$$

# Appendix D Optimal Stopping for Continuous-Parameter Processes

We discuss briefly in this appendix the problem of optimal stopping for random processes in continuous time. (A similar treatment for random sequences appears in Chapter VI of Neveu (1975).) The results presented here are not the most general one can obtain, but will sufice for the purposes of Chapter 2, where they are used rather extensively. For more general treatments we refer the reader to El Karoui (1981), as well as Bismut and Skalli (1977), Fakeev (1970, 1971), Xue (1984), and Shiryaev (1978) for the Markovian case. 

Throughout this appendix we shall consider a nonnegative process $Y ~ = ~ \{ Y ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 ~ \leq ~ t ~ \leq ~ T \}$ with right-continuous paths and $Y ( T ) \ \leq$ ${ \overline { { \operatorname * { l i m } } } } _ { t \uparrow T } Y ( t ) a . s .$ , defined on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and adapted to a filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ satisfying the usual conditions of right continuity and augmentation by the null sets of ${ \mathcal { F } } = { \mathcal { F } } ( T )$ . We suppose that $\mathcal { F } ( 0 )$ contains only sets of probability zero or one. The time horizon $T \in ( 0 , \infty ]$ is a fixed constant; if $T = \infty$ , we interpret $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } ( \infty ) \stackrel { \triangle } { = } \sigma \left( \bigcup _ { 0 \leq t < \infty } \mathcal { F } ( t ) \right) } \end{array}$ and $Y ( \infty ) \triangleq { \overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } } _ { t  \infty } Y ( t )$ . We denote by $s$ the class of $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \}$ -stopping times with values in [0, T]. For any stopping time $v \in S$ , we set $S _ { v } \overset { \triangle } { = } \{ \tau { \in } S ; \tau \geq$ v a.s. . 

The optimal stopping problem consists in 

(i) computing the maximal “expected reward” 

$$
Z (0) \triangleq \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S}} E Y (\tau),\tag{D.1}
$$

(ii) finding necessary and $1 / \mathrm { o r }$ suficient conditions for the existence of a stopping time $\tau _ { * }$ that is “optimal,” i.e., its expected reward $E Y ( \tau _ { * } )$ attains the supremum in (D.1), and then 

(iii) characterizing such a $\tau _ { * }$ and studying its properties. 

Throughout this appendix, we assume 

$$
0 <   Z (0) <   \infty .\tag{D.2}
$$

Under this assumption, we construct the so-called Snell envelope $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ of $Y ( \cdot )$ , namely, the smallest RCLL supermartingale that dominates $Y ( \cdot )$ . A stopping time $\tau _ { * }$ is optimal if and only if $\{ Z ^ { 0 } ( t \wedge \tau _ { * } ) , \mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq \dot { T } \}$ is a martingale and $Z ^ { 0 } \bar { ( \tau _ { * } ) } = Y ( \tau _ { * } )$ a.s. (Theorem D.9). In order to prove the existence of an optimal stopping time, we shall impose the stronger condition $E [ \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } Y ( t ) ] < \infty$ , under which the stopping time 

$$
D _ {*} (0) = \inf \{t \in [ 0, T ]; Z ^ {0} (t) = Y (t) \}
$$

can be shown to be optimal if, in addition, the paths of $Y ( \cdot )$ are continuous (Theorem D.12). Following this result, we decompose the Snell envelope into the diference of a martingale and a nondecreasing process, and use this decomposition to characterize optimal stopping times. 

The key to our study is provided by the family $\{ Z ( v ) \} _ { v \in { \cal S } }$ of random variables 

$$
Z (v) \triangleq \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S} _ {v}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ], \quad v \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{D.3}
$$

(See Appendix A for the definition and properties of essential supremum.) We shall see in Proposition D.2 that the assumption (D.2) guarantees $E Z ( v ) \ < \ \infty$ for all $v \in S$ . The random variable $Z ( v )$ is the optimal conditional expected reward for stopping at time v or later. Since each deterministic time $t { \in } [ 0 , T ]$ is also a stopping time, (D.3) defines a nonneg ative, adapted process $\{ Z ( t ) , \mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ . For $v \in S$ , it is tempting to regard $Z ( v )$ as the process $\{ Z ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ evaluated at the stopping time v. We shall see in Theorem D.7 that there is indeed a modifica tion $\{ Z ^ { 0 } ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ of the process $\{ Z ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ i.e., $P [ Z ^ { 0 } ( t ) = Z ( t ) ] = 1$ for all $t { \in } [ 0 , T ]$ , such that for each $v \in S$ we have 

$$
Z (v) (\omega) = Z ^ {0} (v (\omega), \omega), \quad P \text {-a.e.} \omega \in \Omega .
$$

This process $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is the Snell envelope of $Y ( \cdot )$ 

We now begin an examination of the family of random variables $\{ Z ( v ) \} _ { v \in { \cal S } }$ 

Lemma D.1: For any $v \in S$ and $\tau { \in } S _ { v }$ , the family $\{ E [ Y ( \rho ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] \} _ { \rho \in \mathcal { S } _ { \tau } }$ is closed under pairwise maximization. Furthermore, there is a sequence $\{ \rho _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ ofstopping times in $S _ { \tau }$ such that the sequence $\{ E [ Y ( \rho _ { n } ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ is nondecreasing and 

$$
\operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\rho \in \mathcal {S} _ {\tau}} E [ Y (\rho) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = \lim _ {n \to \infty} E [ Y (\rho_ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ].
$$

Proof. Let $\rho _ { 1 }$ and $\rho _ { 2 }$ be in $S _ { \tau }$ and set 

$$
A = \{E [ Y (\rho_ {1}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \geq E [ Y (\rho_ {2}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \}, \quad \rho_ {3} = \rho_ {1} 1 _ {A} + \rho_ {2} 1 _ {A ^ {c}}.
$$

Because $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { v }$ , the random time $\rho _ { 3 }$ is a stopping time. In particular, $\rho _ { 3 } { \in } S _ { \tau }$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r} E [ Y (\rho_ {3}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = 1 _ {A} E [ Y (\rho_ {1}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] + 1 _ {A ^ {c}} E [ Y (\rho_ {2}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \\ = E [ Y (\rho_ {1}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \vee E [ Y (\rho_ {2}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ]. \end{array}
$$

The remainder of the lemma follows from Theorem A.3 in Appendix A. ␀ 

Proposition D.2: For any $v \in S , \sigma \in S$ , and $\tau { \in } S _ { v }$ , we have 

$$
Z (v) = Z (\sigma) \quad a. s. \quad o n \{\sigma = v \},\tag{D.4}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Proof. To prove (D.4), note that the event $B \ { \stackrel { \triangle } { = } } \ \{ v = \sigma \}$ belongs to $\mathcal { F } _ { v } \cap \mathcal { F } _ { \sigma } = \mathcal { F } _ { v \wedge \sigma }$ (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Lemma 1.2.16). Given $\tau { \in } S _ { v }$ we define $\tau _ { B } = \tau \cdot 1 _ { B } + T \cdot 1 _ { B ^ { c } }$ , so $\tau _ { B } { \in } S _ { \sigma }$ . From the definition of conditional expectation and from Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Problem 2.17(i) and solution (p. 39), we have

$$

for every $\tau { \in } S _ { v }$ . Therefore, $Z ( v ) \leq Z ( \sigma )$ almost surely on B. Reversing the roles of v and $\sigma .$ , we obtain (D.4). 

For (D.5), use Lemma D.1 to choose a sequence $\{ \rho _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ in $S _ { \tau }$ such that $\{ E [ Y ( \rho _ { n } ) | \mathcal { F } ( \tau ) ] \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ is nondecreasing and $\begin{array} { r } { Z ( \tau ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } E [ Y ( \rho _ { n } ) | \mathcal { F } ( \tau ) ] } \end{array}$ By the monotone convergence theorem for conditional expectations, we have 

$$

$$

$\mathrm { O n }$ the other hand, $Z ( \tau ) \geq E [ Y ( \rho ) | \mathcal { F } ( \tau ) ]$ holds for all $\rho { \in } S _ { \tau }$ , and tak ing conditional expectations on both sides of this inequality we obtain $E [ Z ( \tau ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] \ge E [ Y ( \rho ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ]$ . This implies 

$$
E [ Z (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \geq \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\rho \in \mathcal {S} _ {\tau}} E [ Y (\rho) | \mathcal {F} (v) ],
$$

proving (D.5). Since ess sup $\begin{array} { r } { { \bf \Phi } _ { \rho \in S _ { \tau } } E [ Y ( \rho ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] \leq \exp { \sf s u p } _ { \rho \in S _ { v } } E [ Y ( \rho ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] } \end{array}$ $= Z ( v ) , ( \mathrm { D } . 6 )$ follows from (D.5). We obtain (D.7) by setting $v \equiv 0$ in (D.5) and (D.6). ␀ 

For $v \in S$ , let us now define $S _ { v } ^ { * } ~ \stackrel { \triangle } { = } ~ \{ \tau { \in } S _ { v } ; \tau > v { \mathrm { a . s } } $ . on $\{ v < T \} \}$ and introduce the family 

$$
Z ^ {*} (v) \triangleq \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S} _ {v} ^ {*}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ], \quad v \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{D.8}

The random variable $Z ^ { * } ( v )$ is the optimal conditional expected reward for stopping strictly later than v (except that on the event $\{ v = T \}$ , stopping must be done at time $T$ and $Z ^ { * } ( v ) = Y ( T ) )$ . Since $Y ( \cdot )$ has right-continuous paths, it is no surprise that $Z ( v ) = Z ^ { * } ( v )$ holds almost surely (Corollary D.4 below). Before proving this equality, let us observe that the proof of Proposition D.2 can be trivially altered to show that the family $\{ Z ^ { \ast } ( v ) \} _ { v \in { \cal S } }$ possesses analogues of the properties established in that proposition for the family $\{ Z ( v ) \} _ { v \in { \cal S } }$ . Furthermore, $\{ Z ^ { * } ( v ) \} _ { v \in { \cal S } }$ has the right-continuity property (D.10) below. 

Proposition D.3: For any $v \in S$ , and for any decreasing sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ in $\boldsymbol { S } _ { v } ^ { * }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { v = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } v _ { n } \quad a . s . } \end{array}$ , we have

Using the analogue of Lemma D.1 for $S _ { v } ^ { * }$ , we choose a sequence $\{ \rho _ { k } \}$ of stopping times in $S _ { v } ^ { * }$ such that $\{ E [ Y ( \rho _ { k } ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ is nondecreasing and 

$$
Z ^ {*} (v) = \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S} _ {v} ^ {*}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = \lim _ {k \to \infty} E [ Y (\rho_ {k}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

The monotone convergence theorem and (D.14) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {A} Z ^ {*} (v) d P = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {A} E [ Y (\rho_ {k}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] d P \\ = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {A} Y (\rho_ {k}) d P \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} Z ^ {*} (v _ {n}) d P. \end{array}\tag{D.15}
$$

This, combined with (D.11), yields (D.10). 

Corollary D.4: For any $v \in S$ , we have $Z ^ { * } ( v ) = Z ( v ) \ a . s$ 

Proof. For any decreasing sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ in $\boldsymbol { S } _ { v } ^ { * }$ with $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } v _ { n } = v .$ the right continuity of $Y ( \cdot )$ and Fatou’s lemma for conditional expectations imply 

$$
Z ^ {*} (v) \geq \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} E [ Y (v _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \geq E [ \lim _ {n \to \infty} Y (v _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = Y (v) \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

The conclusion follows from (D.9). 

As mentioned earlier, we may take the stopping times $v$ in (D.3) to be deterministic and thereby obtain a nonnegative, adapted process $\{ Z ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ . From $\left( \mathrm { D } . 6 \right)$ we see that this process is a su permartingale. Because the function $t \mapsto E Z ( t )$ is right continuous (from (D.10) and Corollary D.4), there exists a supermartingale $\{ Z ^ { 0 } ( t ) , \mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq$ $t \leq T \}$ with RCLL paths that satisfies 

$$
P [ Z (t) = Z ^ {0} (t) ] = 1, \quad \forall t \in [ 0, T ]\tag{D.16}
$$

(cf. Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Theorem 1.3.13). Recall that $Y ( T ) \ { \stackrel { \triangle } { = } }$ $\overline { { \mathrm { l i m } } } _ { t  \infty } Y ( t )$ if $T = \infty$ , and thus 

$$
Z ^ {0} (\infty) = Z (\infty) = \varlimsup_ {t \to \infty} Y (t) \quad \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

The nonnegative RCLL supermartingale $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is called the Snell envelope of $Y ( \cdot )$ . It is the smallest supermartingale that dominates $Y ( \cdot )$ in the sense of the following definition. 

Definition D.5: Let $X _ { 1 } ( \cdot ) = \{ X _ { 1 } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ and $X _ { 2 } ( \cdot ) = \{ X _ { 2 } ( t ) ; 0 \leq$ $t ~ \le ~ T \}$ be arbitrary processes. We say that $X _ { 1 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $X _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ if $P [ X _ { 1 } ( t ) \geq X _ { 2 } ( t ) , \forall 0 \leq t \leq T ] = 1$ 

Remark D.6: If $X _ { 1 } ( \cdot )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ are right-continuous processes and $P [ X _ { 1 } ( t ) \geq X _ { 2 } ( t ) ] = 1$ for all t in $[ 0 , T ]$ (or even in a countable, dense subset of $[ 0 , T ] )$ , then $X _ { 1 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $X _ { 2 } ( \cdot )$ 

The following theorem permits us henceforth to focus our attention on the RCLL supermartingale $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ rather than the more awkward family of random variables $\{ Z ( v ) \} _ { v \in S }$ . In (D.17), $Z ^ { 0 } ( v )$ denotes the process $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ evaluated at the stopping time v, whereas $Z ( v )$ stands for the random variable of (D.3). 

Theorem D.7: The Snell envelope $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ of $Y ( \cdot )$ satisfies 

$$
Z ^ {0} (v) = Z (v) \quad a. s.\tag{D.17}
$$

for every $v \in S$ . Moreover, $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $Y ( \cdot )$ , and $i f X ( \cdot )$ is another RCLL supermartingale dominating $Y ( \cdot )$ , then $X ( \cdot )$ also dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ 

Proof. For any $v \in S$ there is a decreasing sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ of stopping times in $S _ { v } ^ { * }$ with values in $\{ T \} \cup \mathbf { D }$ (where D is the set of dyadic rationals) and with $v = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } v _ { n }$ a.s. (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Problem 1.2.24). From Doob’s optional sampling theorem (ibid., Theorem 1.3.22), we have 

$$
E [ Z ^ {0} (v _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \leq E [ Z ^ {0} (v _ {n + k}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \leq Z ^ {0} (v) \quad \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

for all positive integers n and k. Therefore, for $A \in { \mathcal { F } } ( v )$ , the sequence $\textstyle \{ \int _ { A } Z ^ { 0 } ( v _ { n } ) d P \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ is nondecreasing and bounded above by $\textstyle \int _ { A } Z ^ { 0 } ( v ) d P$ ; hence lim $\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { l } _ { n \to \infty } \bar { \int } _ { A } \bar { Z } ^ { 0 } ( v _ { n } ) d P \ \le \ \int _ { A } Z ^ { 0 } ( v ) d P } \end{array}$ . The reverse inequality fol lows from Fatou’s lemma and the right continuity of $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . Coupling these observations with (D.10), Corollary D.4, and (D.16), we deduce 

$$
\int_ {A} Z (v) d P = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} Z (v _ {n}) d P = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} Z ^ {0} (v _ {n}) d P = \int_ {A} Z ^ {0} (v) d P.
$$

Since $A \in { \mathcal { F } } ( v )$ is arbitrary, (D.17) must hold. 

Finally, let $X ( \cdot )$ be an RCLL supermartingale dominating $Y ( \cdot )$ . For $t \in$ $[ 0 , T ]$ and $\tau \in S _ { t }$ , the optional sampling theorem implies $E [ Y ( \tau ) | \mathcal { F } ( t ) ] \leq$ $E [ X ( \tau ) | { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ] \leq X ( t )$ almost surely. Therefore, for each $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , we have 

$$
Z ^ {0} (t) = Z (t) \stackrel {\triangle} {=} \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in S _ {t}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] \leq X (t) \quad \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

Remark D.8: $\mathrm { I f ~ } \left\{ X ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t < T \right\}$ is an RCLL supermartingale satisfying 

$$
P [ X (t) \geq Y (t) ] = 1, \quad \forall t \in [ 0, T),
$$

then it is still true that X( ) dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . To see this, first use the right continuity of $X ( \cdot )$ and $Y ( \cdot )$ to see that $P [ X ( t ) \geq Y ( t ) , \forall t \in [ 0 , T ) ] = 1$ Then use the submartingale convergence theorem (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Theorem 1.3.15) to establish the almost sure existence of $X ( T ) \overset { \triangle } { = }$ $\mathrm { l i m } _ { t \uparrow T } X ( t )$ . For $0 \leq s < T$ and with $T _ { n } \uparrow T$ , we have 

$$
E [ X (T) | \mathcal {F} (s) ] \leq \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} E [ X (T _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (s) ] \leq X (s) \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

from Fatou’s lemma for conditional expectations, so that $\{ X ( t ) ; 0 \ \leq$ $t \leq T \}$ is an RCLL supermartingale. Moreover $X ( T ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \uparrow T } X ( t ) \geq$ $\overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } _ { t \uparrow T } \dot { Y } ( t ) \geq Y ( T )$ . Thus the supermartingale with last element $\{ X ( t )$ $\mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ dominates $\{ Y ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ . Now apply Theorem D.7. 

Theorem D.9: A stopping time $\tau _ { * }$ is optimal, i.e., 

$$
E Y (\tau_ {*}) = Z ^ {0} (0) = \sup _ {\rho \in \mathcal {S}} E Y (\rho),\tag{D.18}
$$

if and only if 

$$
Z ^ {0} (\tau_ {*}) = Y (\tau_ {*}) \quad a. s.\tag{D.19}
$$

and the stopped supermartingale 

$$
\{Z ^ {0} (t \wedge \tau_ {*}), \mathcal {F} (t); 0 \leq t \leq T \} i s a m a r t i n g a l e.\tag{D.20}
$$

Proof. Suppose that $\tau _ { * }$ is optimal. From (D.7) we have $E Y ( \tau _ { * } ) ~ =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \rho \in { \cal S } _ { \tau _ { * } } } E Y ( \rho ) \ = \ E Z ^ { 0 } ( \tau _ { * } ) } \end{array}$ , as well as $\begin{array} { r } { E Y ( \tau _ { * } ) ~ = ~ \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \rho \in S _ { \sigma \wedge \tau _ { * } } } E Y ( \rho ) ~ = ~ } \end{array}$ $E Z ^ { 0 } ( \sigma \wedge \tau _ { * } )$ , for any $\sigma \in \mathcal { S }$ . Now, $P [ Z ^ { 0 } ( t ) \ \ge \ Y ( t ) , \forall t \in [ 0 , T ] ] \ = \ 1$ and $E Y ( \tau _ { * } ) = E Z ^ { 0 } ( \tau _ { * } )$ give (D.19), whereas the fact that $E Z ^ { 0 } ( \sigma \wedge \tau _ { * } )$ does not depend on $\sigma \in S$ yields (D.20) thanks to Problem 1.3.26 in Karatzas and Shreve (1991). Conversely, (D.19) and (D.20) give $E Y ( \tau _ { * } ) = E Z ^ { 0 } ( \tau _ { * } ) =$ $Z ^ { 0 } ( 0 ) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \rho \in S } E Y ( \rho )$ ␀ 

Having characterized optimal stopping times in Theorem D.9, we now seek to establish their existence. We begin by constructing a family of stopping times that are “approximately optimal.” For $\lambda \in ( 0 , 1 )$ and $v \in S$ define the stopping time 

$$
D ^ {\lambda} (v) \triangleq \inf \{t \in (v, T ]; \quad \lambda Z ^ {0} (t) \leq Y (t) \} \wedge T\tag{D.21}
$$

in $S _ { v }$ . Because of the right continuity of $Y ( \cdot )$ and $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , the process $\{ D ^ { \lambda } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ is right continuous. Furthermore, for any $v \in S$ we have the inequality 

$$
\lambda Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) \leq Y (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) \quad \text { a.s. }\tag{D.22}
$$

(This inequality holds even on the set $\{ D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) = T \}$ , because $Z ^ { 0 } ( T ) =$ $Y ( T ) . )$ 

Proposition D.10: For $0 < \lambda < 1$ and every $v \in S$ , we have 

$$
Z ^ {0} (v) = E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \quad a. s.\tag{D.23}
$$

Proof. Define the family of nonnegative random variables ${ \begin{array} { l l } { { \boldsymbol { J } } ( v ) } & { { \stackrel { \triangle } { = } } } \end{array} }$ $E [ Z ^ { 0 } ( D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) ) | \mathcal { F } ( v ) ] , v \in \mathcal { S }$ . From (D.6) and the fact that $D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) \in \mathcal { S } _ { v }$ we note that 

$$
J (v) \leq Z ^ {0} (v) \quad \text { a.s., } \quad \forall v \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{D.24}
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, we shall show that $J ( \cdot )$ has an RCLL su permartingale modification $J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ that dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . For $v \in S$ and $\tau { \in } S _ { v }$ we have from (D.6) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ J (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = E [ E \{Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (\tau)) | \mathcal {F} (\tau) \} | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (\tau)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \\ = E [ E \{Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (\tau)) | \mathcal {F} (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) \} | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \\ \leq E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = J (v). \end{array} \tag {D.}\tag{D.25}
$$

It follows that $\{ J ( t ) , \mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ is a supermartingale and that $t \mapsto$ $E J ( t )$ is a nonincreasing function. By Fatou’s lemma and the right conti nuity of $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ and $D ^ { \lambda } ( \cdot )$ we also have $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { s \downarrow t } E J ( s ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { s \downarrow t } E Z ^ { 0 } ( D ^ { \lambda } ( s ) ) \geq } \end{array}$ $E Z ^ { 0 } ( D ^ { \lambda } ( t ) ) = E J ( t )$ . Therefore, the mapping $t \mapsto E J ( t )$ is right contin uous; and by Theorem 1.3.13 in Karatzas and Shreve (1991) there is an RCLL supermartingale $J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot ) = \{ J ^ { 0 } ( t ) , \mathcal { F } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T \}$ such that 

$$
P [ J (t) = J ^ {0} (t) ] = 1, \quad \forall t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{D.26}
$$

In the spirit of the first part of Theorem D.7, we now extend (D.26) to the statement 

$$
P [ J (v) = J ^ {0} (v) ] = 1, \quad \forall v \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{D.27}
$$

Fix $v \in S$ and let $\{ v _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a decreasing sequence of stopping times in $ { \boldsymbol { S } } _ { v }$ with $v = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } v _ { n }$ a.s. and with values in $\{ T \} \cup \mathbf { D }$ , where D is the set of dyadic rationals. For any given $A \in { \mathcal { F } } ( v )$ , we have from (D.25) 

$$
\int_ {A} J (v _ {n}) d P = \int_ {A} E [ J (v _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] d P \leq \int_ {A} J (v) d P, \quad \forall n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

so that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  { } \infty } \int _ { A } J ( v _ { n } ) d P \leq \int _ { A } J ( v ) d P } \end{array}$ . On the other hand, Fatou’s lemma implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} J (v _ {n}) d P & = \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v _ {n})) | \mathcal {F} (v _ {n}) ] d P \\ & = \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v _ {n})) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] d P \\ & \geq \int_ {A} E [ \varliminf_ {n \to \infty} Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v _ {n})) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] d P \end{array}
$$

$$
= \int_ {A} E [ Z ^ {0} (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] d P = \int_ {A} J (v) d P.
$$

It follows that 

$$
\int_ {A} J (v) d P = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} J (v _ {n}) d P.
$$

A similar argument, using the optional sampling theorem instead of (D.25), shows that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} J ^ {0} (v _ {n}) d P = \int_ {A} J ^ {0} (v) d P.
$$

Finally, (D.26) implies that $\textstyle \int _ { A } J ( v _ { n } ) d P = \int _ { A } J ^ { 0 } ( v _ { n } )$ dP for all n. It follows from these equations that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { A } ^ { \cdot } J ( v ) d P = \bar { \int _ { A } } \bar { J ^ { 0 } } ( v ) d P } \end{array}$ . Since $A \in { \mathcal { F } } ( v )$ is arbitrary, (D.27) must hold. 

We show next that $J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . Consider the RCLL supermartingle $\lambda Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot ) + ( 1 - \dot { \lambda } ) { \bar { J } } ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . Fix $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . Then on $\{ D ^ { \lambda } ( t ) = t \}$ we have 

$$
\lambda Z ^ {0} (t) + (1 - \lambda) J ^ {0} (t) = \lambda Z ^ {0} (t) + (1 - \lambda) E [ Z ^ {0} (t) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] = Z ^ {0} (t) \geq Y (t)
$$

from Theorem D.7. On the other hand, the definition (D.21) of $D ^ { \lambda } ( t )$ implies that on the event $\{ D ^ { \lambda } ( t ) > t \}$ we have 

$$
\lambda Z ^ {0} (t) + (1 - \lambda) J ^ {0} (t) \geq \lambda Z ^ {0} (t) \geq Y (t).
$$

The right continuity of $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot ) , J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , and $Y ( \cdot )$ allows us to conclude that the supermartingale $\lambda Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $Y ( \cdot )$ , and thus dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ as well. It follows that $J ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ , and consequently $P [ J ^ { 0 } ( v ) \geq Z ^ { 0 } ( v ) ] = 1 , \forall v \in S$ . Combining this with (D.24) and $\mathrm { ( D . 2 7 ) }$ , we obtain $P [ J ( v ) = Z ^ { 0 } ( v ) ] = 1 , \forall v \in S$ . This is (D.23). ␀ 

For fixed $v \in S$ the family of stopping times $\{ D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) \} _ { 0 < \lambda < 1 }$ is nondecreasing in λ, so we may define the limiting stopping time 

$$
D _ {*} (v) \triangleq \lim _ {\lambda \uparrow 1} D ^ {\lambda} (v) \quad \mathrm{a.s.}\tag{D.28}
$$

Under the assumption that $Y ( \cdot )$ has continuous paths and that 

$$
E \left[ \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} Y (t) \right] <   \infty\tag{D.29}
$$

holds, we shall show that $D _ { * } ( 0 )$ is optimal (i.e., attains the supremum in (D.1)). As one might expect, this argument relies on the $l e f t$ continuity of $Y ( \cdot )$ . The following example illustrates that in the absence of the assumption (D.29), there need not exist an optimal stopping time. 

Example D.11: (Nonexistence of an optimal stopping time): Set $T = \infty$ and $Y ( t ) = \exp \{ W ( t ) - { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } t - { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { t + 1 } } } \} , 0 \le t < \infty$ , where $W ( \cdot )$ is a onedimensional Brownian motion and $\{ \mathcal { F } ( t ) \}$ is the augmentation by null sets of the filtration generated by $W ( \cdot )$ . According to the “strong law of large numbers,” lim $_ { i  \infty } \frac { W ( t ) } { t } = 0 \mathrm { a . s }$ . (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Problem 2.9.3 and solution, p. 124), and we have $Y ( \infty ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \infty } Y ( t ) = 0$ almost surely; however, the condition (D.29) is not satisfied. We show that the Snell envelope of $Y ( \cdot )$ is 

$$
M (t) \triangleq \exp \left\{W (t) - \frac {1}{2} t \right\} = Y (t) \exp \left(\frac {1}{t + 1}\right) > Y (t), \quad 0 \leq t <   \infty .
$$

The process $\{ M ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t < \infty \}$ is a martingale, and when we include the last element $M ( \infty ) \equiv 0$ we have a continuous supermartingale $M ( \cdot ) =$ $\{ M ( t ) , { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) ; 0 \leq t \leq \infty \}$ dominating $Y ( \cdot )$ . According to Theorem D.7, $M ( \cdot )$ dominates the Snell envelope $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ . Furthermore, for each $t \in [ 0 , \infty )$ we have from the same theorem that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Z ^ {0} (t) = \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S} _ {t}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] \\ \qquad \geq \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {t \leq s <   \infty} E [ Y (s) | \mathcal {F} (t) ] \\ \qquad = M (t) \cdot \sup _ {t \leq s <   \infty} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{s + 1} \right\} = M (t) \quad \text {a.s.} \end{array}
$$

Hence $M ( \cdot )$ is the Snell envelope of $Y ( \cdot )$ ; in particular, 

$$
\sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S}} E Y (\tau) = Z ^ {0} (0) = M (0) = 1.
$$

There is no stopping time $v \in S$ satisfying $E Y ( v ) = 1$ , because condition (D.19) of Theorem D.9 is satisfied only by $v \equiv \infty$ but $E Y ( \infty ) = 0$ . For $\lambda { \in } ( 1 / e , 1 )$ , we have 

$$
D ^ {\lambda} (0) \triangleq \inf \{t \geq 0; \quad \lambda M (t) \leq Y (t) \} = - \frac {1}{\log \lambda} - 1,
$$

and lim $\begin{array} { r c l } { { \ O _ { \lambda \uparrow 1 } E Y ( D ^ { \lambda } ( 0 ) ) } } & { { = } } & { { \operatorname * { l i m } _ { \lambda \uparrow 1 } \lambda } } \end{array} = 1$ , but the limit $\begin{array} { l l } { D _ { * } ( 0 ) } & { \triangleq } \end{array}$ $\mathrm { l i m } _ { \lambda \uparrow 1 } D ^ { \lambda } ( 0 ) = \infty$ of these “approximately optimal” stopping times is very clearly “suboptimal,” since $E Y ( D _ { * } ( 0 ) ) = 0$ 

It is of course possible to introduce a deterministic time change in this example, so that T is finite and there still is no optimal stopping time. 

Theorem D.12: Suppose that $Y ( \cdot )$ has continuous paths and that the assumption (D.29) holds. Then, for each $v \in S$ , the stopping time $D _ { * } ( v )$ defined by (D.28) satisfies 

$$
E [ Y (D _ {*} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = Z ^ {0} (v) = \operatorname{ess} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {S} _ {v}} E [ Y (\tau) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \quad a. s.\tag{D.30}
$$

In particular, $D _ { * } ( 0 )$ attains the supremum in $( D . 1 )$ . Furthermore, for any $v \in S$ : 

$$
D _ {*} (v) = \inf \{t \in [ v, T ]; \quad Z ^ {0} (t) = Y (t) \} \quad a. s.\tag{D.31}
$$

Proof. Proposition D.10 and the inequality (D.22) imply 

$$
Z ^ {0} (v) = E \left[ Z ^ {0} \left(D ^ {\lambda} (v)\right) | \mathcal {F} (v) \right] \leq \frac {1}{\lambda} E \left[ Y \left(D ^ {\lambda} (v)\right) | \mathcal {F} (v) \right] \quad \text { a   .   s   . }
$$

Now, for all $\lambda \in ( 0 , 1 )$ we have $Y ( D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) ) \leq { \bar { Y } }$ , where 

$$
\bar {Y} \triangleq \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq T} Y (t),\tag{D.32}
$$

so we may use the dominated convergence theorem for conditional expectations, coupled with the left continuity of $Y ( \cdot )$ , to conclude that 

$$
Z ^ {0} (v) \leq \lim _ {\lambda \uparrow 1} E [ Y (D ^ {\lambda} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] = E [ Y (D _ {*} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

Because $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ is a supermartingale dominating $Y ( \cdot )$ , we have the reverse inequality 

$$
E [ Y (D _ {*} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v) ] \leq E [ Z ^ {0} (D _ {*} (v)) | \mathcal {F} (v)) ] \leq Z ^ {0} (v) \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

and (D.30) is proved. 

From (D.30) and the supermartingale property, we have 

$$
E Y (D _ {*} (v)) = E Z ^ {0} (v) \geq E Z ^ {0} (D _ {*} (v)).
$$

But $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ dominates $Y ( \cdot )$ , so it must be true that $Y ( D _ { * } ( v ) ) = Z ^ { 0 } ( D _ { * } ( v ) )$ a.s. and 

$$
D _ {*} (v) \geq \inf \{t \in [ v, T ]; Z ^ {0} (t) = Y (t) \} \quad \text { a.s. }
$$

For the reverse inequality, observe first that the definition (D.21) of $D ^ { \lambda } ( v )$ implies $Y ( t ) < \lambda Z ^ { 0 } ( t ) \leq Z ^ { 0 } ( t )$ for all $t { \in } ( v , D ^ { \lambda } ( v ) )$ and $\lambda { \in } ( 0 , 1 )$ . Hence 

$$

Theorem D.13: Under the condition $_ { ( D . { \mathcal { Q } } { \mathcal { Q } } ) }$ , the RCLL supermartingale $Z ^ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ admits the Doob–Meyer decomposition

# Appendix E The Clark Formula

We ofer in this appendix a brief overview of the formula of J.M.C. Clark (1970) for the stochastic integral representation of Brownian functionals. The approach is that of Bismut (1981), as presented in Rogers and Williams (1987). 

Let $W _ { t } ( \omega ) = \omega ( t ) , \ 0 \leq t \leq T$ , be standard, one-dimensional Brownian motion on the canonical space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P ) , \{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ with $\Omega = C ( [ 0 , T ] )$ ), the space of continuous functions $\omega : [ 0 , T ] \to \mathbb { R }$ , and with $P$ taken to be Wiener measure. Here $\mathcal { F } = \mathcal { F } _ { T }$ is the P-completion of the σ-algebra generated by $\{ W _ { s } ; ~ 0 \le s \le T \}$ , and $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ is the σ-algebra generated by $\{ W _ { s } ; 0 \leq s \leq t \}$ and augmented by the P-null sets in ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { : }$ , for $0 \leq t \leq T$ 

Let F be a square-integrable Brownian functional, i.e., an $\mathcal { F } _ { T } \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e }$ mapping from Ω to R with $E F ^ { 2 } ( W ) < \infty$ . The martingale representation theorem for Brownian functionals (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Propo sition 3.4.18) states that there exists a unique (up to a.e. equivalence on $[ 0 , T ] \times \Omega ) \ \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \}$ -progressively measurable process $\psi$ with $\begin{array} { r } { E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } \psi _ { s } ^ { 2 } d s < \infty } \end{array}$ such that 

$$
F (W) = E F (W) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \psi_ {s} d W _ {s} \quad \mathrm{a.s.}\tag{E.1}
$$

In the construction of hedging portfolios, it is important to obtain the process $\psi$ explicitly. 

Taking conditional expectations on both sides of (E.1) with respect to $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ , we obtain $\begin{array} { r } { \Lambda _ { t } \stackrel { \triangle } { = } E [ F ( W ) | \mathcal { F } _ { t } ] = E F ( W ) + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \psi _ { s } d W _ { s } } \end{array}$ , which we may 

write in diferential notation as 

$$
d \Lambda_ {t} = d _ {t} \left(E [ F (W) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ]\right) = \psi_ {t} d W _ {t}.\tag{E.2}
$$

If the diferential of the L´evy martingale Λ can be computed, then $\psi$ will be determined. Here is an example of such a computation. 

Example E.1: Let ${ \underset { \land } { F ( \omega ) } } \ \triangleq$ ma $\mathsf { \Omega } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \omega ( t )$ , and define $\begin{array} { r l } { \boldsymbol { M _ { s , t } } } & { { } \overset { \triangle } { = } } \end{array}$ max ${ \bf { \sigma } } _ { s \leq u \leq t } W _ { u }$ and $M _ { t } \stackrel { \triangle } { = } \dot { M _ { 0 , t } }$ , so that $F ( W ) = M _ { T }$ . From the reflection principle we have 

$$
P [ M _ {T} > b ] = 2 P [ W _ {T} > b ] = 2 \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {b}{\sqrt {T}}\right) \right], \quad b > 0,
$$

and therefore 

$$
P [ M _ {T} \in d b ] = 2 \frac {\partial}{\partial b} \Phi \left(\frac {b}{\sqrt {T}}\right) d b = \frac {2}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} e ^ {- \frac {b ^ {2}}{2 T}} d b, \quad b > 0,
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \Phi ( x ) \stackrel { \triangle } { = } \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } \int _ { - \infty } ^ { x } e ^ { - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \xi ^ { 2 } } d \xi } \end{array}$ (e.g., Karatzas and Shreve (1991), 2.8A). It follows easily that $E F ^ { 2 } ( W ) < \infty$ . For $0 \leq t \leq T$ and $m \geq 0$ we have 

$$
P [ M _ {T} > m | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = 1 _ {\{M _ {t} > m \}} + 1 _ {\{M _ {t} \leq m \}} P [ M _ {t, T} > m | W _ {t} ],
$$

and thus $P [ M _ { T } > m | \mathcal { F } _ { t } ]$ depends only on $W _ { t }$ and $M _ { t }$ . For $a < b < m$ and $b > 0$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P [ M _ {T} \in d m | W _ {t} = a, M _ {t} = b ] = P [ M _ {T - t} \in d m - a ] \\ & \qquad = \frac {2}{\sqrt {2 \pi (T - t)}} e ^ {- \frac {(m - a) ^ {2}}{2 (T - t)}} d m. \end{array}
$$

Furthermore, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P [ M _ {T} = b | W _ {t} = a, M _ {t} = b ] = 1 - P [ M _ {T} > b | W _ {t} = a, M _ {t} = b ] \\ = 1 - P [ M _ {T - t} > b - a ] = 2 \Phi \left(\frac {b - a}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) - 1. \end{array}
$$

If follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ M _ {T} | W _ {t} = a, M _ {t} = b ] = 2 b \cdot \Phi \left(\frac {b - a}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) - b \\ \qquad + \int_ {b} ^ {\infty} \frac {2 m}{\sqrt {2 \pi (T - t)}} e ^ {- \frac {(m - a) ^ {2}}{2 (T - t)}} d m \\ \qquad = 2 (b - a) \Phi \left(\frac {b - a}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) - b + 2 a \\ \qquad + \sqrt {\frac {2 (T - t)}{\pi}} \exp \left\{- \frac {(b - a) ^ {2}}{2 (T - t)} \right\}, \end{array}
$$

or equivalently, 

$$
\Lambda_ {t} \triangleq E [ M _ {T} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = 2 (M _ {t} - W _ {t}) \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right)
$$

$$
- M _ {t} + 2 W _ {t} + \sqrt {\frac {2 (T - t)}{\pi}} \exp \left\{- \frac {(M _ {t} - W _ {t}) ^ {2}}{2 (T - t)} \right\}.
$$

A tedious calculation, based on the Itˆo formula and on the identity $\Phi ^ { ^ { \prime \prime } } ( x ) =$ $- x \Phi ^ { \prime } ( x )$ , leads to 

$$
d \Lambda_ {t} = 2 \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) \right] d W _ {t} - \left[ 1 - 2 \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) \right] d M _ {t}.
$$

Because the process $M$ is flat of the set $\{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; M _ { t } - W _ { t } = 0 \}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \Phi ( 0 ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , the $d M _ { t }$ term on the right-hand side of this last equation drops out, and we have identified the integrand $\psi$ in (E.1) as 

$$
\psi_ {t} = 2 \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) \right].\tag{E.3}
$$

While many more examples along these lines can be given, the calculations become increasingly laborious and tedious. The Clark formula is a theoretical characterization of the integrand in (E.1) that sometimes shortens these computations substantially. As presented here, the derivation of this formula requires the Brownian functional $F$ to satisfy the following three conditions: 

$$
E F ^ {2} (W) <   \infty ;\tag{E.4}
$$

there is a nonnegative Brownian functional h 

satisfying $E h ^ { 2 } ( W ) <$ and a function 

$$
g: [ 0, \infty) \to [ 0, \infty) \text {   satisfying   } \overline {{\lim _ {\varepsilon \downarrow 0}}} \left(\frac {g (\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right) <   \infty ,
$$

such that with $\| \cdot \|$ denoting the supremum norm, 

$$
| F (\omega + \varphi) - F (\omega) | \leq h (\omega) g (\| \varphi \|), \forall (\omega , \varphi) \in \Omega^ {2};\tag{E.5}
$$

there is a measurable mapping 

$$
\omega \mapsto \partial F (\omega ; \cdot): (\Omega , \mathcal {F} _ {T}) \to (\mathbf {M}, \mathcal {M}),
$$

where M is the set of finite Borel measures on 

$$
\mathcal {B} ([ 0, T ])
$$

the topology of weak convergence on M, that satisfies 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \frac {1}{\varepsilon} [ F (\omega + \varepsilon \varphi) - F (\omega) ] = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \partial F (\omega ; d t), \\ \forall \varphi \in C ^ {1} ([ 0, T ]), P \text {-a.e.} \omega \in \Omega . \end{array}\tag{E.6}
$$

Note that if the mapping $\partial F$ in (E.6) exists, then it must be unique up to P-equivalence. 

Theorem E.2: (Clark (1970)): Under the conditions $( E . 4 ) - ( E . 6 )$ , the process $\psi$ of (E.1) is the predictable projection of the (not necessarily adapted) process $\partial { \cal F } ( W ; ( t , T ] )$ $0 \leq \textit { t } \leq T$ . Equivalently, for 

Lebesgue-almost-every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , we have 

$$
\psi_ {t} = E [ \partial F (W; (t, T ]) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] \quad a. s.\tag{E.7}
$$

Proof. Let X be a bounded, continuous $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \}$ -adapted process; define $\begin{array} { r } { \varphi _ { t } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } X _ { s } d s } \end{array}$ for $0 \leq t \leq T$ ; and introduce the exponential martingales and the probability measures 

$$
Z _ {t} ^ {\varepsilon} \triangleq \exp \left[ \varepsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {s} d W _ {s} - \frac {\varepsilon^ {2}}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {s} ^ {2} d s \right], Z ^ {\varepsilon} \equiv Z _ {T} ^ {\varepsilon},
$$

$$
P ^ {\varepsilon} (A) \triangleq E [ Z ^ {\varepsilon} \cdot 1 _ {A} ], A \in \mathcal {F} _ {T},
$$

for $\varepsilon \in \mathbb { R }$ . Then $\{ W _ { t } - \varepsilon \varphi _ { t } , \mathcal { F } _ { t } ; 0 \le t \le T \}$ is a $P ^ { \varepsilon }$ -Brownian motion, according to the Girsanov theorem (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), 3.5), and we thus have the invariance principle 

$$
E F (W) = E ^ {\varepsilon} F (W - \varepsilon \varphi) = E [ Z ^ {\varepsilon} F (W - \varepsilon \varphi) ], \quad \forall \varepsilon \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{E.8}
$$

A stochastic calculus of variations (known as the Malliavin calculus) can be based on (E.8). In the spirit of this calculus, we first rewrite (E.8) and then we diferentiate with respect to ε. From (E.8) we have for $\varepsilon \neq 0$ that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{\varepsilon} E [ F (W) - F (W - \varepsilon \varphi) ] + E \left[ \frac {Z ^ {\varepsilon} - 1}{\varepsilon} \{F (W) - F (W - \varepsilon \varphi) \} \right] \\ = E \left[ F (W) \frac {Z ^ {\varepsilon} - 1}{\varepsilon} \right]. \end{array}\tag{E.9}
$$

Using the representation $\begin{array} { r } { Z _ { t } ^ { \varepsilon } = 1 + \varepsilon \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } X _ { s } Z _ { s } ^ { \varepsilon } d W _ { s } } \end{array}$ , one can show first that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \varepsilon \downarrow 0 } E \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } ( Z _ { s } ^ { \varepsilon } - 1 ) ^ { 2 } d s = 0 } \end{array}$ , and then that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { Z _ { t } ^ { \varepsilon } - 1 } { \varepsilon } \xrightarrow [ \varepsilon \downarrow 0 ] { L ^ { 2 } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } X _ { s } d W _ { s } } \end{array}$ for every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . Upon letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ in (E.9), we obtain from these considerations, (E.5), (E.6), and the dominated convergence theorem that 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi_ {s} \partial F (W; d s) = E \left[ F (W) \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {s} d W _ {s} \right].\tag{E.10}
$$

The left-hand side of (E.10) is equal to 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} 1 _ {\{0 \leq t <   s \leq T \}} X _ {t} d t \partial F (W; d s) = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {t} \partial F (W; (t, T ]) d t
$$

(Fubini’s theorem), whereas the right-hand side equals (see (E.1)) 

$$
E \left[ \left\{E F + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \psi_ {s} d W _ {s} \right\} \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {s} d W _ {s} \right] = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {t} \psi_ {t} d t.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
E \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {t} \partial F (W; (t, T ]) d t = E \int_ {0} ^ {T} X _ {t} \psi_ {t} d t
$$

holds for every bounded, continuous, and $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} \mathrm { - a d a p t e d }$ process X, and (E.7) follows. ␀ 

Example E.3: We return to Example E.1, where $F ( \omega ) = \operatorname* { m a x } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \omega ( t )$ This maximum is attained at a unique number $\eta ( \omega ) \in [ 0 , T ]$ (Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Remark 8.16, p. 102), so $F ( \omega ) = \omega ( \eta ( \omega ) )$ , for a.e. $\omega \in \Omega$ Conditions (E.4) and (E.5) are clearly satisfied, and as for (E.6), we have 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac {1}{\varepsilon} [ F (\omega + \varepsilon \varphi) - F (\omega) ] = \varphi (\eta (\omega)), \quad \forall   \varphi \in C ^ {1} ([ 0, T ]),
$$

for $P \mathrm { - a . e . } \omega \in \Omega$ . Thus $\partial F ( \omega ; ( t , T ] ) = 1 _ { \{ \eta ( \omega ) > t \} }$ , and in the notation of Example E.1 we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\psi_ {t} = E [ \partial F (W; (t, T ]) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = P [ \eta > t | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = P [ M _ {t, T} > M _ {t} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ]} \\ & {\qquad = P [ M _ {T - t} > b ] | _ {b = M _ {t} - W _ {t}}} \\ & {\qquad = 2 \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) \right] \mathrm{a.s.}} \end{array}
$$

We have recovered the expression (E.3). 

Example E.4: With $\sigma \mathrm { ~  ~ { ~ > ~ } ~ } 0 .$ , take $G ( \omega ) \stackrel { \triangle } { = } { e } ^ { \sigma F ( \omega ) } = \exp \{ \sigma \ .$ $\operatorname* { m a x } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \omega ( t ) \}$ . Then G satisfies (E.4) and (E.5) with $h = G , g ( \varepsilon ) =$ $e ^ { \sigma \varepsilon } - 1$ . Furthermore, $\partial G ( \omega ; ( t , T ] ) = \sigma G ( \omega ) 1 _ { \{ \eta ( \omega ) > t \} }$ for $P \mathrm { - a . e . } \ \omega \in \Omega .$ where $\eta ( \omega )$ is as in Example E.3. In the notation of Example E.1, it follow that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ \partial G (W; (t, T ]) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = \sigma E [ \exp (\sigma M _ {T}) 1 _ {\{\eta (W) > t \}} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] \\ \qquad = \sigma E [ \exp (\sigma M _ {t, T}) 1 _ {\{M _ {t, T} > M _ {t} \}} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] \\ \qquad = \sigma E [ \exp (\sigma (M _ {T - t} + a)) 1 _ {\{M _ {T - t} > b - a \}} ] \Big | _ { \begin{array}{c} a = W _ {t} \\ b = M _ {t} \end{array} } \\ \qquad = \frac {2 \sigma e ^ {\sigma a}}{\sqrt {2 \pi (T - t)}} \int_ {b - a} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \frac {m ^ {2}}{2 (T - t)} + \sigma m} d m \Big | _ { \begin{array}{c} a = W _ {t} \\ b = M _ {t} \end{array} } \\ \qquad = 2 \sigma e ^ {\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2} (T - t) + \sigma W _ {t}} \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}} - \sigma \sqrt {T - t}\right) \right]. \end{array}
$$

According to the Clark formula, we have 

$$
d \Lambda_ {t} = 2 \sigma e ^ {\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2} (T - t) + \sigma W _ {t}} \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}} - \sigma \sqrt {T - t}\right) \right] d W _ {t}
$$

for $\Lambda _ { t } \triangleq E [ G | F _ { t } ]$ . This last displayed equation can also be verified directly by first computing 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\Lambda_ {t} = e ^ {\sigma M _ {t}} \left[ 2 \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}}\right) - 1 \right]} \\ & {\qquad + 2 e ^ {\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2} (T - t) + \sigma W _ {t}} \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {M _ {t} - W _ {t}}{\sqrt {T - t}} - \sigma \sqrt {T - t}\right) \right]} \end{array}
$$

and then applying $\mathrm { I t o } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ formula. 

Example E.5: Consider now the Brownian motion $\tilde { W } _ { t } \stackrel { \triangle } { = } W _ { t } + \nu t , 0 \leq$ $t \leq T$ , with drift $\nu \in \mathbb { R }$ , and define $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { M } _ { s , t } \overset { \triangle } { = } \operatorname* { m a x } _ { s \leq u \leq t } \tilde { W } _ { u } , \tilde { M } _ { t } \overset { \triangle } { = } \tilde { M } _ { 0 , t } } \end{array}$ . By analogy with Examples E.3 and E.4, we consider the functionals 

$$
\tilde {F} (\omega) \stackrel {{\triangle}} {{=}} \max _ {0 \leq t \leq T} (\omega (t) + \nu t) \quad \text { and } \quad \tilde {G} (\omega) \stackrel {{\triangle}} {{=}} \exp (\sigma \tilde {F} (\omega)), \quad \forall \omega \in \Omega ,
$$

so that $\tilde { F } ( W ) = \tilde { M } _ { T } , \tilde { G } ( W ) = \exp ( \sigma \tilde { M } _ { T } )$ . According to Girsanov’s the orem, W<sup>˜</sup> is a standard Brownian motion under the measure given by $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { P } ( A ) = E [ \exp ( - \nu W _ { t } - \frac { \nu ^ { 2 } } { 2 } t ) 1 _ { A } ] = E [ \exp ( - \nu \tilde { W } _ { t } + \frac { \nu ^ { 2 } } { 2 } t ) 1 _ { A } ] } \end{array}$ for all $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { t }$ and all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . From the reflection principle for Brownian motion, we have 

$$
\tilde {P} [ \tilde {M} _ {t} \in d b, \tilde {W} _ {t} \in d a ] = \frac {2 (2 b - a)}{\sqrt {2 \pi t ^ {3}}} \exp \left[ - \frac {(2 b - a) ^ {2}}{2 t} \right] d a d b, a \leq b, b \geq 0
$$

(cf. Karatzas and Shreve (1991), Proposition 2.8.1), and then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P [ \tilde {M} _ {t} \in d b, \tilde {W} _ {t} \in d a ] = \exp \left[ \nu a - \frac {\nu^ {2}}{2} t \right] \cdot \tilde {P} [ \tilde {M} _ {t} \in d b, \tilde {W} _ {t} \in d a ] \\ & \qquad = \frac {2 (2 b - a)}{\sqrt {2 \pi t ^ {3}}} e ^ {2 b \nu} \exp \left[ - \frac {(2 b + \nu t - a) ^ {2}}{2 t} \right] d a d b, \end{array}
$$

for $a \leq b , b \geq 0$ . Consequently, 

$$
P [ \tilde {M} _ {t} \in d b ] = 2 e ^ {2 b \nu} \left[ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi t}} e ^ {- \frac {(b + \nu t) ^ {2}}{2 t}} - \nu \left\{1 - \Phi \left(\frac {b + \nu t}{\sqrt {t}}\right) \right\} \right] d b, b \geq 0,
$$

or equivalently, 

$$
P [ \tilde {M} _ {t} > b ] = f (t, b) \triangleq 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {b - \nu t}{\sqrt {t}}\right) + e ^ {2 \nu b} \left[ 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {b + \nu t}{\sqrt {t}}\right) \right], b \geq 0.\tag{E.11}
$$

As in Examples E.3 and E.4, we obtain 

$$
E [ \partial \tilde {F} (W; (t, T ]) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = P [ \tilde {M} _ {T - t} > b ] | _ {b = \tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}} = f (T - t, \tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}),
$$

as well as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E [ \partial \tilde {G} (W; (t, T ]) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = \sigma E \left[ \exp (\sigma (\tilde {M} _ {T - t} + \tilde {a})) 1 _ {\{\tilde {M} _ {T - t} > \tilde {b} - \tilde {a} \}} \right] \Big | _ {\tilde {a} = \tilde {W} _ {t}} \\ & \qquad = \sigma e ^ {\sigma \tilde {W} _ {t}} \int_ {\tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\sigma m} P [ \tilde {M} _ {T - t} \in d m ] \\ & \qquad = \sigma e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} f (T - t, \tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}) \\ & \qquad + \sigma^ {2} e ^ {\sigma \tilde {W} _ {t}} \int_ {\tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}} ^ {\infty} f (T - t, \xi) e ^ {\sigma \xi} d \xi , \\ & E [ \tilde {G} (W) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] = E \left[ e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} 1 _ {\{\tilde {M} _ {t, T} \leq \tilde {M} _ {t} \}} + e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t, T}} 1 _ {\{\tilde {M} _ {t, T} > \tilde {M} _ {t} \}} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] \\ & \qquad = e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} P \left[ \tilde {M} _ {T - t} \leq \tilde {b} - \tilde {a} \right] \Big | _ {\tilde {a} = \tilde {W} _ {t}} \\ & \qquad = e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} P \left[ e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} 1 _ {\{\tilde {M} _ {t, T} > \tilde {W} _ {t} \}} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right]. \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & + E \left[ \exp (\sigma (\tilde {M} _ {T - t} + \tilde {a})) 1 _ {\{\tilde {M} _ {T - t} > \tilde {b} - \tilde {a} \}} \right] \Big | _ {\tilde {a} = \tilde {W} _ {t}} \\ & {= e ^ {\sigma \tilde {M} _ {t}} + \sigma e ^ {\sigma \tilde {W} _ {t}} \int_ {\tilde {M} _ {t} - \tilde {W} _ {t}} ^ {\infty} f (T - t, \xi) e ^ {\sigma \xi} d \xi .} \end{array}
$$

There is also an extended Clark formula (E.13) below, which is described as follows. Consider a smooth Brownian functional, i.e., a function ${ \cal F } : \Omega $ R of the form $F ( \omega ) ~ = ~ f ( \omega ( t _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , \omega ( t _ { n } ) )$ for some $n \_ { \mathrm { ~ \scriptsize ~ \in ~ } }$ $\mathbb { N } , ( t _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n } ) \in [ 0 , T ] ^ { n }$ , and some element f in the space $C _ { b } ^ { \infty } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ of functions with continuous and bounded derivatives of every order. Conditions (E.4)–(E.6) are satisfied by $F$ , with 

$$
\partial F (\omega ; (t, T ]) = D _ {t} F (\omega) \triangleq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {j}} f (\omega (t _ {1}), \dots , \omega (t _ {n})) 1 _ {[ 0, t _ {j})} (t), 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

For every $p \geq 1$ , introduce the norm $\| \cdot \| _ { p , 1 }$ on the space S of smooth Brownian functionals by the formula 

$$
\| F \| _ {p, 1} ^ {p} \triangleq E \left[ | F (W) | ^ {p} + \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} (D _ {t} F (W)) ^ {2} d t\right) ^ {p / 2} \right],\tag{E.12}
$$

and denote by $\mathbf { D } _ { p , 1 }$ the Banach space that is the completion of S unde $\| \cdot \| _ { p , 1 }$ . As shown by Shigekawa (1980), $D F$ is well-defined by continuity on the entirety of $\mathbf { D } _ { p , 1 }$ . We have the following “extended Clark formula.” 

Theorem E.6: (Ocone (1984); Karatzas, Ocone, and Li (1991)): For every $F \in \mathbf { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ the process $\psi$ in $( E . 1 )$ is given as the predictable projection of $D _ { t } F , \ 0 \leq t \leq T$ . Equivalently, for Lebesgue-almost-every $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , we have 

$$
\psi_ {t} = E [ D _ {t} F | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] a. s.\tag{E.13}
$$
